2be6ca455d900b8d: MIAMI: A majestic and all-but-indestructible 20th-century ocean liner that once ferried royal leaders, movie stars and even the "Mona Lisa" to the United States was being deliberately sunk on Wednesday to become the world's largest artificial reef.

Experts were conducting a controlled flooding of the 302-metre vessel, a veteran of more than 800 transatlantic crossings in the 1950s and 60s, which is set to reach its final resting place on the Gulf of Mexico's sandy floor, some 40km south-west of Destin-Fort Walton Beach, Florida.
"Two of the valves have been opened. The deployment process has started," said an official on the livestream operated by the city.

Florida's Okaloosa County, gambling that such a huge new reef would boost local tourism and attract diving and fishing enthusiasts, bought the long-decommissioned SS United States from a conservancy group for US$1 million in 2024.

The vessel — longer than the Titanic and the holder of the transatlantic speed record — will become the centrepiece of Okaloosa's undersea garden of sunken ships, including World War II vessels, tugboats and even a casino boat.

Captain Tim Mullane of Alabama-based maritime company Coleen Marine, which led the repurposing, has described it as "a great honour to put this fine vessel to rest... where it's going to serve a second life" promoting marine fauna, diving and fishing.
A year-long process of cleaning the vessel, removing all toxins such as fuel, paint and wiring, towing, environmental remediation, safety assurances and eventual sinking cost roughly US$13.5 million.
The SS United States, the result of a celebrated feat of mid-century American engineering, made its maiden voyage in 1952.

In its heyday, the luxury liner carried countless celebrities, including president John F. Kennedy, former King Edward VIII, Grace Kelly, Elizabeth Taylor and Salvador Dali. Future president Bill Clinton travelled on board on his way to study at Oxford.
Perhaps its most famous passenger was Leonardo da Vinci's "Mona Lisa", the 16th-century painting that visited America in 1963.
Within two decades of being built, the liner was out of service, falling victim to the growing popularity of air travel. It remained docked in Philadelphia for 29 years.
While the ship will rest at a depth of 180 feet, its top decks will be just about 55 feet below the water's surface, making them accessible to beginner divers.
Until now, the largest artificial reef was an aircraft carrier sunk 20 years ago off the coast of Pensacola, also in Florida.
Repurposing the SS United States keeps its heritage alive, said Okaloosa County tourism director Jennifer Adams Kemp.
"She's our country's flagship," she told CNN shortly before the sinking. "Why wouldn't we want to preserve that?"
4b883b58a47d0560: WASHINGTON: A US military guard was seen loudly reprimanding Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and his group on Veterans Day, after they laughed and chatted near a sacred tomb at Arlington National Cemetery.

"All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times!" a US Army sentinel yelled loudly, after laughter and chatter could be heard.

The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier is a sacred burial ground for American soldiers who were killed during World War I, World War II and the Korean War. It also includes an empty burial site for a Vietnam War soldier, in honour of missing soldiers who died in service to their country.

CNN identified the group taking photos on the steps near the tomb with Hegseth as his wife Jennifer, chief of staff Ricky Buria, deputy chief of staff Patrick Weaver and senior adviser Tami Radabaugh.
Chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell told NBC News that Hegseth and the department "have always honoured" the sacrifices of the military.
"While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum," Parnell said.
Democrats were quick to react to the defence secretary's gaffe on a sacred day for the US military.

"Pete Hegseth continues to demonstrate his utter lack of fitness for his office. One day after narrowly avoiding impeachment, he shows his contempt for our men and women in uniform by disrespecting the sanctity of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier," congresswoman Gwen Moore of Wisconsin posted on X.

9caca5da5cc3c99d: WASHINGTON: President Donald Trump defended the war against Iran on Wednesday at a US Veterans Day commemoration that saw his defence secretary publicly admonished for a lack of decorum.
"The bravery and skill of our amazing American warriors has absolutely been incredible," Trump said in an address at Arlington National Cemetery just outside Washington.
"When this conflict is over, and it will be soon, the entire world will be a much safer and better place, more peaceful place, and a place without the kind of danger that we had to suffer."
The war, which began on Feb 28 with US and Israeli strikes against Iran, has so far cost the lives of 23 US service members and wounded several hundred more, according to the latest Pentagon figures.

Trump said in his remarks that the conflict was started not by Washington but by Teheran, which "has been waging war on America since 1979". He stressed that US forces were acting to halt Iran's capacity to build a nuclear weapon.
Trump, 80, attended a wreath-laying ceremony at the cemetery's Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, a sacred symbol for America's lost service members.
During his speech before troops, veterans and top officials in his administration, Trump namechecked Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, who was in attendance, saying he had "done a fantastic job".

Republicans in the US House of Representatives on Tuesday blocked an effort — launched by an outgoing Republican lawmaker — to impeach Hegseth for allegedly waging war without congressional authorisation and abusing his powers as Pentagon chief.

Hegseth stirred even more controversy at the ceremony: an army sentinel watching over the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier reprimanded a small group of people that included Hegseth, his wife and several aides, when some of them laughed after posing for a picture in front of the sacred site.

"All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times," the sentinel called out, halting his patrol to face the group as they walked up some stairs to leave. Hegseth turned around to look at the guard.
During his remarks, Trump brought up the issue of the 76-metre-tall triumphal arch he hopes to build just outside the cemetery, saying it would be dedicated "soon".

On Tuesday, the family of John F. Kennedy asked a court to prevent its construction, arguing that the massive structure would block views and cast shadows over the gravesites of the slain president and other Kennedy relatives buried at Arlington National Cemetery.
The project also faces lawsuits from a group of veterans, the city of Washington and the state of Virginia.

3237b6c42201e119: MEXICO CITY: Mexico is working to block steel from China and other countries from being rerouted through Mexico into the US under North America's trade pact, a Mexican official said on Wednesday, as the country presses Washington for relief from steel, aluminium and auto tariffs.

Luis Rosendo Gutierrez, Mexico's deputy economy minister for foreign trade, told journalists that the government had tightened traceability measures and was ensuring that products were not reaching the United States by exploiting Mexico's trade preferences.
Steel has become a politically sensitive issue in US-Mexico trade, with Washington determined to block Chinese goods and inputs from entering the US market through third countries.
"We want to guarantee — and we are guaranteeing — that there is no triangulation of steel or other products that reach the United States taking advantage of our trade agreement," Gutierrez said.

Gutierrez said Mexico had removed around 1,100 steel mills from its approved registry, many of them in Asia, after finding that they did not actually exist. The move helped cut steel imports from Vietnam by 80 per cent in recent months.

He added that Mexico had reduced steel and aluminium imports from third countries, including China, South Korea and India, by about 30 per cent, equivalent to some 13 billion pesos (US$698.54 million) in imports.
Mexico's priority, Gutierrez said, was to reduce the impact of US Section 232 tariffs on autos, steel and aluminium rather than focus on a broader review of the US-Mexico-Canada trade pact.
About 80 per cent of Mexican exports to the United States already enter tariff-free, he added.
Gutierrez said US officials had welcomed proposals from Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard, and that Mexico hoped for positive news in the coming weeks before year-end.
Analysts argue that Mexico is not a hub for steel "transshipment", in which goods are routed through another country before reaching their final destination, typically to avoid tariffs.

Still, a report last month by Washington-based think tank the Center for Strategic and International Studies said certain goods may undergo significant processing in Mexico before being exported to the US, rather than simply passing through the country.

KUALA LUMPUR: Healthy ageing must not become a privilege reserved only for those who can afford it.
Sultan of Perak Sultan Nazrin Muizzuddin Shah said that while longer and healthier lives were among modern civilisation's greatest achievements, access to their benefits should not depend on wealth.
"A society is ultimately judged by whether the opportunities it creates remain within the reach of its most vulnerable citizens.
"Healthy ageing must be inclusive by design. The environments, services and technologies we develop should widen access rather than deepen existing inequalities.
"This is more than good social policy. It is a moral obligation and a mark of respect for our elders.
"The ability to age with health, dignity and purpose should never be determined by wealth," he said in his opening address, titled "The Silver Economy: A Foundation for Shared Prosperity".
He delivered the address at the High-Level Forum on the Silver Economy 2026, themed "Healthy Longevity for Economic Growth".
At the event, Sultan Nazrin was presented with the Baroness Sally Greengross Award for Healthy Longevity Innovation by Global Coalition on Ageing chief executive officer Michael Hodin.

Sultan Nazrin said the Kuala Lumpur Declaration on Ageing: Empowering Older Persons in Asean, adopted by the bloc's leaders in 2015, recognised the need for equitable access to healthcare, public services, preventive measures and support throughout life.
He said the foundations of healthy ageing did not begin at 60, but were laid through choices made decades earlier.
"If we delay intervention until frailty has taken root, our options narrow drastically.
"We must therefore design environments that do not merely accommodate declining capabilities but help preserve them."
He added that healthy ageing required the right infrastructure, not simply the right services.
"We can no longer treat housing, healthcare, financial security and technology as separate areas of policy. They are interconnected corridors in the same lived environment."
Citing an Asean study, Sultan Nazrin said demand for aged-care services in the region was projected to more than double over the next two decades.
"Any serious discussion on longevity must address the economics, as pressures on public finances and families are real.

"The Malaysia Care Strategic Framework and Action Plan cites research suggesting that every ringgit invested in care can generate up to RM7 in economic benefits through increased economic activity, employment and income."

KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysian food exporters have generated RM420.35 million in sales at the Salon International de l'Alimentation Paris 2026 — the world's largest biennial international food industry trade show.
The Malaysia External Trade Development Corporation (Matrade) said 43 Malaysian companies participated in the event, which was held from Oct 17 to 21 at Paris Nord Villepinte in France.
The Malaysian exhibitors came from eight states, with Selangor contributing the largest contingent of 23 companies.
"This was followed by Johor (five), Kuala Lumpur (four), Kedah (three), Perak (three), Sarawak (three), Penang (one) and Terengganu (one)," Matrade said.

It added that the results reflected growing interest among European importers, distributors, retailers and food service operators in Malaysian suppliers, particularly those offering private-label products, original equipment manufacturing and food ingredient solutions.
It noted that the products showcased at the Malaysia Pavilion included processed food, convenient meal solutions, beverages, snacks and plant-based innovations.

Matrade deputy chief executive officer (Export Acceleration) S. Jai Shankar said the Malaysian companies had demonstrated their readiness to compete not only as consumer brands, but also as reliable partners in Europe's food supply chain.
"European buyers are looking for suppliers who can guarantee consistent quality, traceability and reliable capacity, and our companies demonstrated that they can meet these expectations.
"Matrade's priority now is to help them convert these leads into long-term supply contracts."

Matrade said Malaysia's internationally recognised halal certification framework, administered by the Department of Islamic Development Malaysia, had further strengthened confidence in the integrity and traceability of Malaysian food products.

It added that demand trends in France, particularly for authentic Asian flavours, ready-to-eat and ready-to-heat meals, plant-based alternatives and diverse culinary ingredients, presented opportunities for Malaysian manufacturers.

As one of the European Union's largest consumer markets, France offers established retail networks, food service channels and distribution infrastructure that could serve as a gateway for Malaysian companies to expand.

ISLAMABAD: Former prime minister Imran Khan was taken to a hospital in Islamabad for treatment on Tuesday before being returned to prison, sources said.
Khan, who is being held at Adiala Jail in Rawalpindi, underwent an eye examination at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences, an official said.
"He had some blood pressure problems and received the necessary treatment last night. He has been moved back to his prison cell," the official said.
The cricketer-turned-politician has faced multiple corruption cases since his government was ousted in a no-confidence vote in 2022. He has been in prison since August 2023.
All but one of Khan's convictions have been suspended or overturned, with appeals pending. He ​denies wrongdoing and says the charges are politically motivated, a claim the government denies.
Khan's lawyers say the 74-year-old's health has deteriorated in prison and that he has suffered significant vision loss in his right eye.
It was the first known time Khan had been taken to hospital and returned to jail since August, when a previous hospital visit was cut short.
His party also said a court had ordered prison authorities to allow Khan's legal team and his wife to meet him.
Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf deputy chairman Shah Mahmood Qureshi was also taken from prison to a hospital in Lahore on Tuesday. He remains in hospital.

53eb9391a0681516: WARSAW: Tens of thousands of Polish nationalist sympathisers gathered in Warsaw Wednesday for an annual Independence Day March, just days after a deadly shooting spree in Krakow that shook the country.
The event is held each Nov 11 to commemorate the ending in 1918 of 123 years of partition by Russia, Prussia and Austria.
The march began with the national anthem, which rang out as participants lit flares that blanketed the demonstration in thick smoke.
"There are surely over half a million Poles," Rafal Buca, a spokesperson for the event's organisers, told AFP when asked about the number of participants.
City authorities said as many as 250,000 people took part.
Conservative-nationalist president Karol Nawrocki -- who in the past has participated in the demonstration both in his current role and as a private citizen -- was among those marching.
The event is a magnet for all shades of Poland's right wing -- from conservative-nationalists aligned with its Law and Justice (PiS) party to far-right and radical groups.
Xenophobic slogans, including "Make Europe white again", could be seen on posters carried by demonstrators.
Others read "Poland is not for sale" or likened the country's pro-European Prime Minister Donald Tusk to a "dictator".
"This march is a protest against those who govern us," Jedrzej Kozak, a 28 year-old IT specialist from the northern city of Torun told AFP.
Justyna Plaszczyk, 42, came to the march to "show her solidarity with the Polish nation".
Asked about her opinion on her country's place in the EU, she told AFP: "It goes without saying we must leave the European Union because Poland should be a sovereign state."
Anti-Ukrainian slogans were also present, with nationalist and far-right circles opposing the "Ukrainisation of Poland".
Nevertheless, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote in a post on X: "We are glad that Poland is European, strong, and free".
"We in Ukraine are grateful to Poland for its support – for Ukraine's independence, our state, our defence, our people, and our aspiration to be a European, strong, and free country too."
While generally peaceful, some past marches have been marred by clashes with police or counter-demonstrators.
But Mayor Rafal Trzaskowski assured Wednesday afternoon that "for the moment, we have not observed any serious troubles, apart from the use of smoke flares".
Warsaw was on high alert after deadly shootings in the second city of Krakow, which shocked the country of 38 million.

A 24-year-old man opened fire with a semi-automatic rifle in a packed market square on Saturday, killing six people and wounding 15 others before he was fatally wounded by police. The bodies of his parents and a sister were found at the family home.
On Tuesday, Justice Minister Waldemar Zurek said the killer had been interested in neo-Nazi Anders Behring Breivik, who killed 77 people in Norway in 2011.

Wednesday's march also took place amid a political battle pitting Prime Minister Donald Tusk's centrist government against the nationalist right over the country's highest court -- the Constitutional Tribunal.
The court's legitimacy has been disputed for years because of controversial appointments made under previous right-wing governments.
The governing coalition says it wants to correct "political" reforms and appointments made by the far right, which it deems contrary to democratic standards.
But nationalists have accused Tusk of undermining constitutional order and right-wing protesters have been camping outside the tribunal for several weeks.
Last week, riot police moved onto the tribunal site to block access, and a judge appointed by the ruling majority announced she was assuming the court presidency role on an interim basis.
She suspended the sitting president, who is close to Nawrocki.
The authorities feared political tensions could spill over and that some demonstrators may try to storm the Constitutional Tribunal.
In addition to the march, masses, a military parade, and concerts took place in Warsaw, organised by the state authorities or by the centrist city hall of the capital.
1f6e4782d49c5df0: PRAGUE: Spain coach Luis de la Fuente said Wednesday he is optimistic Barcelona winger Lamine Yamal will be fit to face England in the Nations League at the weekend.
The 19-year-old winger will miss the world champions' visit to face the Czech Republic in Prague on Thursday with a knee problem and is set to join up with Spain after that game.
Yamal played for Barcelona in the 2-1 La Liga win over Atletico Madrid on Sunday and on Monday Spain said he would not travel to face the Czechs.

"He got hurt in the last match, he had some discomfort in one knee, he went for the usual treatment, a scan in Barcelona, and they saw he had inflammation and fluid in the knee - that meant he needed rest," De la Fuente told reporters.
"Our medical staff and his medical staff have a fantastic relationship, and I decided that his trip here should be avoided without knowing whether he'd be in any condition to play."
The coach said he had spoken to the winger and his recovery was looking positive ahead of England's visit to Madrid on Sunday.
"He's doing a series of exercises with his physio and with the club that indicate the recovery is going well," continued De la Fuente.
"We believe, I'm optimistic, that on Friday he'll be with us."
De la Fuente dismissed the idea that Yamal, who came third in the Ballon d'Or voting in October, has any special privileges compared to his La Roja teammates.
"He has no privileges, and his teammates are relaxed about it, because we treat everyone the same," added the coach.
"In similar situations we would have done exactly the same for any other player, and the players know that."
Unstoppable run

a64e2b4f2753c0b8: WASHINGTON: Stacy Keach, the prolific and acclaimed American tough-guy actor who thrived in theatre, film and television, and whose roles ranged from Hamlet to detective Mike Hammer, has died, his wife said Wednesday. He was 85.

Malgosia Tomassi confirmed the news in a statement to Hollywood publication "Variety," saying her husband died Tuesday "after a long and difficult battle with a serious heart condition and heart failure."

The versatile and prolific Keach was a force of nature when he burst onto Broadway in the mid-1960s, winning praise as one of America's greatest Shakespearean actors and earning a Tony Award nomination for his role in "Indians."
His silver screen debut in "The Heart is a Lonely Hunter" kicked off a six-decade career that spanned more than 100 movies.

In "Fat City," the unsentimental 1972 film directed by John Huston and co-starring Jeff Bridges, Keach earned critical praise for his gritty portrayal of a washed up boxer, and it established him as one of Hollywood's most serious actors.
He also delivered top-tier performances as Doc Holliday in "Doc" from 1971, "The New Centurions" and "The Long Riders."

Keach was widely celebrated for his role as the seen-it-all private eye in the hit TV series "The New Mike Hammer," based on the gruff noir detective in the pulp novels of Mickey Spillane, whom Keach revered and eventually befriended.

Keach -- who claimed in his autobiography "All in All" that he shared the same drug dealer as John Belushi -- nearly saw his career derailed when he was arrested in 1984 at London's Heathrow airport trying to smuggle cocaine in a shaving cream can.
"Busted, like some common perp on 'Mike Hammer.' I knew how stupid I had been," he wrote. Keach pleaded guilty, and served six months in jail at England's Reading Prison.

He bounced back with a Golden-Globe-winning portrayal of writer Ernest Hemingway in the 1988 television miniseries "Hemingway," and he drew new fans in the 2010s by playing New York's archbishop in the long-running CBS drama "Blue Bloods," and with a recurring voice role on iconic series "The Simpsons."

fa483c45db8466fb: <!--kg-card-end: html--> Scientists have discovered a bizarre “invisible” object in space that challenges our understanding of stellar evolution and could help resolve longstanding astronomical mysteries, according to a study published on Wednesday in Science Advances. Its orbit and mass are so strange, in fact, that researchers ran thousands of simulations and couldn’t reproduce them.

The hidden object is likely an ultra-rare supermassive neutron star, which is the collapsed core that is left over after a massive star goes supernova. Located in a system called J0008+0128,, the object was detected through its gravitational effects on its companion, a red giant star.

Massive stars that go supernova either collapse into neutron stars or black holes, both of which belong to a wider family of dead stars known as “stellar remnants.” But for decades, astronomers have puzzled over the so-called “mass gap" between neutron stars and black holes, which is the observed scarcity of remnants between 2.5 and five times as massive as the Sun.

The object lurking in J0008+0128 could be up to 2.8 times as massive as the Sun, which “potentially places the unseen companion within the mass gap between neutron stars and black holes,” according to the new study. The colossal mass, combined with its unusually wide orbit of 1,218 days, challenge our understanding of how these objects form.

“We search for compact objects (mainly neutron stars and black holes) using large spectroscopic surveys,” said Song Wang, an associate researcher at the National Astronomical Observatories, Chinese Academy of Sciences, who co-authored the study, in an email to 404 Media. “We have found more than 10 neutron stars, and J0008+0128 is the most massive one among them.”

Generally speaking, stars that are over 25 times as massive as the Sun will form black holes, while stars that are about 10-to-25 times as massive will become neutron stars. Stars with masses similar to the Sun, meanwhile, are destined to spend their afterlives as white dwarfs, which are much larger and less dense than neutron stars. For instance, neutron stars are mere miles in diameter, whereas white dwarfs are about the size of Earth.

Because they are dense pressure cookers, neutron stars are filled with disassembled components of atoms, especially neutrons—hence the name—but also protons and electrons. Supermassive neutron stars like the one in J0008+0128 can shed light on the poorly understood “equation of state” in these objects, which is the relationship between their immense pressures and densities.

“The equation of state of neutron stars is a long-standing unsolved problem in astrophysics, and neutron star masses can provide crucial observational tests,” said Wang. “This is particularly true for massive neutron stars: how massive a neutron star can become depends on how ‘stiff’ its internal matter is in resisting gravitational collapse.”

“The discovery and measurement of supermassive neutron stars (i.e., those above two solar masses) can place important constraints on the equation of state of matter at extreme densities, helping to identify the theories that truly describe the behavior of matter under such extreme conditions,” he added.

In other words, J0008+0128 could open a window into the churning atomic stew within these exotic objects. But the system is weird for reasons beyond the supermassive object lurking in the dark. Indeed, the team ran thousands of simulations but none of them “reproduced physical and orbital properties similar to J0008+0128,” according to the study.

The wide orbit between the neutron star and the red giant star is particularly difficult to explain. Neutron stars could become supermassive by gravitationally tugging material off of their stellar companions, but this object is too far away from the red giant for this mechanism to make sense.

“In fact, many compact objects discovered in recent years cannot be explained by standard binary evolution models and supernova mechanisms,” Wang noted, citing two other examples, known as Gaia BH2 and G3425.

Wang and his colleagues proposed a few alternate scenarios to account for these outliers. It may simply be that supernovas can form supermassive neutron stars within the mass gap in rare cases. The researchers also speculated that this system once contained three objects, and that two of them merged together to form the supermassive neutron star.

“There may be two massive stars forming an inner binary,” Wang explained. “They can merge at different stages. For example, a neutron star merges with a normal star, or two neutron stars merge. Either case could produce the supermassive neutron star that we observe today.”
“In addition, if J0008+0128 formed through single-star evolution, its discovery would suggest that supernovae can produce massive neutron stars,” he added.

Studying systems like J0008+0128 could illuminate the murky limits that determine the afterlives of massive stars. They are also helpful for understanding the dynamics of neutron star mergers, which scientists can detect through gravitational waves, which are ripples in spacetime.

Wang and his colleagues were able to make this new discovery with the help of sophisticated sky surveys, including astrometric data from Europe’s Gaia space telescope. The team hopes that the forthcoming data release from Gaia, due out next month, will help to narrow down the possible mass of the unseen object in J0008+0128.

“The discovery of J0008+0128, together with other systems discovered in these years (e.g., Gaia BH2 and G3425), suggests that much work remains to be done on binary evolution and supernova explosion theory,” Wang concluded.

36fe20458ab3346e: The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world’s most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.

Operating since September 2022, the Russia-based ransomware group Qilin is the currently the most industrious ransomware-as-a-service gang, according to a report (PDF) this month by the cybersecurity firm NCC Group (KrebsOnSecurity profiled the administrator of the second most active ransomware group — The Gentlemen — in June).
The Qilin ransomware administrator “Haise” advertising his affiliate program on the cybercrime forum RAMP. Image: Ke-la.com.

Qilin attracts affiliates to hack into companies and deploy ransomware by offering them at least 80 percent of any extortion amount paid by victims. Its members practice the “double extortion” model, stealing sensitive data before encrypting systems and threatening to publish the files online. Unlike most ransomware partnerships based out of Russia, Qilin is happy to team with English-speaking affiliates, and its leader has shared on Telegram that they’ve worked with ransomware groups like Scattered Spider and RansomHub.

The head of Qilin goes by the handle “Haise,” but they weren’t always known by this nickname. It is not uncommon for cybercriminals to change their handle periodically as an operational security (opsec) measure. Doing so is generally a smart move, because it helps to sever one’s ties to older identities that may not have been as careful on basic opsec, such as separating their real life identity from their cybercrime activities. But even those cautious criminals will sometimes have to reference their past monikers when applying for membership at a new forum. And forums eventually get hacked or seized. That is precisely what happened with Haise.

The cyber intelligence platform Intel 471 records that in June 2022, Haise applied for membership to RAMP, a closely-guarded Russian cybercrime forum that was created as a haven for ransomware affiliate programs. Intel 471 has indexed direct messages from RAMP (the forum was seized by the FBI in January 2026), and those missives show the RAMP administrator approved Haise’s application, referring to this user as Haise and by their Telegram username: Alexbigboss44.

Searching Intel 471 for Alexbigboss44 reveals this was the Telegram account name shared by the user Rjun on the Russian cybercrime forums Exploit and XSS two years earlier in 2020. The cyber intelligence platform Flashpoint finds Alexbigboss44 is a prolific participant in cybercriminal forums and Telegram channels, primarily focused on the illicit trade of traffic, logs, and corporate access [full disclosure: Flashpoint is an advertiser on this blog].
The Qilin administrator once used the nickname “Rjun” on several forums, and shared their Telegram handle as “Alexbigboss44.” Image: Ke-la.com.

Flashpoint says this user was engaged in high-volume acquisition of Facebook logs and Google Ads accounts to facilitate fraudulent advertising and gambling schemes, and that they functioned as a broker and operator — managing a network of traffickers and purchasing compromised data to fuel their operations.

The link between the Qilin administrator Haise and the much older Rjun and Alexbigboss44 accounts was shared privately earlier this month by IntelHawk, which describes itself as an AI-based platform capable of de-anonymizing threat actors based on historical usernames, stylometry and other signals.

IntelHawk founder and chief technology officer Leo Bogod said an analysis of these identities shows a progression from novice arbitrageur and credit card fraudster in 2018–2019 to a more experienced participant and organizer of complex cybercrime-related activities in 2020–2023, with increasing attention to malware, botnets, and payment infrastructure.

Where does this connection between these threat actor identities lead? Intel 471 finds that by the time Alexbigboss44 was applying for membership to RAMP, Rjun was already a longtime member of several other Russian crime forums, including Darkmarket, Verified, and Zloy. Intel 471 says Rjun signed up at all of these sites with the email address mail-30a@mail.ru.

The identity threat protection firm Spycloud found the email address mail-30a@mail.ru at one time used the password “Rjun132” [Spycloud is also an advertiser on this blog]. A search for that email at the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence shows that it appeared in records maintained by gosuslugi.ru, the official digital platform for state and municipal services in the Russian Federation.

Gosuslugi was breached in late 2025, reportedly exposing more than 20 million records with full names, birth dates, and mobile numbers. According to the leaked Gosuslugi records (via Constella), the address mail-30a@mail.ru belongs to 36-year-old Aleksey Mikhailovich Yakovtsev from St. Petersburg, Russia.

Flashpoint finds Haise has long used a Telegram account with the user ID 118329521, recording more than 5,000 messages from this user since 2018. Records from Russia’s education watchdog Rosobrnadzor reveal that Mr. Yakovtsev went to grade school in Murmansk and that he holds a master’s degree in computing and information systems.

A search on this Telegram ID in Constella shows it is linked to the Russian phone number +79602347275. Pivoting on that phone number in Constella reveals it is connected to the email addresses aleksey1990yakov@mail.ru and rjun123321@mail.ru. IntelHawk finds that +79602347275 belongs to Yakovtsev’s biological sister, and that Aleksey often used his sister’s email address when registering at different websites.

That phone number appears on several airline flight records at Russian travel agencies that have experienced a data breach in recent years, and those records show Aleksey Yakovtsev, born August 18, 1990, flew between St. Petersburg and Murmansk at least three times between 2013 and 2014.

More recent flight records show that while Mr. Yakovtsev has not traveled by plane outside of Russia, he does fly frequently between Saint Petersburg and Sochi. Often called the “Russian Riviera,” Sochi is Russia’s largest resort city, situated along the coast of the Black Sea and about 1,200 miles south of Saint Petersburg by plane.
Attempts to reach Mr. Yakovtsev via email and phone were unsuccessful.

Further reading: Gang Exposed, an anonymous Twitter/X account that has a history of successfully deanonymizing suspected ransomware actors, reached similar conclusions about Haise’s real-life identity, crediting IntelHawk’s platform for helping to connect the dots.
The Qilin ransomware admin Haise’s now-deleted Telegram account, advertising the affiliate program in July 2024. Image: justpaste.it/iosba.
bbb1fb8ef5e681ba: The Trump administration’s fight to stop suspected leaks of top-secret military information on LinkedIn can’t sweep in “a vast number of confidential sources” of random journalists “who have no conceivable relationship” to the Department of Justice’s investigation, an appeals court ruled Tuesday.

The order came after the DOJ asked LinkedIn to turn over 18 months of communications from targeted journalists who collectively published more than 1,000 articles on many different topics over that time period. The request was not limited to journalists involved in a controversial report from a news outlet that Trump said exposed confidential military information in a foreign country. (The outlet is not being named to protect national security secrets.) Instead, the DOJ cast a wide net, requesting extensive LinkedIn data on journalists who had any possible link to the journalists around the time the report was drafted.

The majority of journalists have LinkedIn accounts and publish their contact information to encourage sources to connect on the platform, LinkedIn argued. So allowing that government overreach went beyond harming targeted journalists and threatened to undermine a critical platform where journalists frequently connect with confidential sources, judges ruled. Even more concerning, the Trump administration secured a secrecy order barring LinkedIn from telling anyone about the sweeping request for a year. That left journalists unaware for far too long that their First Amendment rights had been compromised, judges ruled.
34b737938b531fa1: Datacenter power consumption in the US is growing roughly ten times faster than grid capacity, meaning facilities may soon need to find a large chunk of their own electricity from other sources.

Surging demand for AI infrastructure is driving a wave of new server farms across America, but it is exposing long-term underinvestment in the grid networks required to deliver power where it's needed.
Insurance broker Howden calculates that datacenters would need to source up to 58 percent of their power off the grid by 2030 just to keep their share of grid capacity from growing.
Gartner warned in June that the energy consumed by AI datacenters is on track to grow 26 percent this year, and grid supply may be unable to keep pace with demand by the end of this decade.

Howden's analysis of data from the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) and S&P Global found that since the year 2000, power being fed to data campuses has risen 19 percent a year on average, while the electricity grid expanded capacity by just 2 percent per annum over the same period.
Datacenters' share of US grid capacity was circa five percent in 2025, up from 0.1 percent in 2000 – a 50-fold increase.

Management consultancy Bain & Company issued a report two years ago warning that energy companies must switch gear and invest in building out grid capacity faster, as energy draw by server farms is expected to more than double by 2030.

This doesn't mean that datacenters are in danger of eating all of America's electricity, at least not in the immediate future. The graph makes it appear that the two lines are about to cross, but the chart uses different scales: 1,400 gigawatts on the left axis for grid capacity, versus just 80 on the right for datacenters.

Keeping datacenters at five percent of grid capacity requires 110 gigawatts of behind-the-meter capacity by 2030, Howden estimates – an expansion it considers unlikely. Instead, it expects a combination of greater reliance on the grid, slower development at power-constrained sites, and alternative supplies.
For the largest, most power-constrained projects, Howden warns that grid delays of two to six years could mean $800 million to $2.4 billion in forgone revenue.
"Power availability is becoming one of the defining challenges of the datacenter boom," says Howden head of Natural Resources Stuart Adam.
"As demand for AI infrastructure accelerates, developers are increasingly looking beyond traditional grid connections to secure the electricity they need."

Howden's business is insurance, and so Adam also notes that on-site generation introduces new operational and financial exposures, as operators take greater responsibility for their power infrastructure. ®

350f41e59919203e: The results of the US midterms on November 3 delivered a resounding victory for the Democrats, and a major loss for US president Donald Trump and the Republican party. Gaining control of the Senate and the House of Representatives has emboldened the Democrats, giving them a renewed sense of political legitimacy and a mandate to pursue their agenda. But will this shift translate into meaningful changes in US climate change policy? The Democratic sweep will change the political dynamics around US climate policy and how the country cooperates with the international community on this issue. Although there was no official US presence at the 2025 Cop conference, held in Brazil, a coalition of 100 local US leaders, including governors, mayors and other top city and state officials, attended as part of the US Climate Alliance. Former US vice-president Al Gore, and former US secretary of state John Kerry are part of an unofficial US group at the 2026 gathering. Kerry said in a speech there: “Americans are committed to taking back their future, and we will build and rebuild our partnerships as we do that.” Being on the ground at Cop is important. As the US has a decisive role to play in global climate policy, sending a non-official coalition signals that many Americans are still working to combat climate change. Trump has repeatedly stated that climate change is a hoax and refused to attend the Cop31 climate talks being held in Turkey. But 20 Democratic members of Congress will be attending, although they have been denied official state department funding for the trip. During the first and second Trump administrations, the US has been an outlier among wealthy countries when it comes to fighting climate change. Trump has actively backed the use of fossil fuels, undermining clean energy projects, and rolled back legislation that stipulated emission standards for vehicles. Trump also weakened greenhouse gas reporting requirements and methane regulation. Then in February 2026, the Trump administration rescinded the Environmental Protection Agency’s 2009 finding that greenhouse gases threaten the health and welfare of the public, which had regulated the emissions from new cars and other vehicles. This had provided the legal foundation for regulation under the Clean Air Act. On the international front, Trump was equally determined to undermine global efforts to fight climate change. Famously, he withdrew from the Paris agreement, part of a global initiative to address climate change, and refused to attend Cop summits. But the Democrats’ seismic midterm win may be a sign of optimism for those fighting to address climate change. World leaders arrive at Cop31, but what will be the role of the unofficial US delegation? Data centres are big issue The biggest issues of the midterms were affordability, corruption and the Iran war, but issues related to fighting climate change were also on voters’ list. There is growing concern about data centres. As many as 56% of US voters felt that data centres and AI were either a major or even crucial factor in influencing who they voted for, with only 13% saying it was not a factor at all. Data centres require millions of gallons of water for cooling systems, and this is expected to rise to 73 billion litres of water a year by 2028. Over half of planned AI facilities in the US will be situated in areas that have significant water shortages or drought conditions. After the midterms, Zoe Lofgren, a Democrat, is likely to become the chair of the House of Representatives’ committee on science, space and technology once the new session starts in January. She wants to tackle the administration’s “climate denialism”. Lofgren’s leadership, along with new Democratic members of the committee, may offer it more power to reverse some of the Trump administration’s changes to science policy. However, the Democrat midterm wins will not mean that the US is automatically back at the negotiating table at Cop nor that the US will be able to rejoin the Paris Accords while Trump is president. Trump still has the power to make these decisions and can continue to keep the US out of international climate initiatives, regardless of who controls Congress. The US Constitution says nothing about withdrawing from treaties, which creates uncertainty for what the Senate’s role might be. The election, however, does signal that there is considerable domestic opposition to his approach. And while Congress has not passed follow-up legislation prohibiting presidential withdrawal from the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), it has continued to fund several UNFCCC initiatives. During the Biden administration, the US significantly increased climate finance from US$1.5 billion (£1.1 billion) a year in 2021 to US$9.5 billion in 2023. Democrats could also push back on Trump’s current policies, using their power to hold hearings, investigate the administration’s dismantling of climate programmes and challenge cuts to scientific research. The Democrats can also use the power of Congress’s control of spending to protect or restore funding to some of these environmental initiatives. They could also try to introduce legislation that reinstates some of the clean energy initiatives that had been implemented in past administrations to strengthen emissions standards and support clean energy. The big issue, however, is that Trump has made it clear that he is going to be very active in using his veto power, and without a two-thirds majority in Congress, the Democrats will not be able to override this. What does this mean globally? What this all means is that the world cannot expect the US to be a reliable and constructive partner at Cop with Trump still in power. Trump will probably continue to forge ahead with expanding fossil fuel production, while weakening international climate cooperation, even if the electorate disapproves of these policies. Ironically, Trump’s greatest contribution to the fight against climate change was his initiation of the war with Iran, which helped to cut global fossil fuel carbon dioxide emissions by 0.4% due the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. But climate scientists note this is not a long-term solution. While the Democrats’ electoral victory offers a glimmer of hope for renewed climate action, both domestically and internationally, restoring US climate leadership will take time, especially while Trump remains in power. Natasha Lindstaedt does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

44cfb07dc808a31b: ANTALYA: With conflicts and defence spending surging worldwide, several leaders and environmental groups on Wednesday urged heads of state at the UN climate summit to redirect funds from wars to saving the planet.
"We are told there is no money, but the spending on war grows," said Marshall Islands President Hilda Heine, whose country is among the most vulnerable to rising sea levels.
"The greatest security threat we face remains underfunded. I appeal to you: find money for life, not death," she told the COP31 conference in Turkiye.
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who has presided over a sharp drop in deforestation in the Amazon rainforest, said climate change had "disappeared" from the global agenda.
"We've turned to talking more about arms and tariffs than the survival of future generations," he said.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan echoed the warning.
"Nature – no less than people – is also paying a heavy price for armed conflicts. The starkest example of this is Gaza," he told the summit in the Mediterranean city of Antalya.

With wars in Ukraine, the Middle East and elsewhere and geopolitical volatility spurring widespread rearmament, global defence spending hit nearly US$3 trillion in 2025, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiga summed up the environmental impact of his country's war, from "poisoned soil" to deforestation and birds building nests from drones' fibre-optic cables.
"For most countries here, the energy transition is a matter of policy. For Ukraine it's a matter of survival," he said.
"Russia is at war with our people and with our land, our water, our air."
Climate campaigner Tasneem Essop said discussion of soaring defence spending was lacking at the annual talks.
"Rich nations come here to say, we don't have public finance. And yet they have the public finance to spend so much on wars," Essop, head of the Climate Action Network, told AFP.
Host country Turkiye plans to increase military spending by 229 per cent in 2027, as it and fellow Nato members bolster their defence budgets.
Turkiye's COP31 president, Murat Kurum, had nevertheless said in September: "Every cent allocated to defence should also be allocated to preserving life on this planet."

bfe3427d01364c99: NEW DELHI: India's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party has accused opposition leader Sonia Gandhi of whitewashing historical wrongs by her Congress party in a memoir, sparking a new faceoff between the two sides ahead of key state elections.
Congress party leaders have in turn accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi's BJP of trying to create a spectacle and give the book a "political spin."

Titled "Belonging" and released on Tuesday, the memoir captures Italian-born Gandhi's journey from her student days in England, where she met her husband and Nehru-Gandhi dynasty scion Rajiv, to her integration into India's most powerful political family that gave the country three prime ministers.

Gandhi, 79, herself turned down the prime minister's job in 2004, but her family continues to control the party that has ruled India for periods totalling nearly 55 years since independence from British colonial rule in 1947.

"Sonia Gandhi could have titled her memoir 'Whitewashing', instead of 'Belonging' because the motive of this book appears to be sugar-coating the historical wrongs perpetrated by the Nehru-Gandhi family, and camouflaging the cardinal sins committed by the Congress party," BJP spokesperson C.R. Kesavan said in a video statement.
Kesavan cited the anti-Sikh riots of 1984 which erupted after then-prime minister and Sonia's mother-in-law Indira Gandhi was assassinated by Sikh bodyguards. Nearly 3,000 people were killed.
Rights activists accuse Congress of turning a blind eye and say that some party leaders helped orchestrate the carnage.
In the book, Sonia describes the riots as a "tragic and shameful chapter", accusing some officials of looking the other way or even fuelling the violence.
She defends husband Rajiv — who succeeded his mother as prime minister — against allegations of complicity, while acknowledging failures of governance and delayed justice.
Kesavan accused Sonia of trying to "normalise and justify" the notorious Emergency imposed by Indira.
The 21-month state of Emergency in 1975 involved suspending civil liberties, censoring the press and jailing opposition leaders in one of the most controversial periods of India's history.
Sonia writes that Indira felt increasingly isolated and politically cornered before imposing the Emergency.
She says Indira was never entirely comfortable with it but felt compelled to continue it amid the prevailing political turmoil.
Although Sonia has herself not responded to the accusations, she said in the book's prologue that it is a "personal memoir, one for which politics is the background, a kind of framework."
A Congress spokesperson did not respond to a Reuters request seeking Sonia's comment.
The release comes at a time when Congress is leading the charge against Modi's government over a controversial revision of voter lists, with Sonia's son Rahul at the helm.

The street protests have emerged as the worst political crisis for Modi since he came to power in 2014, and ahead of elections in the key states of Uttar Pradesh and Sikh-majority Punjab early next year.
The book has dominated social media conversations with posts praising and criticising it in equal measure, mirroring the country's political divide.
The book has also been covered extensively by newspapers, with many publishing excerpts about major events over the last half a century.

HarperCollins India, which agreed to publish the book after discussions failed between Sonia's team and Penguin Random House India, did not respond to a request from Reuters seeking comment on how the book had been received.
On Wednesday, the book — considered expensive at 1,299 rupees (US$14) — topped Amazon India's bestseller list.

5fbec81ac7cecc8c: The image of the red ring around the black hole M87, produced by the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) array, made front-page news around the world in 2019. There was one problem: there was a slim chance the depiction might be wrong.
This week, a small team of four Australian researchers have published their work confirming the result based on a new machine learning algorithm using the same base data.

The 2019 Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) image came from hundreds of scientists working together to capture the first direct view of a black hole's shadow. The measurements were taken at eight telescopes around the world, at locations including Chile, the US, and Antarctica.

Reconstructing the image from the data so geographically distant meant instrument and environment errors could influence the accuracy of the resulting image. Potentially, alternative analyses of the data could have reconstructed an image without the iconic ring shape.

Samuel Lai – a postdoctoral fellow at the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO) in Western Australia – and his team created an independent imaging algorithm to process the historic dataset to validate the result. The new approach used closed triplets (using three telescopes for error correction) rather than station pairs in an effort to reduce error.
To the relief of the EHT team, the new image recreated the iconic ring-like image seen in the original, according to a paper published in Nature today.
In a prepared statement, Lai said taking pictures of black holes was not easy. "It is like standing in your backyard and trying to take a photo of a doughnut on the Moon," he said.

He explained that when his team applied new advanced machine learning and artificial intelligence techniques to the original Event Horizon Telescope dataset, they found a black hole almost identical in size and shape to the historic EHT image.

"Importantly, our model had no idea what a black hole looked like when we applied it to the M87 data. This is the first truly independent validation of the EHT image, an important step in the scientific process," he said.

Event Horizon Telescope director Laurent Loinard welcomed the new study. "It is extremely gratifying to see that an elegant, entirely independent method recovers the ring structure of M87 across several years, in excellent agreement with the EHT Collaboration's published results," he said. ®

ea473d0a35b43727: A tiny, US$900 wearable device being developed by an Indian billionaire entrepreneur and showcased by some of the country's top sportspersons has sparked criticism from doctors who say its claims of tracking blood flow to the brain are exaggerated.
The Temple device is less than 2.54 cm wide and weighs under two grammes. It sticks to the side of the head between the forehead and the ear, or the temple area.

Promotional materials for the device, developed by Deepinder Goyal, say that its BrainFlow feature shows how well the brain is being supplied with blood in real time and its Entropy feature can detect how hard the body works to shed heat.
It can also measure thermal, immune, digestive, cognitive and emotional readings that help to transform how a person regulates their health, they say.
Priced at 85,000 rupees (US$907), the device comes in six colours.
India's cricket captain Shubman Gill and Olympic medal-winning badminton player P.V. Sindhu have worn it.
Some well-known doctors in the country, however, are sceptical of the claims, saying the device's capabilities are not backed by peer-reviewed research.
In prime-time shows and on social media, they are calling for the device to come under the purview of medical regulators.
Prominent Indian hepatologist Cyriac Philips, known as "TheLiverDoc", has been criticising the device on his X account with 328,000 followers, calling Temple "the biggest health scam."
"People must be aware of wellness hacks such as wearables also, even though they are not marketed as health devices," he told Reuters.
On one prime-time TV discussion, paediatrician and nephrologist Sanjeev Bagai called Temple a "gimmick", saying it had "no formal approval or clearance."
Goyal has hit back at the criticism from doctors, saying Temple is a "fitness tracker, and wellness device", not a medical one.

Indian doctor Jason Philip wrote on X that assessing blood flow to the brain was not easy, and optical signals placed over the temple skin would only give data on the "superficial temporal artery" that supplies blood to the face and skin.

In a statement to Reuters, Temple said BrainFlow and Entropy were new metrics "with emerging science", and that more research would follow, adding that some metrics would eventually need regulatory approval.
India's health ministry did not respond to Reuters queries, and the government has so far not reacted to the public debate.
SCRUTINY ON WEARABLES MAKERS
The debate on Temple comes as wearable makers overseas also face questions on when a fitness feature becomes a medical one.
Some Apple Watch features, such as hypertension notifications, have received US Food and Drug Administration clearance as software-based medical features.
Last year, the US FDA warned Whoop, saying its wrist-worn fitness tracker's blood-pressure feature looked like a medical one — a view the company disputes.
Goyal is best known for co-founding Eternal, which houses India's biggest listed food-delivery company Zomato and has a market value of about US$35 billion.
The 43-year-old stepped down as chief executive of Eternal this year to focus on Temple.
Temple, which has professors from the University of Ottawa and Harvard on its advisory board, raised US$54 million in February at a valuation of about US$190 million.
Goyal said Temple has received orders from more than 62 countries since Nov 1.
On its website, Temple says it is also working on detecting conditions including snoring and jaw clenching.

2ef828b51c4bc407: It’s that time of year again: Thousands of delegates, lobbyists, and journalists are gathered for the annual UN climate talks, taking place this time in Antalya, Turkey.

COP31 officially kicked off on November 8, marking the beginning of negotiations on one of the biggest stages of the climate world. Turkey and Australia are cohosting this year’s talks, which are scheduled to wrap up on November 20.

This annual gathering can often serve as an indicator of where the world stands on addressing and adapting to the climate crisis. And this year’s talks are sure to be a doozy—expect a lot of back and forth on fossil fuels and climate finance in particular. Here’s what you should know about COP31.

In recent years, the tension always feels high when COP rolls around. (COP stands for “Conference of the Parties.”) But this year feels especially charged: The world is still grappling with the ongoing war in Iran, which has disrupted the Middle East and sent economic shock waves around the world as energy prices have spiked.

This year’s COP will be the second without a formal delegation from the US. President Trump formally withdrew the country from the Paris Agreement earlier this year and is in the process of withdrawing from the UN Framework Committee on Climate Change. That’s the treaty that allows formal participation in negotiations.

Meanwhile, things aren’t looking good for the Paris Agreement, which was established at UN climate talks 11 years ago, setting a goal of limiting warming to 1.5 °C over preindustrial levels. In a report published in September, the UN Environment Program acknowledged that global warming is set to exceed that 1.5 °C goal, “likely within the next few years.”

So as climate talks kick off, there’s an obvious, urgent question looming about how to quickly cut emissions to limit warming. There’s also the major issue of how to pay for efforts to address emissions and to help a warming world endure the inevitable damage.

Two years ago, talks ended in a goal of mobilizing $300 billion per year by 2035 to help pay to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change. (Rich nations provided $136.7 billion in 2024, according to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development.) And last year, the COP30 agreement included a goal of tripling the money for adaptation over that period. (Such funding has been quite flat over the past few years.)

The world got a tragic reminder of just how high the stakes are earlier this year, when a glacier collapse caused devastating flooding in the Himalayas. The flood killed approximately 1,500 people, left over 5,000 missing, and caused nearly $5 billion in damage. The UN loss and damages fund committed $20 million to helping Nepal recover (less than 1% of the total estimated cost to the country).

Another key trend to watch is how the formal negotiations engage with the topic of fossil fuels. Three years ago, the final agreement text explicitly called for a transition away from them. But it felt as if things took a step back last year, when the final agreement didn’t even mention the phrase “fossil fuels” once. This will be an interesting conversation, especially because cohosts Turkey and Australia have both faced criticism over their relationships with these fuels—Australia is a major exporter of coal and natural gas, and Turkey’s grid relies heavily on fossil fuels, including coal.

Outside the formal negotiations, COP31 president Murat Kurum, Turkey’s environment minister, is spearheading a side agenda, including two informal initiatives that will be worth watching. These wouldn’t be part of the official agreement text, but countries could sign on to signal support.

One is a pledge to make AI more sustainable; this is almost comically squishy, even as voluntary COP pledges go. The text includes explicit wording that it creates no new obligations for countries, so don’t expect anything resembling enforcement there.

The COP leadership is also pushing to make electricity a larger part of member countries’ energy use. Today, only about 23% of global energy is used in the form of electricity. Fossil fuels, like gasoline in vehicles or natural gas for heating, make up the bulk of the rest. Shifting to more electricity use, and relying on cleaner sources for that electricity, could help drive down emissions. The new pledge’s target is for electricity to make up 35% of total energy consumption by 2035.

With leadership billing this as an “implementation COP,” it would be great to see some real, tangible progress on the global challenge of addressing climate change. I’m not expecting anything groundbreaking, but we’ll be tuned in to see what the final agreement shapes up to be.
This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review’s weekly climate newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here.

3bd8eba50bd0c212: LONDON: UK media on Tuesday published allegations that British comedian and children's author David Walliams groomed teenage fans and sexually assaulted a 15-year-old girl as well as harassing young female colleagues.
The claims, published by The Guardian newspaper and ITV news channel, came after a joint investigation into allegations by multiple women dating as far back as 2003.

Walliams, who lost a High Court battle against being identified in the UK media and did not appeal, denied targeting teenagers and using his fame to manipulate them to have sex, his lawyers told media.
His lawyers did not respond to a request for comment from AFP.
The Guardian published a letter Tuesday from Walliams, saying he "behaved thoughtlessly" in casual relationships.
But he said: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law."
Now 55, Walliams starred in the BBC's "Little Britain" sketch show in the early 2000s and was a judge on commercial broadcaster ITV's "Britain's Got Talent."
He also penned books such as "Mr Stink", "Gangsta Granny" and "The Boy in the Dress", with his work translated into more than 50 languages and reportedly selling 50 million copies.
When seeking to block the publication of the reports, Walliams' legal team argued he was "highly likely" to die by suicide if they were published.
The High Court heard he made two suicide attempts this year and was detained in a secure hospital last month.
Almost all the women making claims were identified only by first names, some changed at their request.
- 'I WAS GROOMED, 100 PER CENT' -
In a particularly grave allegation, one woman, named as Jade, said Walliams contacted her in 2007 via her social media page showing her age as 15.
Then aged 36, he invited her to his house and pulled up her top and sucked her breast, she said, with her words read by an actor in a documentary released by ITV.
"It's a sexual assault, it's a grooming, it's completely wrong in every way," she said.
It is illegal in Britain for someone aged over 18 to intentionally communicate with a child under 16 for a sexual purpose.
Walliams' lawyers said he never engaged in grooming young women and denied sexual contact with Jade.
Another woman, named as Alex, told The Guardian Walliams first met her when she was a 15-year-old aspiring comedy writer and he was 32.
He phoned her and gave her tickets to shows. They had sex for the first time at his home when she was 17 and he was 34, she said.
She said this was consensual but Walliams was "pushy" and treated her "like a prostitute."
"I think I was groomed, 100 per cent. We met when I was 15 and he was promising to help me ... He used that power," she said.
Walliams' lawyers told The Guardian he believed she was 18 and that she had got back into contact with him.
The investigation also claims Walliams messaged teenage models and invited teenage fans back to his dressing room and his house.
His publisher, HarperCollins, dropped him last year after he faced accusations of harassing female staff, which he denied, and he has not posted on social media since.
The latest allegations prompted more organisations to distance themselves from the former star.
A BBC spokesperson told AFP it has taken down some shows involving Walliams from its platforms, including all episodes of "Little Britain", which ran between 2003 and 2006.
A spokesperson for his literary agents, Independent Talent Group, told AFP that after the latest claims, "we are no longer representing him in any capacity."
The ruling Labour Party is also understood to have suspended Walliams as a member.--AFP

55b84366c52c976c: MADRID: Thousands of Spaniards left their workplaces and hit the streets on Wednesday as a general strike sought to crank up pressure on the key issue of housing weeks before a snap election.

In Barcelona, school lunch monitor Ines Oliveras said she wanted "to live a normal life, have my own space, my own home, not have to count every euro just to be able to buy food."
"It's not just my problem, but a shared one... it's very intergenerational," the 29-year-old told AFP.
The size of later demonstrations planned in Madrid and Barcelona will be seen as an indicator of public discontent before the Nov 29 vote, which the right-wing opposition is predicted to win.
- TRAINS DISRUPTED -

In Barcelona, the metro and bus networks were out of action after offering minimum services during the morning rush hour, but Madrid's suburban trains reported little impact on services.
Public rail operator Renfe said 24 per cent of its high-speed services were cancelled, while around 20 per cent of trains were scrapped in the sprawling commuter networks of Madrid and Barcelona.
UGT union leader Pepe Alvarez told public broadcaster RTVE that the participation was "massive", with a "total" stoppage in some regions making the strike "a huge success."
But his union acknowledged participation was "uneven", with large mobilisation in the car manufacturing, petrochemicals and meat sectors and in coastal regions.
The CEOE organisation, which represents business leaders, said in a statement that the impact varied by region and area of work, with a "low participation" in most sectors.
Electricity demand had fallen by around five percent, "significantly lower" than in previous strikes, the CEOE said.
- 'LISTEN TO EVERYONE' -
The main UGT and CCOO unions called the strike following a wave of nationwide protests over access to housing, sparked by the eviction in September of an 87-year-old Madrid pensioner.

Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez called the election, initially scheduled for 2027, after his minority government failed to secure parliamentary approval for a package of housing measures proposed in response to the demonstrations.
Business groups and the right have rejected the strike, seeing an election-related gambit instead of a genuine labour dispute.
But the unions have insisted the strike is directed against all levels of the state and not only the right, which voted down the government's housing decrees.
They have defended the walkout as an exceptional measure intended to generate broad social pressure for action on soaring housing costs.
Living costs are another major concern, with inflation hitting 4.9 per cent in September and October – its highest level in more than three years.

Isabel Iglesias, a nurse who lives in Madrid, said housing was the issue "that is affecting me the most." She pays a rent of 1,000 euros (US$1,100) with her partner but earns just 1,700 euros a month.
Iglesias, 27, said Sanchez, who has been in power since 2018, "could have done much more" on housing, urging the next government "to listen to everyone and get their act together."--AFP

ea6183d1a08c38b6: PESHAWAR: Gunmen attacked a police convoy on its way to an illegal gold mining operation in Pakistan's northwestern region on Wednesday, killing eight officers, officials said.
A senior administrative official in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province's Kohat district told AFP eight police personnel were killed and 13 others were injured.
Militants set two police vehicles on fire during the assault, while two other police vehicles and one private vehicle were missing, the official said.
He said the officers were travelling to an illegal gold mining operation near Gumbat.
A security official in Peshawar confirmed the toll of eight officers killed.

No group immediately claimed responsibility for the shooting in the border province where security forces are battling an intensifying militancy they say emanates from Afghanistan – an accusation its Taliban government denies.

A spokesman for a local emergency service earlier on Wednesday said there had been a "firing incident involving police personnel" in Kohat district, adding that rescue workers were treating a dozen wounded officers.

Relations between Pakistan and Afghanistan have been fraught since the Taliban authorities took power in 2021, and worsened after deadly border clashes in October last year that led to near-total closure of the border.
Clashes subsided after mediation, but the conflict intensified again in February, with Pakistan declaring "an open war" on its neighbour.
Islamabad accuses Kabul of allowing militants responsible for deadly attacks on Pakistani territory to operate from its soil. Afghanistan's Taliban authorities have denied the allegations.
Hundreds of civilians have been killed in fighting between the two countries since October last year, according to figures from the United Nations' mission in Afghanistan.
Earlier this month, militants in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa killed two police officers assigned to protect a polio vaccination team travelling near the Afghan border.
The province was placed under emergency rule last month in a move authorities said came in reaction to the failure by the provincial government to act against militancy.
The imposition of emergency measures sidelined the last remaining bastion of power for jailed former prime minister Imran Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party.
The special constitutional measures also set off a province-wide crackdown on Khan's supporters, with hundreds of detentions.--AFP

5f8e26b36ac467ac: Apple's first touchscreen MacBook got a mixed reception from iFixit's teardown specialists, who praised its easily replaced lid but found fans and USB-C ports buried beneath the logic board.

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display was unveiled at the end of October. It features a tandem OLED screen that stacks two layers of organic light-emitting pixels, eliminating the need for a backlight, and adds touch capability to the MacBook line for the first time.
Although the vendor was patted on the back in recent years for improving the repairability of its famously locked-down products, this machine shows Apple still has some way to go.
The good? The entire lid comes off relatively easily. Its three-screw hinges closely resemble those on the M6 14-inch MacBook Pro, while streamlined display cable brackets simplify removal.

Apple's Repair Assistant tool also handled a full system board swap well. Despite concerns about Touch ID fingerprint authentication, everything went relatively smoothly when iFixit paired a touchscreen from one machine with a logic board from another. On the first boot, Repair Assistant recognized the battery, display, and Touch ID sensor, and touch control needed no separate calibration.

The bad? Replacing the panel alone is not possible. When iFixit tried to separate it from the lid, the glass delaminated, cracking the OLED and touch-sensitive layers beneath. That could make for a costlier repair than bargained for.
Under the bottom cover, the PROLED has a similar internal layout to the last few models of MacBook Pros, with the fans, board, speakers, and trackpad all in the same places.

That means the same annoyances persist. The MagSafe power connector can be removed via two screws and a bracket, yet the USB-C ports can't be extracted the same way because the logic board is in the way. The headphone jack and the fans also require removing the system board first, and the HDMI port and SDXC card reader are soldered to the board itself, as is the storage and memory.
Another gripe is that this MacBook's battery pack is hard to remove, though at least it is removable, unlike in many thin-and-light laptops. The tested Pro weighs 1.38 kg or about 3 pounds.
For these reasons, the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display earns a 5 out of 10 repairability score from iFixit, but this is actually a one point increase over the score it gave the M5 MacBook Pro.

The Apple logo has its own lighting. Older MacBooks with illuminated logos borrowed light from the LCD backlight shining through an apple-shaped window in the lid. This model uses a strip of LEDs along one edge of the logo, passing through a diffuser for an even glow. Because it sits behind the display panel, it would be nearly impossible to repair if it failed, especially if the panel is destroyed during removal.
Under a microscope, the PROLED XDR display looks very different from earlier MacBooks: the blue subpixel is significantly larger than the green and red ones.
The reason, we're told, is that blue OLED materials wear out faster, so a larger subpixel can emit the same amount of light while putting less strain on the material. ®
