cf38731f04c15c11: If you want to watch four billionaire/billionaire wannabes cope with the election results, you could watch the absolutely dreadful hosts of All-In talk across a livestream and a follow-up podcast for four hours, or you could just watch the Lucille Bluth “What could a banana cost, Michael,” clip on repeat until your eyes and ears bleed.

Throughout their post-election breakdown podcast episode released over the weekend, the All-In bros seem to be on the verge of grasping why Americans are so mad and who they’re mad at, but are still trying to find the guy who did this. They appear to finally grasp that Americans are mad at something called “oligarchs” but largely do not seem to know who they are (it’s them). Populist anger at the oligarchs is a “perception” or “narrative” problem. The four hosts — David Sacks, Chamath Palihapitiya, Jason Calacanis, and David Friedberg— spend much of the episode considering whether they are out of touch, or whether the children are wrong. Let’s see how they did.

“We lost all the podcast bros,” David Sacks, a Trump sycophant billionaire most famous for leading anti-DEI witch hunts against college administrators and writing interminable, book-length tweets, said on the most recent episode. “We lost a huge part of our base. The Republicans in particular are dependent on the podcast circuit. Let’s call it alternative media. Why? Because the mainstream media hates us. Legacy media hates us.”

“And they’re 90 percent left, so it is what it is,” Jason Calacanis, a man who seems singularly focused on discussing how he moved away from California three years ago to move to now-Blue Texas, responds.

“Without them, we don’t have any media that supports us,” Sacks says, seemingly unaware of the existence of Fox News, CBS News and 60 Minutes under Bari Weiss, the Paramount-Skydance (and CNN) merger, Jeff Bezos’s Washington Post, the concept of Elon Musk’s X, to say nothing of Democratic pseudo-scandals being ginned up by the New York Times.

The podcast, like their election night coverage last week (which features, among other guests, Ted Cruz and the CEO of Polymarket explaining at length how little he knows about elections), goes on and on like this.

In the aftermath of last week’s election, the schadenfreude of watching right-wing figures crash out as they realize just how unpopular Trump’s policies have become has been particularly satisfying. But there’s something special about watching smarmy Silicon Valley weirdos who sound like they haven’t spoken to anyone who hasn’t founded a startup in several decades advance their theory of the case about what just happened, and what Trump could do next to “save his legacy.” Calacanis, for example, suggested a policy of “no taxes on people under a certain revenue, uhh, income threshold.” He catches himself, perhaps realizing that most people don’t think of their paychecks as their “revenue” because they are not businesses. Palihapitiya says something must be done to “allow the wage earning class to feel more ownership of the United States economy.” Calacanis has come to the realization that “the bottom half of non-equity holders” are mad about the state of the country. Sacks says the wave happened because of “this narrative around affordability plus the perception of the lack of affordability” that has put the public “in a very ornery mood.” “It doesn’t matter how good the economy actually is,” he says. “It matters how good people perceive it to be,” adding that “the economy is not that bad. I mean, in fact it’s quite good.” In fact, data shows this is deeply out of touch with what people across the country are experiencing: More than half of Americans can’t afford to have an emergency fund or save for the future, and most Americans report having to cut back on their lifestyles to afford to live. Housing affordability is at crisis levels.

41bbf09b55324917: Users are having difficulty installing Microsoft's latest Windows patch.

Patch Tuesday contained a truckload of fixes for Microsoft products. However, for some users, installing the update, KB5132061, is proving challenging. In the hours after the patch was released, multiple complaints began to surface that the download and installation were failing, with some customers reporting a 0x800F0993 error code. Others say they received a 0x800F0989 error.
Microsoft does not currently list any known issues with the update and is yet to make a statement or provide explanation for the glitch.

In addition to the security fixes, this patch resolves a number of known issues from previous updates, including a problem where USB Audio 1.0 devices might fail to start and display an error code 10 in Device Manager.

In the absence of a statement from Microsoft, several users have taken to sleuthing. One, with the handle of Forceflow on the ElevenForum site, suggested the bug might be related to Windows Sandbox, and said that after disabling the feature and rebooting, the patch installed successfully.

However, others reported problems regardless of Windows Sandbox status, and alternative solutions included using DISM (Deployment Image Servicing and Management) to check the package or downloading the update manually.
It's an important patch to install, since it addresses 726 vulnerabilities in Windows alone, and the difficulties affected users face are less than ideal.

Microsoft patches have lately displayed more gremlins than usual. Out-of-band releases are depressingly regular after updates break functionality. A September Out-of-band release, for example, was hurriedly pushed out after the September 2026 Windows security update caused trouble for Remote Desktop Services.

The October Patch Tuesday for Windows Server sent Exchange Servers toppling, with a registry edit workaround suggested. There was no out-of-band update - Microsoft said the problem had been resolved in the November update.
At least this latest release appears to be failing before users get a chance to see what is broken this time.
The Register has asked Microsoft to comment. ®

adfaa2db826924ea: NEW DELHI: India's cabinet approved on Wednesday a mega-museum showcasing the country's history and civilisation, which the government said will cost around US$340 million and have the largest display area in the world.
First announced in 2023, the project received approval as Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Hindu nationalist government renewed its emphasis on the country's pre-colonial cultural identity.
The museum's name, Yuge Yugeen Bharat, translates roughly as "India through the ages" and invokes the country's ancient Sanskrit name, Bharat.
It will occupy former civil service offices in New Delhi, known as North and South Blocks, which were designed by British architects Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker in the 1920s.
In a statement, the cabinet said the museum will be "spread over a proposed built-up area of approximately 178,509 square metres".
"Benchmarked against major international museums, Yuge Yugeen Bharat Museum is going to be the museum (with) the largest display area in the world," it added.
India's cabinet said the Yuge Yugeen Bharat is "envisaged as a landmark civilisational museum showcasing the continuity, diversity and richness of Bharat's (India's) civilisational heritage".
The first gallery is expected to open to the public by the end of 2027, with project completion scheduled for financial year 2030-31.
Modi came to national power in May 2014, and has since taken multiple steps to glorify the country's heritage and culture.
His government built the world's tallest statue, a 182-metre monument to Vallabhbhai Patel, for his role in bringing princely states into India.
Modi also backed the revamp of New Delhi's historic administrative district in his second term and moved lawmakers to a new parliament building in 2023.

"The Museum is envisaged as a national public cultural institution... it will provide opportunities for learning, research, cultural engagement and appreciation of India's civilisational heritage," the government statement said on Wednesday.
Around 1.8 million objects have been identified from national and state museums, archaeological collections and private holdings for potential display.
The museum is designed to accommodate up to 10 million visitors a year.

"This is a very important moment for us, we had an Argentine pope and he wasn't able to come, that hurt me," said 76-year-old Estela Adorno.
The 71-year-old pontiff is on a 12-day tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru less than a month after undergoing surgery for lung cancer.

The South America tour has been cast as a double homecoming, bringing Leo to Argentina, birthplace of Francis, before taking him to Peru, where he spent years as a missionary and church leader before becoming pope.

Throughout his stay in Argentina, Leo has pointedly urged leaders to build a more inclusive economy and protect society's most vulnerable, comments widely interpreted as criticism of President Javier Milei's government.

Those social concerns were visible in the crowd at Lujan. One group unfurled a banner reading "land, housing and work for the people," while a woman held a sign calling for the release of a man she said had been wrongly imprisoned.
Adorno said the pope's message had resonated in a country marked by political and economic divisions.
"Everything that helps society is welcome. People were deeply moved, I was deeply moved. With everything that is happening in the country, it will always be welcome," she added.
Volunteers handed out water in the crowd as pilgrims continued streaming into Lujan under the spring sun.
Inside the basilica, choir members prepared for a Mass they described as a once-in-a-lifetime occasion.

"It is a unique opportunity, full of emotion. From the moment we were told we would participate, through preparing the repertoire and these final days of rehearsals, there has been so much shared excitement," said choir member Nora Jauregui, a 61-year-old retired music teacher.
Earlier Wednesday, Leo visited inmates at Buenos Aires' Devoto prison, where he urged prisoners to use their time behind bars as an opportunity to rebuild their lives.
"Human beings often flourish through limits rather than despite them," the pope told around 75 inmates and family members gathered in the prison gymnasium.
He acknowledged the hardship of prison life, saying he could imagine their sleepless nights and thoughts of loved ones or those they may have harmed.
The US-born pope had refused to reschedule the trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru despite having the lower part of his right lung removed to extract a cancerous tumor.

The spacecraft, which suffered a communications hiccup last month, is traveling at approximately 38,000 mph (61,000 kph) and will mark the 50th anniversary of its launch next year. Before then, it has another distance record to set.
"Light-day" is a bit snappier than 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). NASA puts the crossing at 05:16:07 EST (10:16:07 UTC) on Wednesday, November 18.

For "Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day," participants are invited to flash the mission's three-letter designation – VGR – in Morse code after sunset on November 17, using a flashlight or NASA's website.

According to the space agency, this will create "a symbolic wave of golden light encircling the planet after sunset." It is also a nice way to mark the achievement – Voyager 1 is the most distant human-made object from Earth, and its extraordinary longevity remains a testament to the skill of engineers past and present.
Not that Voyager 1 will be able to detect any flashlights on Earth. Its cameras were turned off decades ago, after the famous Pale Blue Dot image was captured.

NASA has invited the public to join in a spacecraft photo opportunity before. On July 19, 2013, Cassini photographed Earth and the Moon from its orbit around Saturn for "The Day the Earth Smiled," while people back home were encouraged to look up and "just smile at the sheer joy of being alive on a Pale Blue Dot."
Voyager 2, the spacecraft's sibling, is not expected to reach the same milestone for another nine years. It took a different path through the solar system to swing past Uranus and Neptune.
It will, however, be uncertain as to whether Voyager 2 will still be able to communicate by then – even with recent efforts to eke out the probe's dwindling power supply, margins are razor thin. ®

df89be52240b7a85: A 2013 breach of Russian-language cybercrime forum YouHack exposed its members' login details – and millions of credentials they had posted about other victims, according to newly cataloged data.

Have I Been Pwned (HIBP) added the breach on Wednesday, recording 7.2 million unique email addresses. Around 107,000 belonged to forum members, whose exposed data included usernames, IP addresses, and mostly unsalted MD5 password hashes.

Unsalted MD5 is a poor choice for protecting passwords. It's fast to compute, allowing attackers to test guesses at speed, and identical passwords produce identical hashes. Hardly good hygiene for a hacking forum.

You might expect members of a cybercrime forum to know better than to reuse passwords or register with an email address tied to their real identity. Expectations and reality are not always on speaking terms, as AlphaBay founder Alexandre Cazes demonstrated.
YouHack, a longtime cybercrime forum, moved to a different domain after the 2013 breach and remains active, giving cybercrims a place to trade stolen credentials and financial data.
The data collated from that digital burglary was eventually bundled into 2024's so-called Mother of all Breaches – a 12TB, 26 billion-record mega-dump of files taken from myriad data security lapses.

HIBP separately published its findings concerning another Russian data breach today. It said the 2023 breach of Russian bank Sberbank's loyalty program (SberSpasibo) contained records belonging to 48 million users.

The dataset included 3.3 million unique email addresses, alongside phone numbers and dates of birth. Bank card numbers were stored as unsalted SHA-1 hashes, which could let attackers test possible numbers against the leaked hashes for a match.
Reporting on the SberSpasibo breach at the time suggested the records were dated between April 2017 and February 2022, and the attack was claimed by the pro-Ukraine hacktivist outfit NLB.
NLB also claimed responsibility for an attack on Sberbank's internal systems at the same time, and later took partial credit for an attack on Alfa-Bank, Russia's largest private bank. ®
07be24d7a8aa835c: Cape Verde’s presidential election takes place against the backdrop of a democratic record that remains unusual in its regional context. The country, made up of an archipelago of islands off the coast of west Africa, has sustained multiparty competition for more than three decades. It has had peaceful transfers of power and no coups or military takeovers since independence from Portugal in 1975. Cabo Verde (population 530,000) is a semi-presidential republic in which the president is directly elected. The prime minister is appointed by the president in light of parliamentary election results, and heads a government that is politically accountable to the national assembly. The president represents the state and safeguards the constitution, while the prime minister and the government conduct public policy. The presidency nevertheless carries substantial political weight. The president can veto legislation, request constitutional review and, under certain conditions, dissolve parliament. The office also entails responsibilities in foreign affairs and national defence. The president is, therefore, not the principal policymaker. However, the way in which these powers are exercised can become particularly consequential when the president and prime minister belong to opposing political camps. This might indeed be the outcome of the 15 November 2026 election. I am a political communication specialist who has researched the dynamics of Cabo Verde’s presidential elections. In my view the central test for the upcoming poll will be whether the country’s institutions can continue to function effectively while preserving the important distinction between the presidency and the government. The background Cape Verde’s political climate is shaped by a recent change of government. The African Party for the Independence of Cabo Verde returned to office after winning the May 2026 parliamentary election. This ended 10 years of government by the Movement for Democracy, which now forms the opposition. The African Party for the Independence of Cabo Verde’s victory reflected growing voter dissatisfaction with a decade of rule by the Movement for Democracy. This is particularly over poor inter-island transport, economic difficulties, living conditions and public security. The change of government renewed questions about the balance of power between the president, the new government and parliament, as well as the opposition’s ability to hold the ruling party accountable. The forthcoming presidential election will, therefore, test not only party loyalties but also voters’ expectations of the presidency and its role in the political system. The two main contenders are José Maria Neves, backed by the African Party for the Independence of Cabo Verde, and Joana Rosa, supported by the Movement for Democracy. Neves previously served as prime minister between 2001 and 2016. Rosa, a former minister of justice, is the first woman to run for president in Cabo Verde. They face Antero Tavares, Casimiro de Pina, Gilson Alves and Loisito Sousa. These four offer alternatives to the two parties that have dominated national politics since the introduction of multipartyism in 1991. These candidates are unlikely, however, to attract support on a scale that would challenge the two main contenders. The voters Together with political science researchers Danielton Delgado and Susana Rogeiro Nina, I published a paper that offers insight into the dynamics of presidential elections in Cabo Verde. Our 2019 study found that voters didn’t consistently use presidential contests to punish the governing party. Indeed, except in 2011 and 2021, every presidential election in the country was won by the candidate backed by the party that controlled parliament and the executive. Also, there was not a systematic advantage for independent candidates or candidates backed by smaller parties. The short interval – one to six months – between legislative and presidential elections may help explain this phenomenon, as presidential contests often take place during the governing party’s post-election “honeymoon period”. What’s different in the upcoming election? If Neves secures re-election, the presidency and government will be held by figures associated with the same party. This possibility is not unlikely. Since the introduction of multiparty democracy in 1991, every incumbent president who has sought a second term has been re-elected: António Mascarenhas Monteiro in 1996, Pedro Pires in 2006 and Jorge Carlos Fonseca in 2016. A victory for Neves could play out in one of two ways. It could facilitate cooperation, but it could also raise questions about the president’s independence from the government. In turn, a victory for Rosa, mirroring the patterns that emerged in 2011 and 2021, would create a situation of divided leadership, with a Movement for Democracy-backed president working alongside an African Party for the Independence of Cabo Verde government. Such an arrangement is not inherently problematic. Nevertheless, it can require negotiation when constitutional responsibilities and political interests diverge. Cabo Verde has recent experience of this situation: between November 2021 and the formation of the new government in June 2026, Neves dealt with a Movement for Democracy government. This was led by Ulisses Correia e Silva. Despite their partisan differences, relations were generally characterised by institutional cooperation rather than open confrontation. In short, whoever wins will face a distinct institutional challenge. Neves will have to balance his party affiliation with the constitutional responsibility to act as head of state. Rosa will need to establish a working relationship with a government led by her political opponents. José Santana Pereira does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

36d2068d8bbc9dd9: WASHINGTON, Nov 11 — President Donald Trump’s political mantra is “fight, fight, fight.” But he has given decidedly mixed messages about whether he will do so after Republicans were hammered in the midterms.
In the week since becoming a lame duck, Trump named the hardline architect of his migration crackdown as his chief of staff, while admitting his deportation policy was too tough.
The 80-year-old raised eyebrows when he publicly asked Ultimate Fighting Championship boss Dana White to be his new press secretary — then claimed he was just joking.
He has admitted that the Iran war was largely to blame for the midterms rout. But he has strongly backed Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth’s battle against impeachment.
And despite saying on election night that he’d accept the results of the Democratic sweep, he has reverted to type and revived baseless claims of election fraud.
“One of the characteristics of Donald Trump is that he changes his mind on a dime,” Democratic Senator Chris Coons told CNN.
“He’ll be praising someone on Monday, firing them on Tuesday, and pretending he never knew them on Wednesday. So it’s hard to predict exactly what Donald Trump is going to do.”
‘Too tough’
Democrats have promised to rein in Trump and launch a series of investigations into corruption and abuse of power. He could face a third impeachment.

But for a president supposedly facing his last stand, he has at times struck a surprisingly conciliatory tone. As results came in, he congratulated Democrats on seizing Congress and said he could work with them.
Instead of a press conference the next day, he gave reporters a tour of his new White House ballroom — sparking speculation he might spend the rest of his term on his building projects.
But the signs of volatility were still there. In the Oval Office, Trump placed a red baseball cap saying “veto” on his desk.
And when Trump announced on Friday that ultraloyalist Stephen Miller would replace Susie Wiles as his chief of staff, it seemed that the gloves were finally off.
The brains behind the masked immigration raids that left two Americans dead, Miller has also been instrumental in using executive orders to help Trump bypass Congress.
Yet in an interview the same day — though broadcast on Sunday — Trump conceded voters had been turned off by the aggressive deportation push.
“I think it was too tough,” Trump told the CBS News 60 Minutes programme.
Still, the chances of Trump doing a deal with Democrats — possibly even for an amnesty for undocumented migrants — remain low.

“It doesn’t seem likely. Not with this decision to have Stephen Miller running the show,” Sarah Binder, a senior fellow in governance studies at the Brookings Institution, said in a panel discussion this week.
‘Violent fighter’
Trump’s astonishing announcement on Saturday that he wanted “violent fighter and warrior” Dana White to be his new spokesman also seemed to signal a war footing.
If it seemed too ironic to be true, it was. A day later Trump said he was “kidding.”
Ever the showman, the former reality TV star brought the UFC boss to the White House podium for an unexpected visit on Monday, where White turned down the job.
The administration’s biggest fight now is against Hegseth’s impeachment.
It’s a fight Trump appears to be joining with relish — saying that Hegseth “gets an ‘A’ PLUS, PLUS, PLUS” shortly after the Pentagon chief gave a press conference calling the charges a “farce.”
But Hegseth will know that Trump is rarely shy of shaking up his staff. He jettisoned Wiles just over two weeks after saying there was “zero chance” he would sack her.
And Trump himself admitted he isn’t likely to change his stripes.
Asked by CBS if he could forgive his foes, when faced with going to heaven or not, he demurred.
“Can I be honest? I probably cannot do that, no. Because I do hate some of my enemies, and I always will.” — AFP
a312b7ac7ecbcb93: BRUSSELS, Nov 11 — After recent attacks on supermarket fridges, home appliances could be next, the EU’s cyber chief told AFP on Tuesday, as he urged Europe to invest more to counter growing cyber threats.
Supermarkets in at least 12 European countries were hit by cyberattacks in October and November, with France the worst affected.
“Security should not and cannot be an afterthought,” Juhan Lepassaar, executive director of the EU’s cybersecurity agency ENISA, said.
“Today it was fridges, tomorrow it could be routers, the day after tomorrow it could be home appliances and so forth.”
Lepassaar spoke to AFP in Brussels where he unveiled the Athens-based agency’s latest biennial report on the state of the EU’s cybersecurity.

“All incidents can be avoided, but the question is, are we ready to invest to make it happen? Cybersecurity is not cheap,” he said, calling on manufacturers to make products that are secure “by design”.

Cybersecurity is crucial, Lepassaar said, because “every single service that you are depending on as a citizen, as a human being, contains a layer whereby there is a digital element in it, a piece of code which if not protected can be hacked.”
A worst-case scenario would mean losing services “you depend upon: the policemen arriving, the fire brigade arriving, the hospital functioning, the transport giving you a ride from point A to B.”
“These are the things that we depend on to function well and 24-7,” he explained. “And if they don’t, we will have an immediate impact.”

Hundreds of French supermarkets were hit in cyberattacks on October 11 and 12, which raised the temperatures in their refrigerators and freezers, forcing many to throw away entire inventories of perishable food.
France on Monday said it held Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) responsible for the cyberattacks on supermarkets.
Lepassaar would not comment directly on France’s accusation, but said Iranian and Russian “state-aligned actors” were known to target Europe.
He pointed to “a lot of collaboration” between them.
“China, Iran, People’s Republic of North Korea, there are a lot of state-aligned threat actors which do target European companies and European interests,” Lepassaar said.
He welcomed EU cyber rules that will fully enter into force next year, and the bloc’s plans to “double the size of ENISA and also its resources.”
It would “never” be enough, he said, “but it is a first good step”. — AFP
8e9a3c967d1314fc: WASHINGTON, Nov 11 — The scandal engulfing Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang could have its biggest consequences in Washington, where China hawks are seizing on the affair to push a hard line that had been put on the back burner under President Donald Trump.

Huang, who co-founded Nvidia and turned it into the world’s leading supplier of the processors that power artificial intelligence, admitted on Sunday to an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed whom US intelligence officials believe was working for Chinese intelligence.
Trump, who has relied on Huang as an adviser on AI, called him “an honorable guy” and said Huang told him he had no idea the woman was a spy.
Huang has spent years lobbying against curbs on sales of advanced AI chips to China, and Trump last year cleared Nvidia’s H200 chips for export there over objections from hawks in both parties.

“China hawks in policy circles in Washington DC were quite frustrated with the decisions and really wanted to see a more aggressive approach around export controls to China,” said Aalok Mehta of the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
“They will now see some fruits of their efforts.”
Many in Washington see the United States as locked in a Cold War-style race with China for technological and military dominance, and these hawks have bristled at Trump not conforming to that.

“What we are heading into is one of the most serious investigative efforts in a substantial period,” said Kurt Campbell, a former US deputy secretary of state and co-founder of consultancy The Asia Group.
Lawmakers will want to know when the government learned of the alleged links, whether the president was warned and whether the contacts shaped his China policy, Campbell said.
The New York Times has reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed the allegations to Trump in May, but the president chose not to act.

Nvidia committed US$25 million (RM101.85 milliion) to Trump’s White House ballroom — among the largest donations — months after securing his approval to resume chip sales to China, The Washington Post reported. Nvidia has said the gift was independent of its business interests.
Three Republican House committee chairs have asked Huang to attend a closed-door briefing on November 18 about his dealings with Alice Huang and Nvidia’s safeguards against espionage.
Not ‘invincible’
Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution’s John L. Thornton China Center, said Republicans long feared crossing Trump.
But with the party having lost control of Congress and Trump “no longer this seemingly invincible political brand,” some may feel freer to break with him, Chan told AFP.
That could revive the AI Overwatch Act, a bipartisan bill that would let Congress review and block licenses to export advanced AI chips to China and other adversaries.

The revelations have given hawks “new enthusiasm” to push through the stalled annual defense authorization bill with export control measures attached, said Emily Benson, head of strategy at Minerva Technology Futures.
The key question is Trump, she said, who holds a veto that only two-thirds majorities in both chambers can override.

Commerce Department staff have also pushed for new rules, including curbs on Chinese remote access to advanced AI chips, but Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick will not act without Trump’s instruction, tech news outlet The Information reported.
The department has already drawn scrutiny for reportedly halting a probe into Megaspeed’s dealings with Nvidia.
Tighter rules risk upsetting the trade truce Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping reached last year.
Export control legislation seen by Beijing as targeting China “would almost certainly invite swift retaliatory action by Beijing to destabilize US supply chains,” Benson said.
The FBI is looking into the spying allegations, Trump said, while the Justice Department is investigating whether Megaspeed smuggled Nvidia chips into China, NBC News reported.
Megaspeed denies smuggling, and Beijing has dismissed the spying claims as smears.

If wrongdoing were found and Huang forced out, “that would have huge implications for AI in the US, given that he has played such a pivotal role in pushing forward Nvidia but also the whole industry,” Chan said.

89f2ba81c9c8eb00: PARIS, Nov 11 — The cyberattack on supermarket refrigerators that France has blamed on Iran marks a new phase in the asymmetric campaign Tehran is waging against the United States, extending it onto European soil, analysts say.

Scores of French supermarkets were hit in the October 11 and 12 cyberattacks, which raised the temperatures in their refrigerators, in some cases forcing them to throw away entire inventories of perishable food.
France said Iran’s Revolutionary Guards were behind the “unprecedented” cyberattacks, a charge Iran rejected.
While Paris referred only to attacks against French supermarkets, similar incidents were reported in at least 11 other European countries.
Iran has ramped up operations on European soil since the outbreak of the war launched by Israel and the United States in February, security sources and experts said.
Iran has also warned that any renewed strikes would trigger retaliation.

In recent days, “Iran has sent very clear signals to a number of countries, warning that if there is another major US-Israeli bombing campaign, there will be consequences in Europe”, a European security source told AFP.

Tehran has already been accused of plotting various attacks on US interests in Europe, including against two air bases used by the United States in Britain — the US military on Monday withdrew aircraft from Mildenhall Royal Air Force (RAF) base.

It has also been accused of recruiting proxies to carry out attacks, including on a Bank of America branch in Paris this spring, and on Jewish targets, with synagogues attacked in Belgium and the Netherlands.
Paris has also accused Iran of spreading misinformation related to the protests that have rocked France and of mistreating the French embassy’s number two diplomat in Tehran in October.
Intimidation
The war has been at a stalemate for months, with efforts under way to avert a resumption of hostilities.
Threats that Europe could be targeted have been echoed in propaganda circulated by outlets close to Tehran.

In a recent AI-generated propaganda video entitled “Europe On Fire”, circulated by networks close to Iran, several European bases, including RAF Fairford in Britain and Istres air base in France, are shown under attack.

Missile warnings blare in Paris and London as civilians run through the streets. An English-language voiceover says: “You are not our enemies, but anyone anywhere in Europe who helps America harm our women and children, they’re our enemies”.

Intelligence monitoring group SITE reported that on November 8 the Persian-language outlet Teyban published a video targeting what it called “Satan’s Nests” — a reference to US military bases, including some in Europe such as Ramstein in Germany and Bezmer in Bulgaria.

From terrorist threats to cyberattacks, “it is a continuation of Iran’s asymmetric threat strategy and its determination to bring the battlefield onto European soil”, Clement Therme, Iran specialist at the University of Montpellier Paul-Valery, told AFP.

“It is similar to the way Russia conducts operations in Europe to strike at Ukraine’s strategic depth. What is the strategic depth of the US military in its confrontation with Iran? What lies between Iran and the United States? Europe,” he said.
‘Horizontal escalation’
Whereas American or Jewish interests were once the primary focus, the scope of potential targets has expanded, said Therme.
“We are now seeing a horizontal escalation, a geographical widening of the conflict and a shift in the nature of the targets towards civilian infrastructure such as refrigeration systems,” he added.
One advantage of cyber operations is that they allow for plausible deniability.
Iran is among the leading actors in this field.
“Iran has highly developed offensive cyber capabilities” and is “more specialised in sabotage than in data theft”, Anthony Chaix, a cybersecurity analyst at SQUAD, told AFP.
Unlike some other state actors that may hire cybercriminals to carry out operations, “Iran is generally known for conducting such operations itself”.

Most of the time, “sabotage operations are carried out very quickly, the aim is not to stick around under the radar”, Chaix said, although “they clearly also have the capability to conduct more discreet and longer-term operations”.
SQUAD cybersecurity expert Kris Vanhulst said the hack targeting supermarket refrigeration systems differed from previous cyberattacks.
He pointed to “the nature of the target and the message it sends: ‘we can reach anyone in the physical world’.”
“This was not a single company,” he added. “There were hundreds of impacts, it was extremely wide-ranging. The goal was to destabilise.” — AFP

"Our findings so far strongly suggest no sensitive data has been disclosed," the company said.

"The incident is isolated to a local system, and we have found no indication that there has been any impact on other Maersk systems or customer and partner systems that connect to Maersk through integrations such as APIs and EDI."
Maersk described the legacy local system as one "from a previous acquisition," and said it does not expect the attack to have an effect on operations.
Customers were reassured that they can continue to use Maersk platforms to manage their shipments as usual, and to expect updates from the company as and when they're available.
"Cybersecurity remains a constant, ongoing priority for Maersk," it added. "We have rigorous processes in place to identify and prevent incidents and minimize customer impact.
"As always, please treat any unexpected communications claiming to relate to this matter with caution and verify them through your usual Maersk contact.
"Thank you for your patience as we continue to investigate the incident."

Fortunately for those who immediately feel uneasy after hearing "Maersk" and "IT security" mentioned in the same breath, the wording of the shipping giant's disclosure suggests this intrusion won't be as calamitous as the NotPetya disaster in 2017.
Mimicking the Petya ransomware strain, NotPetya was an infamous destructive wiper malware strain that wormed its way across the global economy.
Western intelligence agencies attributed the malware to Russia's Sandworm group, an outfit believed to be part of the country's military intelligence service (GRU).
Maersk said at the time that it expected the attack to result in a circa $300 million bill, owing to remediation and rebuild costs.

Offering a sense of scale, Jim Hagemann Snabe, then chair of Maersk, told World Economic Forum delegates in 2018 that the company's rebuild encompassed 4,000 new servers, 45,000 new PCs, and 2,500 applications – which he said had been completed over just ten days.

In 2020, as exclusively revealed by The Register, Maersk went on to lay off around 150 staffers from its command and control center in Maidenhead, England. The staffers who lost their jobs had played key roles in the recovery. ®

8bf784b0134d532b: "Train in Python, serve in C++" might as well be Google's motto when it comes to much of its ML work.

Python is easy for data scientists to wield, but keeping its interpreter in the serving pipeline can add overhead and deployment headaches. The industry-backed OpenXLA Project provides tools for compiling machine learning computations into native code for different processors.
The latest component of this setup to be open sourced is XSE, short for the XLA Serving Engine.

XSE is not so much suited for large-scale LLM inference (which would be better served by vLLM or SGLang), but rather for smaller, more sharply task-oriented models, of which there are plenty at Google.

"LLM serving gets most of the attention right now, but a significant amount of production inference is still ranking, recommendation, embedding, and vision models. These tend to be short requests with very high [queries-per-second] and tight latency budgets," Nathan Beach, Google director of product management, wrote in a LinkedIn missive Tuesday.
At Google, XSE already handles more than six million queries per second across services including YouTube Shorts, Google Ads, and Search.
These models aren't there for a leisurely chat. They rank results, recommend videos, and make other decisions on the fly, often without users noticing.

A Python interpreter mulling each request would be a bottleneck, if not the end of Google itself. In Google's tests on short requests, XSE delivered two to five times the throughput of its best optimized Python server, using a quarter of the memory.

In this setup, the ML boffins write their model code in Python, using Google's JAX to help with the sums. Google also plans integration with TorchTPU so PyTorch users can export models for C++ serving on TPUs. An export tool packages the model's computations in StableHLO, a portable intermediate representation, alongside its trained weights in an "XLA SavedModel."
Ready to precognate, the C++ serving runtime uses XLA to compile those computations into native code for the target silicon. No Python interpreter to see here.

XLA SavedModels can run on GPUs and CPUs – Google partnered with both Arm and Intel to develop the XLA ecosystem. But Google obviously thinks it'd be a lot cooler if you ran your models on its own line of TPU accelerators.

Python's sluggishness continues to be an issue for the ML community. Beyond XSE, other approaches have been taken, many of which involve jettisoning the Python code as quickly as possible. PyTorch offers a native C++ runtime called LibTorch. Also, Microsoft and its collaborators offer the ONNX Runtime, which supports an open graph format with Python bindings.
Even Python's own reference implementation relies heavily on C, with Rust now getting a foot in the door. ®

69039760698893bd: ZURICH, Nov 11 — Swiss researchers have found a new way of detecting renowned date-rape drug GHB in urine for up to 72 hours after ingestion, in a possible boon to sexual assault investigations.

The University of Zurich said in a statement published Tuesday that the newly discovered biomarker could “indicate earlier GHB intake even when the drug is no longer detectable using conventional analysis”.
“Every hour is critical when it comes to detecting the use of drugs used to render victims unconscious,” it said.

But GHB, which is commonly used for this purpose, including by being slipped into drinks of unsuspecting victims, is excreted rapidly from blood and urine, leaving little time to test for it before all traces vanish.
“The usual detection window is around six hours in the blood and 12 in the urine,” Zurich University pointed out.

A team led by Andrea Steuer at the university’s Institute of Forensic Medicine had in 2021 helped discover a “promising biomarker” for the drug — a compound of GHB and a sugar thought to be ribose, known as GHB-pentose.
“Unlike GHB itself, this biomarker remains detectable in the urine for longer after intake,” the statement said.
The study indicated that the compound “remained detectable for up to three days after GHB intake, representing the longest detection window reported for a direct GHB-related biomarker to date”.
For their study published last week in the peer-reviewed scientific journal Drug Testing and Analysis, the researchers analysed 2,414 anonymised urine samples from genuine forensic cases since 2024.
Highlighting 14 samples, the researchers found that “although GHB levels measured were below the threshold set for the test, GHB-pentose was still detected”.
“In eight of these 14 cases, the case details supported the suspicion that GHB had been taken or administered previously,” the statement said.
Those cases included three suspected criminal offences — two robberies and one alleged sexual assault, in which urine samples were only gathered 13-16 hours after the incident.
“The findings offer the first indication from forensic practice that GHB-pentose remains detectable beyond the usual detection window for GHB,” Steuer said in the statement.
While promising, the researchers said the findings did not yet make it possible to determine the diagnostic reliability or the maximum detection period in any individual case using the method. — AFP

d3cc7bbf481859a0: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 11 — The government has approved a special incentive of about RM15 million a month under the Cooking Oil Price Control Mechanism (MKHMM) to maintain ceiling prices and ensure a stable supply of bottled pure palm cooking oil.

5d1b7e056778e1a9: UK travelers had more than fog to contend with this week, as Linux proved that if Windows could bork anything, it could bork it better.

Spotted by Andy Hinks at Heathrow Airport's Terminal 2, this information display has seen better days. While its neighbors offer walking times and terminal maps, it presents a sideways Linux boot log – useful only if your next connection involves mounting a filesystem.

There aren't many clues to what has befallen the machine behind the screen. The boot messages mention systemd, an Intel PRO/1000 network adapter, and an EXT4 filesystem on what appears to be a logical volume named LV_ROOT. Whether mounting that filesystem is the problem, or simply the last thing displayed before something else went wrong, isn't clear.

Heathrow's information displays clearly accommodate a mixture of technologies. Recent examples ran Microsoft Windows, which had - naturally - suffered a moment of its own. Linux can evidently be just as unreliable in the right hands.

The question is which Linux distribution is having its moment in the sun. Heathrow has been rolling out Raspberry Pi-based signage, although the Intel PRO/1000 adapter leaves the hardware behind this particular display something of a mystery.

Pi hardware makes sense for signage: it's relatively cheap – at least until AI ate all the RAM – and low-powered compared with a full-fat Windows PC. Heathrow's senior product owner for displays described the approach as a "reliable, secure solution that has a significantly lower hardware cost and are 30-40% more energy efficient than our previous hardware."

Readers might be interested to know that Heathrow has spent years working on its new screens. The product owner again: "We've completely re-engineered our content distribution system to be flexible and device-agnostic."
So Windows in one place, and Linux somewhere else. All rubbing along famously. Assuming, of course, the displays can show more than a virtual cough and splutter during boot. ®

aeedc8f8851a7bfc: ABU DHABI, Nov 11 — Russia and Ukraine began a second day of talks in Abu Dhabi on Wednesday, with Washington mediating as the two sides seek progress towards ending the worst conflict in Europe since World War II.

The first trilateral talks since February — when discussions ended in a stalemate and Washington shifted attention to its war with Iran — have so far been praised by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
He has hailed a change in approach by US mediators, led by President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and businessman envoy Steve Witkoff, though he has not yet elaborated on that change.

But the Ukrainian leader has emphasised the need for security guarantees for his country, while Europe has watched nervously after Washington said the talks would include a new security framework for the continent.
After Wednesday’s talks end, “we will hold a separate meeting with our European partners,” Kyiv’s chief negotiator Rustem Umerov said on Telegram.
A source in the Ukrainian delegation told AFP the US envoys would also join that meeting.

Kushner told delegates on Tuesday the United States had “narrowed the gaps” between the warring sides, without providing details, and hoped to move towards a “solution” to the conflict, which began with Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Zelensky, speaking in Copenhagen on Tuesday, said his team had reported that humanitarian issues and security guarantees were among the topics discussed.
He said the first day of talks had been “constructive and quite substantive”.
Asked about changes in the approach to peace talks by Kushner and Witkoff, Zelensky said: “I see changes. I’m very happy with what I hear.”
The Ukrainian president said negotiators were working on a “large-scale exchange of prisoners”, adding that US officials would travel to Russia to discuss the matter further.
But as the talks continued, so did the fighting: Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky said Wednesday that Russia had pummelled “six major electrical substations” in four regions overnight.
In Russia’s Leningrad region, governor Aleksandr Drozdenko posted on Telegram that a Ukrainian drone barrage had sparked a fire at Ust-Luga, a key Baltic port for oil exports.
‘New’ security framework
Europe has been rattled as Trump floated a deal with Russia on rewriting European post-war security, also worrying that Washington will force Kyiv to accept a de facto defeat.
Kushner on Tuesday said the United States hoped to “create a new framework” of security between Ukraine, Russia and Europe that will secure “decades, if not centuries, of peace”.
Ukraine insists Russia end hostilities before there can be any discussion on a future security arrangement for Europe.

Kyiv has warned against a “Yalta 2.0”, referring to Western leaders dividing Europe with the Soviet Union after World War II, and the EU has said security arrangements can only be discussed after a ceasefire.
But Moscow, several weeks before invading Ukraine, issued an ultimatum to Western countries to roll back troops from eastern Europe.
And Putin has repeatedly turned down broader ceasefire offers and vowed his troops will press on in Ukraine.
Moscow pushes security review

A Russian delegation source had said that settling the war was “merely one item on the agenda” for this week’s talks, and that Moscow’s main objective was reviewing security “for the entire continent”.
In a joint statement, the Europeans, Ukraine, the United States and Nato reaffirmed their “shared commitment to a strong post-war European security architecture”.
Kyiv is also pushing post-war support for its army.
A senior Ukrainian source told AFP Ukraine wanted at least 10 years of financial support to sustain an 800,000-strong army able to defend any future Russian attack.
Trump hinted before the talks that Kyiv might have to give up land, saying: “They’re going to end up with a little bit different shape.”
Russia’s troops have ground westwards but have not been able to seize the whole of the coveted Donetsk region, and Moscow demands Kyiv surrender the parts of the embattled area it controls. — AFP

42c2be2b71be4310: AMD's latest sales pitch: Up to 99 percent of the performance with half the DRAM, provided you're willing to buy a Mext license alongside your shiny new Epyc server.

This is made possible by using AI models to load memory pages in and out of cheaper NVMe storage before your operating system or apps ever know they need it — kind of like SWAP or a Windows page file, but smarter.

AMD acquired the tech from Mext back in June, and according to former CEO Gary Smerdon — now CVP of business development at AMD — the tech could cut enterprise server costs by as much as 83 percent by replacing costly RDIMMs with flash storage. Of the initial 145 systems the software has been deployed on so far, he estimates customers have already saved $5 million in avoided DRAM costs.
"Conservatively, 60, 70, even 80 or 90 percent for very large memory systems, of the cost of a server can be in memory," he explained.
Everyone's favorite buzzword to the rescue

Even in systems with high memory utilization, where (say) 95 percent of the memory is "in use," a lot of it isn't actively being used, he explained. He cited a Meta research paper that showed that between 50 and 80 percent of memory pages hadn't been touched in five minutes, ten minutes, or even longer. "Five minutes to Epyc is an eternity."

Mext technology aims to offload those infrequently accessed pages to flash. The challenge, Smerdon explains, is that while flash may be 50x cheaper per bit, 30x lower power per bit, it's also 500x slower.
This is why most folks, when provisioning VPCs or servers, generally avoid swapping out to disk wherever possible: it kills application performance and sends service level agreements out the window.

So for Mext's tech to work, it needed to ensure that any pages offloaded to storage were back in DRAM before they're needed. Kind of like running an errand in the middle of the workday – so long as you're back before your boss needs you again, they'll never know you left your desk.
The problem was that the "R" in DRAM stands for random. Predicting which pages the system was going to need at which time isn't exactly trivial. The solution? (Brace for it.)

"We realized we could use AI to monitor the system and proactively push those pages back into DRAM, so that as far as the application or the operating system knew, they were there the whole time," Smerdon said. In other words: "We transparently make flash appear as DRAM."
So, "instead of buying two terabytes of DRAM for your Epyc-based server, you could buy one terabyte of DRAM, and then the next terabyte comes with Mext."
To do this, AMD’s Mext employs a number of machine learning algorithms.

"The workhorse model is a transformer derivative model, just like ChatGPT or Claude or the other famous models, but instead of predicting, for example, in the case of text, what word is next, what we're doing is predicting what page of memory is going to be required next," Smerdon explained. So long as the pages are in DRAM before they're needed, the pages don't even need to be in the right order, he added.
Training the models to predict memory access patterns accurately presents its own challenges, which, Smerdon says, makes pre-training the models impractical.

Instead, they take a single Epyc core and train the model "in under one second," he explained. From there, the model is further refined and retrained over time until it is able to predict accurately where the pages need to be and when they need to be there.
All of this training, he emphasizes, takes place on the CPU core — no GPU required, which means essentially any Epyc customer can take advantage of the software platform.

While no GPU may be required, it's worth noting that in virtualized environments, the software requires one core per VM or VPC, so the overhead scales with virtualization. Container runtimes presumably don't suffer from this same limitation. We've reached out to AMD for clarification.
99 percent of the perf, half the DRAM

According to AMD, the technology actually works. Initially, Smerdon says, the company targeted memory-hungry applications like electronic design automation (EDA) and content creation, but later expanded to support latency-sensitive applications like databases and agentic AI pipelines.
"When pages of memory are cold, we can push them off to flash, and there's literally no impact on performance," he said.
Smerdon is overstating things just a little here. Depending on the application and how much memory is offloaded to flash, there is a performance penalty.

According to tests against Synopsys' PrimeTime EDA suite, he claims, half the memory can be offloaded to flash using Mext and the system still achieves 95 percent of the performance of DRAM. With 25 percent DRAM and 75 percent flash, performance fell to 80 percent of the DRAM-only baseline in AMD's tests.

EDA tools are extremely memory-hungry, but the amount of data the cores are working on at any given moment is often measured in megabytes. This is why AMD's Epyc X-chips remain so popular with EDA customers and why Mext targeted it initially.
In other scenarios, like Apache Spark, AMD's Mext team says it is seeing 99 percent of the performance even after replacing half the DRAM in the system with flash.

While implementing the tech may cost some performance, AMD is betting that customers will be willing to make that compromise in exchange for substantial DRAM savings, as memory remains constrained thanks to the AI datacenter buildout.

Right now, AMD is working to integrate Mext into its broader enterprise portfolio. The software, we're told, will be exclusive to AMD hardware and will be offered as a license sold through OEM partners.

Systems running Linux require only a kernel driver to take advantage of the software, while a separate RAM View application is being offered to help enterprises understand which systems and workloads it should be enabled on.

The chip designer says it's currently in the first phase of its Mext rollout, which means working with OEMs like HPE to ensure systems are so-called "Mext ready." In the second phase, the company aims to begin selling licenses for the software and shipping Epyc platforms with RAM View preinstalled.®

2337d68ee0356b89: The UK government talks a good game about buying British, but less than £1 in every £6 spent with its biggest technology suppliers goes to British firms, according to research exposing how much Whitehall relies on foreign tech.

A report from the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) found that while 42.5 percent of spending with the public sector's 150 largest technology suppliers appears to go to UK companies, that figure collapses to just 15.4 percent once you look beyond where those businesses happen to be headquartered.
A UK headquarters doesn't necessarily make a company British. Some are owned from overseas, others have most of their staff abroad, and many simply resell technology from US giants such as Microsoft.

In fact, 43 percent of the spending attributed to UK-headquartered suppliers goes to resellers. Bytes and Softcat alone account for around £2 billion, making them two of the three biggest recipients of public sector technology spending.

Once researchers traced reseller contracts back to the companies behind the products, the US emerged as the biggest beneficiary, accounting for £9.2 billion of the £19.2 billion spent with the largest suppliers.

And the money isn't exactly being spread around. Just 150 companies receive 83 percent of public sector technology spending, with the largest 15 accounting for almost half. Smaller suppliers aren't getting much of a look-in either, receiving just 12 percent of government technology spending compared with 27 percent of spending across government as a whole.

Competition is another concern. According to IPPR, 89.9 percent of government IT contracts over the past 12 months had no published record of how many suppliers bid for the work, making it difficult to assess how competitive those procurements were.

Things get murkier when AI enters the picture, naturally. Government spending records show relatively little money going directly to the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic, but that doesn't mean Whitehall isn't buying their technology. Much of it is bundled into existing cloud agreements, enterprise software licenses, and partnerships.

One example is NHS England's rollout of Microsoft 365 Copilot to 505,000 staff, which IPPR says was carried out under a national licensing agreement signed in June 2023, before Copilot was even generally available.

That means AI tools can reach hundreds of thousands of public sector workers through deals negotiated before those products were on the market, potentially leaving rival suppliers without an opportunity to compete.

The report, Locked In: A Realist's Agenda for Digital Sovereignty, warns that Britain's dependence on American technology could become particularly troublesome if Washington restricts access to advanced AI systems. It points to recent US restrictions on Anthropic models and limits on early access for Britain's AI Security Institute as evidence that such concerns are no longer entirely hypothetical.
The government has already committed £500 million to a Sovereign AI Fund, but researchers reckon throwing money at homegrown technology companies won't be enough to loosen Silicon Valley's grip.

Instead, they want Whitehall to negotiate technology contracts as a single customer, make it easier to switch suppliers, and work with countries including France, Germany, Japan, and South Korea to secure access to advanced AI.

Roa Powell, senior research fellow at IPPR, said: "But we cannot do it alone, and building domestic capability can't be our only bet. The UK should be working with other middle powers, pooling our buying power to shape markets and using shared leverage to secure access to frontier AI."
Darren Jones MP, who wrote the report's foreword, made a similar argument, saying Britain should work with international allies rather than attempting to build everything itself.

"We can change how the state buys technology, back industries where the UK has a genuine opportunity to lead the world, and shape markets – but we can't go it alone. We need to join with natural allies like France, Germany, Japan and Korea and make ourselves indispensable together," he said.

Whitehall might have grand plans for digital sovereignty, but it's going to be a tough sell when so much of its technology comes from across the Atlantic. And with AI already bundled into software contracts worth billions, US tech giants aren't making it easy for the government to shop elsewhere. ®

86393ff07c7e1bde: The world cannot build prosperous economies, peaceful societies or resilient democracies while neglecting its people’s everyday justice needs.
Originally published on Global Voices
Image courtesy HiiL

This post by Jude Udo Ilo is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Imagine visiting a hospital with a serious illness, only to discover that every patient receives the same medication, regardless of their symptoms. We would rightly call this a failure of healthcare. Yet this is remarkably close to how justice is delivered in much of the world.

We have built justice systems around institutions rather than people, procedures rather than problems, and legal traditions rather than lived realities. We measure progress by the number of courts constructed, judges appointed and laws enacted, while paying insufficient attention to whether ordinary people can actually resolve the disputes disrupting their lives.

This institutional obsession reflects a deeper failure in how we understand development. Justice is not simply a legal service or a moral aspiration. It is essential for economic and social infrastructure. Our collective failure to treat it as such is undermining development, deepening inequality and threatening global stability. With the level of discontent across the world, distrust in institutions, poverty and inequality, and growing footprints of violent conflict, we need to refocus on what is necessary to heal our bleeding world.
The missing infrastructure of development

When governments and international financial institutions discuss infrastructure, the conversation invariably turns to roads, bridges, electricity and digital connectivity. These investments matter. But what happens when a highway project becomes trapped in unresolved land disputes; when a small business cannot recover payments from a supplier? When a woman cannot claim her inheritance, or communities cannot secure remedies for environmental destruction?

Physical infrastructure cannot deliver its promised benefits when the institutions and mechanisms for resolving grievances are inaccessible, ineffective or distrusted. Justice is the soft infrastructure that allows economies and societies to function.

For businesses, it provides the certainty necessary for investment, contract enforcement and growth. For individuals, it protects rights, livelihoods and opportunities. For communities, it creates peaceful pathways for addressing grievances before they escalate into confrontation.

Without functioning justice systems, economic development becomes fragile and social stability increasingly precarious. The World Justice Project estimates that the economic costs of legal problems, including lost income, health impacts and expenses of seeking resolution, average 1.7 percent of GDP across the countries studied.

The scale of the problem is staggering. The Justice for All report estimates that 5.2 billion people lack meaningful access to justice. HiiL's research demonstrates that everyday legal problems are widespread, while effective, satisfactory resolutions remain elusive. This is a crisis of development.
When injustice becomes insecurity
Across the world, unresolved grievances are quietly eroding the foundations of social cohesion.

In parts of Africa, disputes over land ownership, natural resources and community rights have contributed to recurring tensions. In fragile and conflict-affected societies, the absence of credible mechanisms for resolving grievances can deepen mistrust and reinforce cycles of violence.

But justice failures are hardly confined to developing countries. From housing disputes and discriminatory employment practices to unequal access to legal representation, even wealthy democracies struggle to ensure that justice works for everyone.

The consequences extend beyond those directly affected. When people repeatedly encounter institutions that cannot protect their rights or resolve their problems, confidence in public authority deteriorates. When people encounter injustice, they can easily become the enemy of the state. And where legitimate institutions fail, alternative systems of enforcement emerge. Sometimes these are constructive community mechanisms. At other times, they involve coercion, exploitation or violence. We cannot sustainably address insecurity while ignoring the injustices that help fuel it.

This should fundamentally change how governments approach peacebuilding and security. Military and policing investments may respond to immediate threats, but accessible justice can help address grievances before they become security crises.
Justice should therefore be understood as preventive infrastructure, not merely a mechanism for responding to wrongdoing after it occurs.
What the evidence tells us

Fortunately, evidence from across HiiL’s global operations demonstrates how people-centred approaches are transforming the design and delivery of justice services. Rather than relying solely on formal courtrooms or conventional approaches to conflict resolution, community-led initiatives and alternative justice pathways are meeting people where their disputes actually occur.

In Kenya, research informed the Judiciary’s Social Transformation through Access to Justice (STAJ) Blueprint. The Alternative Justice Systems (AJS) centres in Kenya are resolving family, land and other disputes locally, thereby preserving community cohesion. In Ethiopia, government-led community justice centers bridge formal laws and customary traditions to deliver rapid, reconciliation-focused resolution. In Nigeria, pilot community justice centers and domestic violence one-stop shops in Imo and Ogun States provide scalable, data-driven dispute resolution. In Tunisia, digital platforms co-developed for employment disputes directly connect workers, employers, and inspectors to resolve conflicts before they escalate.
Instead of assuming what institutions need, the question is: What justice problems do people actually experience, and what would help resolve them fairly?

Through Justice Needs and Satisfaction (JNS) surveys, we gather data on everyday legal experiences rather than institutional outputs. The data consistently reveal a significant disconnect between supply and demand. In Tunisia, we found that nearly one in three adults experiences a legal problem annually, yet only a fraction reach formal courts. Similarly, research in Nigeria highlights widespread justice needs alongside heavy reliance on community and informal mechanisms. These insights expose the core limitation of traditional justice reform: expanding court capacity alone cannot solve the problem. People facing family, land, employment, or commercial disputes rarely seek lengthy litigation. They need solutions that are fair, accessible, affordable, and timely.

Similar approaches are yielding results. In Bangladesh, a government-led initiative has strengthened village courts, enabling rural communities to resolve minor disputes locally, more quickly and affordably. These courts resolved over 82 percent of reported cases in an average of 25 days, at an average cost of just USD 2.70 to users. In Canada, the Indigenous Justice Program supports community-based initiatives that involve Indigenous communities in designing and delivering culturally appropriate justice services, reflecting their needs and traditions. In Colombia, Houses of Justice bring together formal and informal justice services, providing communities with access to legal information, mediation and dispute resolution through integrated service centres. These examples illustrate how justice services can be brought closer to people and organised around different pathways to better respond to their needs.

This does not make courts obsolete; rather, it underscores that formal courts are only one component of a healthy justice ecosystem. To truly serve society, functional justice infrastructure must integrate formal institutions with trusted community mechanisms, mediation, legal support, and innovative services.
From justice reform to justice investment
If justice is infrastructure, we must fundamentally rethink how we finance, govern and deliver it.

First, governments must stop treating justice as the Ministry of Justice's exclusive responsibility. Economic planners, finance ministries, development institutions, businesses and peacebuilding organisations all have a stake in effective dispute resolution.

Second, justice investments must be guided by evidence about people's needs and outcomes. HiiL's Delivering Justice, Rigorously framework emphasises data, evidence-based practices, scalable services, enabling environments, and accountability.

Third, we must move beyond endless small-scale pilots towards financing solutions that demonstrate results and can reach entire populations. The Justice Financing Framework developed under the Justice Action Coalition offers important proposals for making people-centred justice services financially sustainable.

Finally, justice must become integral to development financing. International financial institutions and development partners should recognize that investments in agriculture, infrastructure, entrepreneurship, gender equality and peacebuilding depend partly on people’s ability to resolve disputes fairly and the credibility of the entire justice system. This is not an argument for diverting resources from development priorities. It is an argument for making those investments more effective and sustainable.
The foundation we cannot afford to ignore

The world faces intersecting crises of inequality, economic uncertainty, democratic distrust and violent conflict. Governments are searching for ways to build more resilient societies, yet one of the most important foundations of resilience remains chronically neglected.
Justice cannot continue to be treated as an institutional afterthought.

A society is not resilient simply because it has strong borders, modern highways or growing financial markets. It is resilient when people trust that grievances can be addressed fairly, rights can be protected, and conflicts can be resolved without violence.

The question is no longer whether we can afford to invest in people-centred justice. It is whether we can afford the economic, social and political consequences of failing to do so. This spotlight provides the argument for the justice case, evidence of what is working and a roadmap of what we must do to make justice work for our societies.
Udo Jude Ilo is the CEO of the Hague Institute for Innovation of Law.
Written by Guest Contributor

14528c1993996feb: NEW YORK, Nov 11 — Anthropic plans to raise up to US$64 billion (RM260.8 billion) in its upcoming initial public offering, the artificial intelligence giant said in a filing yesterday, in a listing that could value the company at up to US$1.4 trillion.
The stock market debut will be the first by one of the leading AI model developers and is being seen as a gauge of how long the AI spending boom lifting the US economy can last.

The maker of the Claude AI models said in a filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission that it aims to sell 825 million shares at between US$70 and US$78 each. The shares will trade under the ticker “ANT.”
Seven tech companies including Google, Nvidia, AMD and Microsoft have also agreed to buy US$26 billion of non-voting shares at the IPO price in a separate private placement, the filing showed.
The companies are investors in Anthropic or major suppliers of its computing power.
Anthropic had been expected to raise up to US$100 billion, which would have made it the largest IPO on record.
Even at the top of its price range, the offering would fall short of the record set by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which raised US$86 billion in its June IPO at a valuation of US$1.77 trillion.
Anthropic has been aiming to go public the week of November 16, and reports said its shares would begin trading on November 19.

Anthropic’s listing is “just another chapter” in investors’ worries over the cost of the AI buildout and how it gets financed, Art Hogan, chief market strategist at B. Riley Wealth Management, told AFP.

“But at the end of the day, I think there are three massive companies that investors have wanted to be part of for the last three years and that’s SpaceX for sure, Anthropic is next, and perhaps next year OpenAI,” he said.

The listing comes as Wall Street digests the results of the US midterm elections, in which Democrats, who are more wary of AI, won control of both chambers of Congress and have vowed to put the brakes on President Donald Trump’s agenda.
The slide has brought volatility to shares of companies linked to the AI boom, with AI chip-maker Nvidia particularly in focus after chief executive Jensen Huang was caught up in a spy scandal.
‘Catastrophic risks’
The company’s revenue reached US$17 billion in the third quarter, up from US$1.4 billion a year earlier, according to the filing.

Its annualised run-rate revenue was about US$81 billion as of October 31, up US$10 billion from the end of September, the company said. This figure describes how much the company expects in a year based on current revenue.
Estimates in recent months had put Anthropic’s valuation as high as US$2 trillion, but they have slipped along with a slide in AI stocks on Wall Street.

Anthropic’s IPO filing devotes extensive space to the technology’s risks, including concerns that advanced AI systems “could pose catastrophic or existential risks to society if not developed and deployed responsibly.”
The company also warns that its public positions on AI regulation and safety could expose it to “political backlash, or disproportionate regulatory action.”
This referred to feuds with the Trump White House. The Pentagon has labeled Anthropic a national security risk after the company refused to lift restrictions on military use of its technology.

Its stratospheric costs have also been underlined, with Anthropic committing hundreds of billions of dollars to computing capacity. It warned that it must make many of those payments even if demand falls short.

Under the governance structure laid out in the filings, the seven co-founders, led by chief executive Dario Amodei and his sister, president Daniela Amodei, will keep just over half of shareholder votes after the listing, so outside investors cannot outvote them. — AFP

“A stronger and more resilient grid also enables TNB to support new economic opportunities, including in digitalisation and industrial growth, through initiatives such as the Green Lane Pathway,” he said.
This initiative accelerates grid connections for eligible data centres without compromising supply reliability or engineering standards.
Beyond Malaysia, these investments further reinforce the nation’s role in the ASEAN Power Grid, contributing to greater regional energy security, connectivity and collaboration, said Shamsul.
Ultimately, grid readiness creates economic certainty, he said.
“By investing ahead of the curve, TNB is ensuring our power infrastructure actively catalyses new investment and long-term national progress,” he added. — Bernama
