e20c3ab504db66f9: BEIJING: If you are looking for evidence of how enthusiastically China is adopting AI, look no further than the country's premier month-long Singles Day shopping festival.

Shopping via chatbots that recommend, direct and complete purchases is on the rise, AI-enabled devices such as toys and robots are being heavily promoted and consumers are snapping up bundles of AI tokens — units of computing that people buy to use AI models.
For e-commerce firms such as Alibaba 9988.HK, JD.com 9618.HK and PDD Holdings PDD.O, artificial intelligence has offered a new way to keep cautious consumers engaged amid fierce competition.
For example, Alibaba platforms — Tmall for established brands and Taobao for a wider range of merchants — offer AI-driven research, virtual try-ons of clothing and tools to help users find discounts.

On short video and social commerce platform Douyin, AI drove roughly 5% of purchases through chatbot links in October, according to data from WPIC Marketing + Technologies. For considered purchases such as supplements, that share exceeded 20%.

"This is still a very new gateway and discovery channel," Jacob Cooke, chief executive of the research firm, said. "I expect it to account for a growing share of direct purchases, comparable to livestreaming or social commerce."
Whether AI has excited consumers sufficiently to boost overall spending, however, remains to be seen.
"Some brands benefit more based on how the platforms are tuned or how the brands are pricing their products," said Ben Cavender, managing director at Shanghai-based China Market Research Group.
But brands can also be hurt "if they are no longer showing up in product searches because the consumer is defaulting to letting an AI assistant do the 'shopping'," he added.
Sales for Singles Day climbed 2.4% between October 7 and October 31, according to third-party data platform Syntun, which will provide an updated figure for the entire event on Thursday.
Singles Day started out as a one-day event but has morphed into month-long festival with discounts galore, albeit with different start dates for different platforms.
The 2.4% figure compares with a 1.1% rise in China's retail sales for the year through to end-September.

AI has become much more embedded in the Chinese shopping experience than in Western markets due to the dominance of super apps. Their AI agents can conduct research, complete transactions, apply coupons and schedule deliveries without the shopper ever having to use a separate app.
Researching specific requirements is also now much easier.

A shopper can ask a chatbot to find a washing machine suitable for a narrow balcony and quiet nighttime use within a specific budget, said Liu Xingliang, a Beijing-based independent technology analyst.
JD.com said its AI shopping assistant, Dongdong, drew nearly 80 million users seeking advice for this year's Singles Day festival, more than triple last year's users.

AI devices are also growing in popularity. AI toys surpassed 100 million yuan (US$15 million) in sales on Alibaba's platforms within one year of launching as a new category, the e-commerce giant said.
One such product is Dr. Look's AI learning camera, which allows children to take a picture of, say, a leaf or an insect, which the camera identifies and then explains its characteristics.
Sales of AI companion robots rose nearly fivefold year-on-year in the second half of October, Alibaba also said, without disclosing how many were sold.

Tmall said sales of AI tokens rose more than 700% between October 15 and November 5, compared with the period from September 15 to October 5. Top livestreamer Austin Li featured AI products for the first time, selling 100,000 monthly subscriptions to Alibaba's QwenWork within 30 minutes.
For some shoppers, AI tools have already become a natural part of buying online.
Amanda Gao, a 40-year-old office worker in Beijing, said she uses Taobao's AI virtual try-on feature whenever she shops for clothes. "I find the function useful and fun," she said.
8c05635dbbc36d55: The transition to electric vehicles should be moving apace, but it is not. And why? Incompetence, expedience and cowardice This is how it works. An industry puts tremendous effort into resisting change: lobbying governments, mobilising the media, pouring money into junktanks. It argues that a transition would threaten jobs, or damage the national interest, or harm poor people, while what it really fears is the cost of retooling its plants or developing new protocols. Then, when the inevitable cliff edge approaches, it whines that change is coming too soon. For reasons beyond its control, it isn’t ready, so the government must delay its plans. This is what triggered the Dutch nitrate crisis, and the UK’s repeated “emergency” exemptions from the ban on a devastating class of pesticides. Now the same dynamic is driving the UK’s crisis over the transition to electric vehicles (EVs). The result is that, as the global climate summit, Cop31, begins, it looks as if our gift to the world will be a major, predictable and entirely avoidable increase in the UK’s greenhouse gas emissions. George Monbiot is a Guardian columnist Continue reading...
6a831db7f7ac5101: BEIJING, Nov 11 — Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang’s relationship with a Chinese businesswoman suspected by US authorities of having links to Beijing’s intelligence services helped facilitate at least US$7.5 billion (RM30.4 billion) in chip shipments to China, according to a report that has intensified scrutiny of the company’s export controls and corporate governance.

US technology news publication The Information reported yesterday, citing two people familiar with Alice Huang, that she had used her connections to Nvidia and its distributors to secure supplies of advanced processors for Chinese companies.
The allegations raise questions about whether Nvidia’s distribution network allowed customers to obtain technology subject to Washington’s restrictions on semiconductor exports to China.
According to Reuters, Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, worked with her husband and sister to establish a network of companies across China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia processors.

Central to the arrangement was Shanghai Century Litong, a Chinese company established in June 2023 that secured preferred cloud partner status with Nvidia four months later, giving it priority access to the chipmaker’s products.
When orders involving export-restricted processors stalled, Alice Huang allegedly drew on her industry connections to obtain supplies.

The network reportedly facilitated shipments of approximately 240,000 H100, H200 and A100 chips to China, some of which ultimately served technology groups Alibaba and Tencent, as well as smaller Chinese artificial intelligence laboratories.

The reported shipments have added to concerns about the effectiveness of US export controls, introduced to limit China’s access to advanced semiconductors capable of powering sophisticated AI systems.
Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed International, in which Alice Huang became the controlling shareholder, has also attracted scrutiny.

The Financial Times reported that several US government agencies had sought to add Megaspeed to Washington’s trade blacklist over national security concerns, but the Commerce Department had delayed the process.
The reasons for the delay remain unclear.
Reuters said it could not independently verify the reports. China’s foreign ministry has rejected allegations that Alice Huang was involved in espionage as “groundless”.
Nvidia has said its board has no reason to believe US national security or company secrets were compromised.
The allegations have nevertheless prompted calls for greater oversight of the company and its leadership.
Republican Senator Kevin Cramer has urged Huang to resign, citing concerns about potential foreign intelligence exploitation.
“The potential for extortion is so tremendous that something as sensitive as Nvidia chips, I just think he’s got to go,” Cramer told Politico.
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer has meanwhile called for tighter restrictions on semiconductor exports to China.
Nvidia’s independent directors have appointed outside legal counsel to investigate the matter, while the FBI is separately examining whether Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation.
Huang, 63, has acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife but has not disclosed details of the relationship.

The controversy has also unsettled investors. Nvidia lost approximately US$430 billion in market capitalisation over two trading sessions, with shares falling 9.5 per cent since the affair became public, according to Reuters.
f71d238cb182a978: In 2019, OpenAI decided not to publicly release a new model because its research uncovered “concerns about malicious applications of the technology.” And on Tuesday, the company announced it has built a kill switch for the models deployed in its research labs, months after some of them displayed disturbing behavior.

“As our models get more powerful and the associated safety and security risks become bigger, it becomes more and more critical that we can detect potential issues, and quickly stop models in their tracks when needed,” OpenAI explains in a Tuesday post.

The company named the kill switch “Control Room” and described it as “a central system to track model workloads across our research infrastructure and stop them quickly when safety or security concerns arise.”
The facility can apparently stop models from producing any output 35 seconds after a decision to pull the plug – and can go faster.

“The 35-second lag comes from a caching layer for inference authorization, to support the required volume of traffic. We are working to drive this number down to zero so that we can end jobs instantly,” the company promises.

A rookie mistake in critical infrastructure design is to build both production and resilience tools on shared resources that could be taken offline by a single incident. OpenAI seems conscious of that risk, because it says the tool “has been built to keep working even when other systems fail, and to stop model output if Control Room itself goes down.”
OpenAI hasn’t explained why it took so long to build a kill switch or why it decided now is the moment when it needs one.

The Register fancies recent examples of agents exceeding their brief in worrying ways – like attacking Hugging Face, causing trouble at the Wikimedia Foundation, or going a little too deep when researching Australian healthcare data – may have influenced the timing of this development.

“Control Room is already deployed across our research infrastructure, where the need is greatest,” the company’s announcement states. “Our external model-serving stack is already much more centralized by nature, with a well-developed operational capability to quickly take down model deployments if needed.”
OpenAI says it plans to “strengthen and expand the system over the coming months, alongside our investments in monitoring for misaligned behavior and security breaches.”

That’s a variant of Big Tech’s usual “We’re sorry and we promise to do better in future” proclamation that follows the latest SNAFU. Yet back in 2019, OpenAI pulled the pin before matters ever reached that state. ®

a5614e5197317cdf: NEW DELHI: India’s airlines operated fewer routes during the peak Diwali travel season, signalling that rising costs and operational disruptions are beginning to cool momentum in one of the world’s fastest growing aviation markets.

Airlines scheduled about 6% fewer flights across October and November than a year earlier, according to data from aviation analytics firm Cirium. That marks the first capacity decline since 2020, when carriers slashed service capacity by nearly 45% amid the pandemic-induced collapse in travel demand.

The pullback comes as India’s aviation sector shows signs of strain as capacity reduction pushes fares up. While domestic passenger traffic had already declined 6.5% in September, festive-season fares on some routes surged to levels where one-way tickets cost as much as round-trip journeys did a year ago - putting air travel out of reach of consumers.

Dinesh Sharma, a 28-year-old marketing professional in Hyderabad, said that despite booking his Diwali travel months in advance, he still couldn’t find an affordable ticket back home to Siliguri in the state of West Bengal.
“One-way fares had crossed 20,000 rupees (US$213), roughly what I would normally pay for a round trip,” he said.

Airlines say demand remains resilient but acknowledged passengers are bearing the burden of higher costs. Speaking on an earnings call last month, IndiGo CEO Willie Walsh said demand had held up “reasonably well,” while noting that airlines had to balance affordability with financial stability.

IndiGo, India’s largest carrier, reduced capacity by 1% and carried 4.5% fewer passengers during the quarter ended September. Despite a more than 34% increase in passenger yields, the airline reported a loss of 18.8 billion rupees during the period as its fuel bill jumped 67%.

The surge in fares reflects mounting pressure on airlines’ cost structures. Indian carriers are being squeezed by a combination of higher fuel prices, a weaker rupee and longer international flight paths caused by airspace restrictions, according to Ajay Prakash, chief executive of Mumbai-based travel agency Nomad Travels.
“Even though this is the festive season, I suppose it’s a question of surviving,” he said. Airlines have had to “rationalize their schedules, cut back wherever they can,” he said.
9b37705e7e7accfe: Australia’s government will consider creating a new criminal offense to punish AI companies which knowingly release harmful models.

Canberra dangled that possibility yesterday when releasing the results of an investigation into OpenAI’s admission that its agents accessed non-public medical records – and that it didn’t disclose the incident for weeks.

Security at the agency which held those records fell short of contemporary best practice but Canberra nonetheless ordered a rapid review into Australia’s ability to handle infosec incidents involving AI.

That review landed yesterday, complete with 18 recommendations including one that would make it mandatory for AI companies to report misaligned behavior or security incidents involving their models, and perhaps impose criminal penalties for “egregious regulatory non-compliance.”

Another recommendation calls for consideration of “A standalone ‘failure to prevent’ offence which would criminalize instances where the company is responsible for developing an AI model that engages in harmful conduct, and the company fails to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm.”
The review suggests two ministries and Australia’s Federal Police consider those reforms, meaning this is not something that will happen in a hurry, if at all, for a couple of reasons.
One is that Australia yesterday proposed a new regulator which will require AI players to do six things:
Maintain security controls across all stages of development and deployment
Identify and manage serious risks associated with their models
Allow independent evaluation of their models
Provide mandatory notification of incidents to the Australian Government rapidly
Maintain and publish safety and security frameworks to ensure good governance, risk management and transparency
Respond to updated standards and rules as technologies change.
If AI companies straighten up and fly right, Canberra might not need to do more.
The other reason Australia might not criminalize AI is economic pragmatism.

Canberra wants to ensure leading AI companies invest in local datacenters, especially facilities where they train and run frontier models. Such investments would mean Australia scores some of the AI boom cash sloshing around the world, while also giving the government the ability to at least point to leading-edge AI running on local shores and therefore theoretically remaining accessible even if war or a diplomatic rupture makes it hard to access advanced AI hosted offshore.

Other nations in Asia, such as South Korea and India, are addressing those risks by building substantial sovereign infrastructure and working to develop sovereign frontier-class models trained on local data and especially data in their local languages.

Canberra can’t match that investment without pouring petrol on its raging inflation problem. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is therefore instead trying to regulate AI without scaring away investment.
Threatening to lock up AI executives is not likely to make them enthusiastic when asked to approve building datacenters down under.
Some sections of Australia’s population won’t mind it if big tech doesn’t show up: Protests against datacenters are already widespread.

Your correspondent recently spoke to the organizer of a protest group opposed to development of a new datacenter which is just three kilometers from four existing bit barns, one of which abuts a sizable apartment complex and has operated without incident or opposition for years. The organizer was blissfully ignorant of those facilities and eventually said their group is opposed to AI in all forms. ®

470fcb377593fa61: From Azam Mohd
Melaka’s new political understanding offers a revealing experiment: can parties cooperate without asking citizens to surrender the right to question them?

The BN–PAS arrangement, described as tafahum siyasi, is significant not because former rivals can share a platform, but because it tests whether political reconciliation can accommodate disagreement, scrutiny and plural representation.

On Oct 21, Barisan Nasional chairman Ahmad Zahid Hamidi announced an understanding under which BN would contest 21 of Melaka’s 28 constituencies, with seven allocated to PAS and its partners. By nomination day, however, the reported arrangement had changed: BN was contesting 23 seats and Perikatan Nasional five.
That revision matters. Negotiated formulas reflect political intentions; the actual ballot determines the choices voters face.

Melaka BN chief Ab Rauf Yusoh subsequently described PAS as a strategic partner and said the parties would coordinate their campaigns and share a manifesto. PAS president Abdul Hadi Awang has indicated that cooperation could extend beyond Melaka.
These statements point to an evolving political relationship, not a binding prediction about future governments or voter behaviour.

The more interesting issue is the meaning of understanding itself. "Tafahum" suggests a willingness to acknowledge differences while finding common ground. In a diverse federation, that can be constructive.
Consent of the governed
Yet political accommodation becomes fragile when leaders mistake agreement among elites for consent among citizens.
Malay political cooperation and Malaysia’s multiracial constitutional character need not conflict, but their compatibility must be demonstrated through policies and conduct.

Consider representation. BN includes component parties whose constituencies and organisational histories differ from those of PAS. A shared campaign must explain how minority interests, religious freedom, education and local economic concerns will be addressed, without assuming that a joint platform erases substantive disagreements.
Equally, voters sympathetic to PAS deserve clarity about which proposals remain party positions and which commitments have been accepted by all partners.

A joint manifesto creates an opportunity to answer those questions. It should identify priorities that can be implemented within state powers, distinguish them from federal responsibilities and specify how competing proposals would be reconciled.
Without such clarity, a manifesto risks becoming a catalogue of agreeable aspirations, with contradictions emerging only after polling.
State and federal ties

There is also a federal dimension. BN participates in the national unity government alongside Pakatan Harapan, while its cooperation in Melaka involves parties associated with the parliamentary opposition.
Such asymmetry is neither inherently unlawful nor unprecedented in coalition politics. Nevertheless, it complicates public understanding of accountability.

Leaders should explain whether state-level cooperation changes their federal commitments and where the boundaries between electoral partnerships and governmental responsibilities lie. This question cannot be answered through rhetoric about loyalty alone.

State administrations make decisions affecting land use, investment approvals, local infrastructure and public services. Business confidence depends less on displays of unity than on whether policies remain clear and decisions can be challenged through established institutions.
Keeping spotlight on
There is no available evidence to establish that this electoral understanding has already changed investment outcomes; that would require separate analysis.

For Pakatan Harapan and other competitors, the appropriate response is substantive scrutiny rather than assuming that cooperation proves ideological inconsistency. Parties routinely negotiate across previous divisions.

What matters democratically is whether voters receive accurate explanations of those negotiations and meaningful policy alternatives. Criticism should focus on documented commitments, not speculative claims about hidden intentions.

The outcome of the Nov 14 election will reveal the choices made by voters, but not necessarily why each choice was made. Turnout, candidates, local grievances and broader party loyalties all interact. Claims that a new Malay consensus has emerged require evidence beyond leadership appearances and seat allocations.
Three questions
Electoral results should be interpreted cautiously, especially when several political relationships are changing simultaneously.

My assessment is that Melaka’s experiment should be measured against three questions: Are shared commitments sufficiently precise to be evaluated? Can participating parties disagree openly without paralysing the administration? And will citizens outside the parties’ principal constituencies enjoy equal access to representation and public services?
That obligation extends to opposition scrutiny, legislative debate and the independence of public institutions.
Political understanding acquires democratic meaning when it protects disagreement as well as cooperation.
Beyond Melaka, BN and PAS face a continuing choice between treating tafahum siyasi as a temporary arrangement among leaders and developing transparent principles that voters can examine.
Malaysia’s political maturity depends not on eliminating differences, but on making cooperation accountable to everyone affected by it.

54a5997f5a41934c: NEW YORK, Nov 11 — US inflation data released yesterday slowed slightly in October but still overshot analyst estimates, raising expectations for further Federal Reserve interest rate hikes.

The consumer price index for October rose 0.4 per cent from September, down from the prior month’s 0.6 per cent increase, according to Labor Department data. Analysts had projected a 0.3 per cent increase.

The improvement from the prior month reflected a significant moderation in energy price increases from September. The prior CPI report had shown the effects of a big jump in fuel prices following renewed clashes in the US-Iran war over the summer.
But food prices shot higher in October, along with medical care, household furnishings and several other categories.
The report follows last week’s US midterm elections in which voters turned sharply against President Donald Trump’s Republican Party in part due to persistent inflation.

The Labor Department was unable to translate the figures into a year-over-year number because there was no report in October 2025 due to a government shutdown. But the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland estimated the jump as 3.8 per cent, well above the Fed’s 2 per cent target.
The report “sets the stage for a December Fed hike,” read the headline on a note from Oxford Economics.
“Though energy prices moderated as expected, it was food inflation that drove the forecast miss of last month’s headline CPI,” Oxford Economics said in the note.
“Grocery-store inflation accelerated notably after a string of quiescent readings, underscoring the lags between energy price shocks and nonenergy consumer prices.”
Price hikes for energy slowed significantly compared with the prior report, with the gasoline index rising 1 per cent — far below the 9.1 per cent spike in September from August.
The index for food rose 0.5 per cent in October after being unchanged in September.
‘Supersize’ rate hike?

Joseph Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM, said the inflation report could keep a “supersize hike on the table at the December Fed meeting,” alluding to comments earlier yesterday from Fed Governor Christopher Waller.

“In my estimation this requires rate hikes by the Fed and we think that a December rate hike is baked in the cake given that this is the final CPI report that the Fed will get to observe,” Brusuelas said.

Futures markets now see a December rate hike as essentially guaranteed, with 85 per cent of trader bets expecting a one-quarter percentage point hike and 15 predicting a half-percentage point increase.

Earlier yesterday, Waller signalled support for a December rate increase due to persistently elevated inflation, saying the central bank must act “sooner rather than later, to return inflation to a path that will reach 2 per cent in the medium term.”

Waller cited inflationary effects from the artificial intelligence buildout and pointed to Fed research that suggests “energy price pressures may pass through to goods and services in a more sustained way than in the past.”
Speaking a few hours before the CPI release, Waller said he was “leaning towards” a 25 basis point rate hike in December even with an October report showing moderation in pricing pressures.
But if October pricing dynamics are similar to last month’s, “then a stronger policy move may be needed,” he said.

“In that case, I believe a 50-basis point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting,” Waller added. “Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take.”

Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan also strongly endorsed additional rate hikes, citing the data as she urged “prompt” action before persistent inflation “becomes baked into behaviour,” she said in a speech late Tuesday morning.
Logan estimated that the Fed funds rate must rise by “at least 50 basis points” in order “to bring the inflation trend back to target,” she said.

Logan acknowledged that energy prices have played a role, but described inflationary trends as “broader than that,” noting that higher prices in categories like visiting the doctor or dining out “aren’t particularly sensitive to tariffs, conflict in the Middle East or surging demand for computer chips.”
“It remains clear to me, given the current outlook, that the FOMC needs to implement at least two more 25-basis-point rate increases,” Logan said. — AFP

1b1e59572933e14d: Citizens in Gabon went 248 days without access to Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, or YouTube
Originally published on Global Voices
Image of a smartphone showing the Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, YouTube, and Messenger apps. Screenshot from the DW Afrique YouTube channel.

After more than eight months of government blockage, Gabon has restored its social media access. But it has come at a cost. This reinstatement comes with a tighter regulatory framework and an unprecedented cooperation between the government and various tech giants, raising serious concerns about freedom of expression and privacy.

On February 17, 2026, Gabon’s media regulator, the High Communication Authority (HAC), suspended major social media networks, including Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube, “until further notice.” According to the regulator, quoted in the daily newspaper L’Essentiel, this measure targeted not only content “undermining national security” but also content involving defamation, cyberbullying, hate speech, and threats to social cohesion.

At first, the suspension had no real impact, with presidential spokesperson Jennyfer Mélodie Sambat claiming it would solely target Meta platforms. However, according to Gabon Media Time, several influencers, content creators, and citizens later experienced access disruptions on YouTube and TikTok, sometimes rendering connections impossible without a bypass tool, such as a virtual private network (VPN).

The global data platform Internet Society Pulse confirmed this observation, revealing major anomalies for Meta, Telegram, TikTok, and YouTube, but not X (formerly Twitter). The online news portal Le360 Afrique consequently reported a surge in VPN usage in the months that followed.
For 248 days, more than 1.84 million individuals, or 71.9 percent of the country’s population of over 2.5 million, were denied regular access to some of the world’s most popular digital platforms.

On October 24, 2026, the HAC lifted this suspension, with Africanews stressing that this ruling didn’t necessarily mean a return to business as usual. It, therefore, remains to be seen whether Gabon, where Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema has been president since September 2023, will restore digital freedoms or establish a new state-controlled online model instead.
From bypassing the suspension to tighter regulatory frameworks

A new legal framework, enacted on February 26, 2026, underpins this reinstatement. According to Gabon Media Time, Ordinance No. 0011/PR/2026 establishes a regulatory framework for digital platform usage, while Ordinance No. 0013/PR/2026 amends the HAC Reorganization Act.

The HAC also invokes a law, enacted on October 5, that ratifies the social media ordinance and establishes a regulatory framework for AI-generated and AI-amplified content, according to reporting by Gabon Review.

What’s more, available data shows that these regulations have introduced joint liability for those who create and share illegal content and require all social media users to provide personal identification information. Purported as tools to combat abuse, these regulations have raised serious concerns about anonymity, personal data protection, and their stifling effect on public debate.
In a country where criticizing public institutions is politically sensitive, the threat of prosecution for posting online could discourage users from expressing dissent.

The issue here isn’t whether the state should combat cyberbullying, disinformation, or hate speech, but rather how. While these are valid concerns, the real worry is whether its measures are transparent, proportionate, and subject to independent scrutiny.
Tech giants enter the regulatory mix

The most decisive development in this saga was undoubtedly the unprecedented cooperation between the government and Big Tech companies. On July 13, 2026, after a meeting at the AI for Good/WSIS summit in Geneva, Gabonese Minister of Digital Economy Mark-Alexandre Doumba announced an agreement with TikTok. Both parties signed a 12-month cooperation agreement, ensuring the platform’s compliance with Gabon’s new regulatory framework.
At the meeting, TikTok presented its Q1 2026 content moderation results, revealing that it had removed more than 23,500 pieces of sensitive content in Gabon.

Meanwhile, the HAC confirmed that it had established an “active cooperation” with TikTok, Meta, and YouTube to “improve content moderation.” The regulator added that, during the suspension, it also held direct discussions with these companies. However, neither the technical details of these exchanges nor the practical operation of the authorities’ reporting tools has been specified.
Find the HAC spokesperson’s full statement here:

These agreements reflect tech companies’ growing influence in digital platform governance. These platforms are also no longer satisfied with merely hosting exchanges between their users; they now shape decisions about what content remains accessible and what does not.

For governments, partnerships with digital platforms provide a direct channel to deal with content they consider harmful, illegal, or threatening to their regime. For tech companies, complying with the state’s requests and distinguishing legitimate moderation from politically motivated censorship poses a significant challenge.
Cooperation is no substitute for transparency
Working alongside digital platforms isn’t inherently problematic. Tech companies ultimately have a responsibility to deal with credible threats, protect vulnerable users, and enforce their own rules.

However, problems arise when the state has direct access to reporting mechanisms — particularly if the public remains unaware of these partnerships. What criteria determine which content is flagged? How are HAC requests processed? Can users challenge a post removal? Are there any safeguards to protect journalists, activists, and government critics?

The line between harmful content and legitimate political expression is often blurred. Without clear procedures, independent monitoring, and an appeals process, critics say these measures risk becoming tools of influence over public debate.

The situation in Gabon represents a much broader trend. As various African states tighten their grip on digital platforms, tech companies face escalating pressure to comply with new national regulations to maintain key market access. The balance of power between governments and tech giants has ultimately become a defining factor in the future of digital rights.
Beyond Gabon: Who is accountable for digital freedom?
Restoring social media access was imperative for Gabonese citizens, journalists, businesspeople, and content creators alike, all of whom suffered under this suspension.

However, access alone doesn’t guarantee freedom. The real test will be whether internet users can participate in online discussions, criticize public policy, and share information without fear of arbitrary sanctions or disproportionate restrictions.

It also depends on Meta, TikTok, and YouTube demonstrating how their cooperation with the Gabonese government complies with international human rights standards, especially freedom of expression, privacy, and access to information.

The current situation in Gabon illustrates how authoritarian control over the digital sphere evolves. Restrictions don’t necessarily end when platform accessibility is restored. Instead, they become regulatory frameworks, personal identification requirements, and tighter government cooperation with private tech companies.

The challenge, therefore, isn’t just about reconnecting citizens to social media, but also about ensuring the digital spaces they return to remain open to criticism, independent information, and public debate.
Although tech giants can negotiate conditions allowing citizens to regain access to digital platforms, they must also ensure those conditions don’t compromise their fundamental freedoms.

60f80913d48f881c: One could be forgiven for thinking the world is hurtling towards an apocalyptic end and that humanity is about to reenact Mad Max, complete with spiked leather jackets and tribal warfare over the last remaining can of baked beans.

This is because more than 30 countries have recently issued “be prepared” warnings, sending preppers – those who prepare for the day when the grid goes down, the shelves go empty, and the world as we know it ends – into another frenzy of stockpiling and repetitions of “I knew it was coming”.

The world has become more dangerous—or at least appears so. With never-ending global conflicts, meteorological tantrums, and the instant, vibrating hum of social media algorithms pinging our dopamine receptors twenty-four hours a day, crises are no longer experienced; they are simulated in our heads before they even happen.

And social media amplifies crises in ways the older generation —who blissfully survived on slow-moving broadsheets and evening radio—never experienced. What once trickled down as boring administrative updates now floods our phones in real-time, inducing a collective, low-grade heart flutter.

When roughly 30 nations update their civil resilience playbooks in the same calendar window, algorithms do what they do best: they hallucinate a conspiracy. Social media sharing stitches these independent notices together into a terrifying mosaic of a coordinated global doom narrative.
Some viral headlines scream that something’s going terribly wrong; others claim governments are secretly preparing us for war and not telling us the whole story.
The world has always had its dangers; the difference today is that mechanisms for broadcasting anxiety have become infinitely more efficient.
The reality, as is so often the case, is wonderfully, boringly mundane.
To understand the October 2026 wave, we must separate routine government weather chores from modern media panic.

Take Malaysia. In late October 2026, the National Disaster Management Agency (Nadma) issued its thoroughly familiar seasonal reminder: citizens should “stock up sensibly” ahead of the northeast monsoon. The call was a practical, sober reminder to prepare for seasonal flooding—a ritual practiced faithfully every year since the 1990s across Southeast Asia.

Yet, this routine tropical memo collided on the calendar with a broader occidental wave, most notably the UK’s newly minted “Be Ready” campaign, launched under Prime Minister Andy Burnham to encourage multi-year resilience against generic short-term infrastructure glitches or cyberattacks.

When a seasonal flood warning in Kuala Lumpur and an all-hazards resilience campaign in London drop in the same fortnight, and more than 30 nations issue similar advisories, digital platforms turn it into a blockbuster movie trailer.
This happened despite every official source emphasizing the same thing: the advice was voluntary, gradual, and completely unrelated to any looming apocalypse.
So why are governments suddenly nagging us about emergency kits? Is the world ending? No. But our infrastructure has quietly evolved.

In the old days, if a local transformer blew out,your neighbourhood went dark, and we used a candle until power was restored. Today, because our banking, logistics, communications, and heating rely on digital infrastructure and interconnected power grids, a minor disruption cascades instantly across sectors.
Governments aren't warning us because war is at the door; they are doing it because hyper-connected societies are inherently fragile to short-term hiccups.

Predictably, human nature did what it always does. In the UK, Malaysia and elsewhere, some took to social media to urge people to stock up on food or actually cleared supermarket shelves of certain items, proving once again that panic is far more infectious than any virus.

They chose to ignore the advice to buy gradually and not panic. So much so that Nadma director-general Meor Ismail Meor Akim felt it necessary to issue a statement saying: “We should avoid such panic-buying messages. Sometimes, panic buying creates another problem, not a northeast monsoon disaster, but a shortage of goods instead. Just buy according to your needs.”
This brings us to the most important distinction of all: the gap between selfish hoarding and civic self-reliance.
When a government tells us to store a 72-hour buffer of water, a torch, and non-perishables, it isn't inviting us to join a doomsday cult. It is an exercise in decentralised pragmatism.

If households are self-sufficient for three days during a sudden power outage or flash flood, it keeps arterial roads uncluttered and emergency phone lines open for people facing actual life-and-death medical emergencies. And for other such emergencies.

An emergency kit isn't a survivalist fetish; it’s an act of civic hygiene. It’s the modern equivalent of bringing your own bucket to a neighbourhood fire instead of standing in the street screaming that the town is cursed.

Ultimately, these advisories don't signal a descent into martial law or long-term catastrophes. They reflect the tedious, necessary business of living in a complex world. Just as learning fire safety or getting vaccinated became the unremarked background noise of twentieth-century life, digital-age resilience is simply the new baseline of modern citizenship.
How should we respond?
We would do well to ignore the merchants of panic—whether they write viral social media threads or sensationalist headlines—and consult sober official sources instead.

By preparing quietly, rationally, and without melodrama, we insulate ourselves against minor tempests while preserving the sanity of the commonwealth at large. After all, if the world truly is coming to an end, panicking in the supermarket checkout queue is a singularly undignified way to greet the final curtain.

d496ec12f3f9f943: Anthropic has introduced three new types of artifacts that show the company tiptoeing into the office productivity market long dominated by Microsoft and Google.

On Tuesday, the Claudefather announced Claude Sheets, Claude Whiteboards, and Claude Data, and promised the imminent arrival of Claude Meetings. These artifact types join existing ones – Docs, Slides, Design, and Motion – to form a nascent Claude-dependent productivity suite.

Anthropic initially used the term artifacts to refer to shareable AI-based interactive tools, like dynamic charts. But the scope of the term has been stretched to cover specific artifact types, which refer to what traditionalists might take to mean files associated with specific hosted applications.
"An artifact is anything Claude makes for you that you'd put in front of someone: a design, a deck, a document, a dashboard, or a small interactive tool," the company explains.

The key thing that distinguishes an artifact from a file is that users are meant to interact with artifacts through Claude, rather than storing and transferring them independently. Think of it more as a container or managed object that opens in Claude (via a sharing URL), because artifacts in fact consist of various content types – .txt, .md, .html, .jsx, .svg, .pptx, .docx, .zip, .pdf, and .mp4, among others.

Anthropic's vision of Claude as a container for other applications goes beyond artifacts. The AI biz has also expanded its interactive connectors, which turn Claude into a landlord for other software applications. Its own promotional video for the feature hammers that point home in its title: "Your apps have moved into Claude."

"Starting today, partners can embed their apps directly in Claude, so you can work in Adobe, Atlassian, and others without switching tabs," Anthropic said. "Plugins from Salesforce (beta), NetSuite, and Workday (beta) come with built-in skills, so sellers can prep for a call, accountants can analyze financial data, and HR teams can handle time off and expenses."

In a prior era, those would be fighting words. Tech companies like Apple, Google, and Microsoft have worked for years to maintain their positions as platform landlords. Anthropic's invitation to become a Claude tenant ought to set off competition alarm bells. But perhaps with LLMs being able to re-create other people's apps on demand, there's less interest in defending app boundaries as if they were moats to keep out rivals. With AI, the call is coming from inside the house.

Alongside the rollout of Claude Sheets, Whiteboards, and Data, Anthropic is pushing the notion that Claude is useful for people working outside of computation and mathematics, the occupational category that, according to the company's own data, accounts for a larger share of Claude usage than any other.
"Inside Anthropic, non-technical teams are starting to get as much out of Claude as our engineers," the biz insists, hauling out canned testimonials from the likes of Accenture and Datadog.
If Anthropic can demonstrate that there's an untapped market of non-coders who would welcome a Claude subscription, investors in the company's pending IPO will be glad to see it. ®

b54179fab9055473: Server consolidation has led Cisco to boost the speed of top-of-rack switches to 100G.
The networking giant last week announced the catchily named N9348C8D-H2, a 1U device packing 48 100G SFP-DD ports and eight 400G QSFP-DD uplinks.

At the Cisco Live event in Melbourne, Australia, this week, Cisco’s senior veep for datacenter and internet infrastructure, Kevin Wollenweber, said one reason the company created the device is that modern servers often feature a pair of fast network interface cards.
The twin cards are needed because sixth-gen server processors from Intel and AMD offer dozens, or even hundreds, of physical processor cores and therefore generate a lot of traffic.

The density of computing power those processors provide has led chipmakers and server manufacturers to suggest replacing handfuls of machines running older, power-guzzling Xeons and Epycs with boxes running more efficient sixth-gen chips.

The Register hears it’s not uncommon to achieve 6:1 server consolidation ratios when moving from third- or fourth-generation Xeons or Epycs to current models. Users who make that move can pack many more server cores into the same rack. Power bills go down, but the quantity of data leaving a rack goes up.
Wollenweber said Cisco realized it had “tons” of switches that offer 25G ports but felt it had a gap in its range for non-AI scenarios like server consolidation that produced increased data flows.

The exec admitted that the 100G ports may be overkill for a modest collection of new servers, but argued users recognize it won’t be long before they grow into the excess capacity – perhaps as they use more agentic AI applications.
Cisco sees traffic from AI agents stressing the north-south connections that link organizations to the cloud and also driving much more east-west traffic across internal networks.
At Cisco Live, the company’s execs suggested that network upgrades are therefore an inevitable necessity.

That’s not entirely self-serving, because agents will vastly outnumber humans and constantly create traffic, compared to the flurries of network activity that happen when humans use generative AI or chatbots.
Cisco argues that deploying agents at scale will therefore only be possible on highly automated networks.
“Humans can no longer comprehend the amount of data that we actually have in a network,” Wollenweber told The Register.
Cisco’s Canvas agentic operations platform aims to at least make humans aware when their attention is needed, by detecting problems and offering to make repairs.

Joe Vaccaro, Cisco’s senior vice president and general manager for Network Platform and Assurance, told The Register he believes network administrators don’t feel threatened by suggestions from AI agents when they concern familiar, routine, low-risk tasks that IT pros are confident the agents can handle. Over time, he said, networking pros will learn to trust agents with more complex work. ®

e0f47e1eef07df75: I drove to Seremban from my humble abode recently and covered 106km, if one rather disreputable GPS app is to be believed. My journey began on the northern route of the North-South Expressway which is numbered E1 as well as AH2 (for Asian Highway 2). If you've ever wondered what those small signs meant, you’re welcome!

At Sungai Buloh, the E1 morphed into the New Klang Valley Expressway (NKVE) and a new Asian Highway designation, the AH141. Later, I was back on some federal and city roads for a while before I rejoined the NSE at Sungai Besi on its southern route, numbered E2. Later at Bangi the E2 became the AH2 again.

On my return journey, the said disreputable GPS app took me through some quaint Seremban back roads where life appeared slower and I was reminded of the Penang I knew from many decades ago. I was then guided out of town and on to another expressway, the E21 or Lekas, yet another fancy acronym in this never-ending battle amongst toll highway concessionaires to pick the coolest name possible for their particular concession.

Lekas – fast in Malay – quickly took me away from Seremban’s charming old town and countryside and handed me over to the E18, the Kajang Dispersal Link Expressway or SILK, which is somehow a Malay acronym because apparently KDLE doesn’t sound very exciting. SILK smoothly took me onto the E27, the East Klang Valley Expressway, or EKVE, which probably means something cool in some language I’m not au fait with, perhaps French.

The E27 took me to the E19, the Sungai Besi Ulu Kelang Elevated Expressway (SUKE), which deposited me on the E33, the Duta Ulu Klang Expressway (DUKE), which also happens to be part of the AH141. I went from SUKE to DUKE, or from happiness to sadness, if your Malay is au courant.

Sad indeed, as there I was in a small sedan and not my usual thirsty but spacious old 4x4, which consumes a litre of petrol just coughing itself to a start. My back and knees and ego hurt while I looked up to other motorists rather than down on them – a rather unnerving and humbling experience indeed.

I duked my way out of the late afternoon traffic on the E33 back to the recently-traversed E1 incorporating the NKVE, and made my way home, which remains a humble abode regardless of how many French words I throw out to the hoi polloi in telling this story.
At this point, you’re probably close to screaming “Is there a point to all this?” Yes, there indeed are some points I’m trying to make, so hold on to your pantalons, dear readers.

I’ve driven on almost all major roads and highways and byways in Malaysia, especially on the peninsular side. But it appears Malaysia’s appetite for building toll expressways far exceeds my capacity to drive on each and every one of them.

I should have paid more attention when rich people objected to yet another expressway running through their neighbourhood and bringing down property values. Or when the conservation-minded people shouted about yet another toll highway cutting through some pristine nature preserve. All these mean yet another highway with a cute name and many toll booths is being born.

I’ve seen expressways that seem to just hang in the sky, and had I chosen the E12 Akleh elevated highway instead of the E33, or better still, taken the E12 and then still went on to the E33, my story would’ve been more fantastique and my knees more swollen.

Had fate and my GPS app taken me on slightly different routes, I could very easily have added the E6 Elite, the E20 Maju and maybe even the E38 SMART Tunnel to the list of highway concessions I helped enrich. With a few more diversions I could’ve also added the E31 DASH, the E23 SPRINT, the E6 Kesas, possibly the E11 LDP and the E13 LKSA, and closer to home, the E25 Latar and perhaps even the E35 GCE.

These are not all. Elsewhere and not quite taking me to Seremban are the E7 CKE, the E8 ECE, the E9 Besraya, the E10 NPE, the E26 SKVE, the E29 SPDH, the E30 NNKSB and the E37 LKS. These are all within the Kuala Lumpur-Seremban metropolitan area, and many of you probably drive on them regularly without realising how magnificent, intricate and widespread our toll highway network is.
But a blessing can also be a curse. More on that when the journey continues.

03f7014d81c48e8e: Advocates for cloud-native software have long argued that their approach to development makes applications portable across different Kubernetes environments. But VMware argues that’s not happening across hybrid clouds, and has taken the lead in an effort to improve matters.
That effort, the new Workload Conformance Working Group in the Kubernetes community, aims to establish a shared standard for how workloads run on Kubernetes.

The group’s web page points out, “Certified Kubernetes tests the cluster, and Kubernetes AI Conformance tests whether a cluster can run AI and ML workloads. Nothing comparable exists for the workloads themselves, so cluster operators still check each application by hand before routine maintenance or a Kubernetes upgrade. Every cluster operator ends up repeating the same assessment, and application maintainers get the same questions from each environment they support,” the group asserts.
The proposed solution? “A common specification with repeatable tests would give both groups the same baseline to start from.”

Prashanth Shenoy, VP of product marketing in Broadcom's VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) division, told The Register that standard is needed in part because applications packaged to run in public clouds don’t always run well in hybrid clouds.

That’s challenging for VMware, and other vendors of hybrid clouds like Nutanix and Red Hat, because they all sell tools to create and run a stack that users can deploy to both on-prem infrastructure and public clouds.
VMware therefore thinks it will find support for an effort to ensure that cloud-native apps run predictably and efficiently in any Kubernetes environment.
The effort to create this standard is in its very early days.

“The first step is deciding which workloads and behaviors the specification covers,” states the announcement of the working group’s formation. “The scope includes security, resilience during disruptions, resource use, networking, storage, API usage, and observability, but the group hasn’t yet agreed on specific requirements or on how to test them.
“However, one rule is already set: every requirement needs an objective test that a test binary can run, so nothing subjective goes into the specification.”
Shenoy thinks application vendors will likely support this effort because they want to package their wares once and have them run anywhere.
VMware this week announced another contribution to Kubernetes by moving its VM API to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) Sandbox.

The CNCF, which maintains Kubernetes, is already home to KubeVirt, a tool that allows users to create and manage VMs inside a Kubernetes cluster. The VM API lets Kubernetes users create VMs that run under other hypervisors – including VMware’s own ESXi.

VMware previously integrated Kubernetes into vSphere with Kubernetes, introduced as part of vSphere 7 in 2020. Chronicling Virtzilla’s long and convoluted attempts to package and sell the container tech it acquired along with Pivotal Software would be a tedious exercise.
Suffice to say past efforts didn’t catch on, and VMware is now trying a different approach to making VMs a first class citizen of Kubernetes.

The CNCF’s interest shows this is not a vanity project for VMware, because while developers generally prefer to write for containers, operations folk often decide to run those abstractions within lightweight VMs. The two abstractions are therefore going to coexist for years to come, both for new apps and as organizations run new containerized apps alongside legacy VMs, and do so in an infrastructure-as-code world in which automated deployments are assumed.
VM API will therefore likely be a welcome addition to Kubernetes, representing another option to make life a little easier for ops and dev teams. ®
d08a653ede684233: It’s another doozy of a Patch Tuesday, with Microsoft fixing 1,094 bugs in its products, including one that attackers exploited before Redmond released a patch. Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence at exposure management firm watchTowr, succinctly said in an email to The Register: “Maybe we should just go home.”

“Most security teams haven’t quite recovered from the last month of bumper-to-bumper critical vulnerabilities, emergency patches, and ‘2shell’-branded everything, and we’re yet again at another Patch Tuesday,” Knott told us.

Starting with the zero-day: It’s an Outlook spoofing vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-124194, and it only garnered a 6.5 out of 10 CVSS rating. But as Dustin Childs, head of threat awareness at TrendAI’s Zero Day Initiative, warns, don’t let the score or the name lull you into thinking it’s OK to put off patching this one.
“It’s labeled spoofing, but the impact is bigger than the name suggests,” Childs said in his monthly Patch Tuesday review.

“An attacker sends a specially crafted message file and convinces a user to open it,” he wrote. “Outlook then connects to an attacker-controlled network location without showing the usual external-content warning, which discloses the user’s NTLMv2 hash. The attacker can use that hash to authenticate as the user.”

Microsoft marked CVE-2026-124194 as exploited, but per usual didn’t say when the attacks started, who is battering this bug, and what they are doing with the access post exploitation. These details will likely start trickling out soon.

Plus, now that there’s a public fix, other miscreants are undoubtedly already scanning for vulnerable versions and reverse engineering the patch for their own attack purposes. So prioritize this fix, and keep an eye on your inbox for any suspicious files.
Back-to-back months of 1K+ CVEs

Despite the second month of more than 1,000 CVEs (October had 1,474), CVE-2026-124194 is the only one under active exploitation, and none of the 1,094 are listed as publicly known. Childs says this shouldn’t give organizations “false comfort.”

“Logging back-to-back months above 1,000 CVEs proves automated bug-hunting has permanently reset patch volume,” he told The Register. “With AI making patch-diffing and exploit generation near-instant, the threat window opens the minute these updates drop.”
For defenders, this means two things, Childs added.

“What defenders need to know and do right now is abandon broad triage and take immediate defensive action: patch Exchange and Domain Controllers (LDAP/Kerberos) first to stop zero-click compromise, ring-fence exposed network services like DNS and DHCP to prevent wormable spread, and verify manual administrative fixes on your cloud services,” he said.
Zero-click threats

There are two zero-click threats in this month’s batch of fixes: CVE-2026-116928 and CVE-2026-119958. Both are critical, carrying 9.8 CVSS ratings, in part because they don’t require any user interaction to exploit.

CVE-2026-116928 is an out-of-bounds write in Microsoft Windows Search Component that could lead to remote code execution. An unauthenticated attacker could abuse this search feature in Exchange “by sending an email containing a specially crafted attachment,” Redmond warned. “Exchange automatically processes the attachment for indexing, so the recipient does not need to open the email or attachment. Successful exploitation could allow the attacker to execute code with the permissions of the affected processing service.”

CVE-2026-119958 is an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in Windows' implementation of the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code remotely without user interaction. This one can be exploited by sending specially crafted LDAP requests to vulnerable systems, potentially compromising domain controllers.

Childs also counts 30 CVEs that pose a “wormable risk,” requiring zero authentication and zero user interaction over a network. All of those are listed in his blog, so prioritize fixing those as well.
And…Xbox remote code execution

And finally, for funsies, a critical flaw in the Windows Xbox Live Networking Service, CVE-2026-112967, that could allow remote code execution also made this month's roundup. It's a heap-overflow vulnerability with a 9.8 CVSS rating that doesn't require authentication or user interaction to exploit.

So don't take a gaming break between testing November's updates. Or, if you do, at least make sure vulnerable Windows systems running the Xbox Live Networking Service are on your patching list, too. ®

bda5de5f5ee664c9: Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month’s Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws — including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook — and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe, Apple, Google and Mozilla.

November’s patch release from Redmond tackles 1,093 vulnerabilities, fixing 63 “critical” flaws that can be exploited to seize control over a Windows system with little or no help from users. Nearly half of those critical bugs are remote code execution vulnerabilities. Overall, 535 of the flaws addressed this month allow an attacker to elevate their privileges on a vulnerable device.

This latest round of updates means Microsoft has shipped more than 5,100 security patches so far this year, a staggering number considering that a year ago Microsoft was averaging around 100 patches per month. Microsoft credits advances in artificial intelligence for helping to find (and fix) such a large volume of security bugs in recent months. Last month, Microsoft pushed more than 1,400 fixes.

According to Redmond, just one of the flaws is already seeing active exploitation: CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing bug in Outlook. The advisory for CVE-2026-124194 says it affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and editions of Microsoft Office.

Several other major software makers pushed security updates this week to fix critical weaknesses in their products. Apple on Monday released out-of-cycle security updates to fix at least nine vulnerabilities in iOS/iPadOS, macOS, watchOS and visionOS. Among the weaknesses reportedly fixed in Apple’s release include an iMessage flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages; the updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined.
Lee Neely, an instructor at the SANS Institute, noted that Apple backported the fix to iOS 18.

“I take notice when Apple releases fixes to more than two versions,” Neely wrote in a SANS newsletter today. “You really need to get to version 27.2.1 of their OSes and push folks who are holding onto devices which cannot run the current version. The best plan often involves setting an upgrade date for old hardware. Run through all your Apple devices and make sure everything is up to date, don’t assume the fixes went out automatically.”

Google this week released Chrome version 157.0.8103.50, which resolves nine security holes, including CVE-2026-125350, the sixth zero-day vulnerability this year for Chrome (this bug also is being patched in Chromium-based browsers like Edge). The latest Chrome version follows its November 3 release, which fixed 213 vulnerabilities. A new version of Mozilla Firefox out today (Firefox 160) resolves almost 100 CVEs, about half of them high severity.

Adobe today released patches for at least 110 vulnerabilities across a range of products, with nearly half of the flaws rated high severity. Adobe said there is no evidence any of the security holes it addressed this month are being actively exploited.

Chris Goettl, vice president of product management at Ivanti, said it’s easy for security teams at large enterprises to feel overwhelmed by the volume and criticality of patches from Microsoft lately. But he notes that while some 95,000 vulnerabilities have been assigned CVEs this year across all vendors, only 217 have so far this year been added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

“Roughly four in ten of this year’s exploited vulnerabilities sit in operating systems, endpoint software, browsers, and server platforms, which a continuous patch strategy can close quickly,” Goettl said.”The rest calls for exposure management alongside patching, especially the 44% that sit in edge devices and IT management or remote access tools, the internet-facing systems that hold privileged access. Teams that can quickly identify those assets, confirm exposure and act on confirmed exploitation can focus on the small slice of vulnerabilities attackers are actively using, while the rest stays on the normal patch cadence.”

Please don’t neglect to back up any important data if you haven’t recently; generally speaking, this is a task best accomplished before applying operating system updates. As ever, if you experience any issues installing this month’s bundle of love from Microsoft, please drop a comment about it in the space below.
629f242331093df8: If you didn't have any privacy concerns about slapping a Ring doorbell on your front door or putting Ring cameras inside, you'll love Amazon's newest offerings, which move around homes and businesses to capture views stationary cameras might miss.

The house of Bezos announced the launch of Ring Robotics on Tuesday along with its first two products: a drone designed for indoor home security, and a wheeled robot with a telescoping camera mast for automated after-hours business patrols. Both are designed to proactively patrol spaces as well as respond to alerts from connected alarm systems and Ring-connected devices.
According to Ring founder Jamie Siminoff, this is something customers actually want, as those stationary cameras just can’t quite see everywhere.
“It’s not just a new category of security; it’s the beginning of a future where proactive, autonomous protection is something every home and every business can have,” Siminoff said.

The consumer-focused Ring Drone Cam launches from its own charging dock that Amazon says keeps the thing “out of sight” when not in use, and when in flight is able to patrol a home by flying around pre-programmed routes to take in the sights with its 148-degree FOV, 2K camera that includes LED illumination for night patrols. Amazon says it can also respond to alerts from cameras, sensors, and alarm systems.

The Ring Rover Cam, designed with businesses in mind, is sort of like a security Roomba that sports a camera on a telescoping mast that Amazon says can be programmed to certain heights to let it see over counters, shelves, and other workplace obstacles. The Rover can also perform 360-degree scans and includes a siren, lights, and two-way audio so you can yell at intruders who aren't dissuaded by its presence. The Rover streams and records video in up to 4K while moving or patrolling and is designed to make regular patrols of businesses during off hours. It can also detect people and respond to alerts from connected Ring devices.

Of course, given that this is Ring we're talking about, these flying and free-wheeling cameras use Amazon's cloud for some processing, likely inviting privacy concerns about what footage and mapping data the company can access and retain.

The Amazon-owned security tech firm has faced a number of privacy complaints over the years, some of which have resulted in multimillion-dollar settlements. Ring agreed to pay $5.8 million in a 2023 settlement with the FTC over allegations that employees and contractors improperly accessed customers' private videos and that the company failed to adequately protect accounts against unauthorized access – just imagine the privacy concerns raised by flying robots.

More recently, the company took heat for partnering with surveillance outfit Flock Safety, a relationship which it has since canceled. Amazon/Ring also invited criticism for a Super Bowl ad earlier this year promoting a new feature called Search Party, which would remotely activate Ring cameras to search for lost pets, suggesting that Amazon had the ability, in theory, to use Ring cameras like a dystopian neighborhood surveillance network.

Another Ring feature, Familiar Faces, which uses AI-powered facial recognition to identify people captured by compatible cameras, prompted a proposed class-action lawsuit filed in June. The complaint alleges that the feature collected biometric information from visitors and passersby without their consent.
If we can’t have iRobot, we’ll do it with Ring

Amazon abandoned its efforts to buy Roomba robot-vacuum maker iRobot in 2024, blaming regulatory scrutiny for the move. The FTC, under then-chair Lina Khan, examined the deal's potential effects on competition and consumer privacy, including concerns about the information Roombas collect while mapping customers' homes. European regulators, meanwhile, raised concerns that Amazon could use its marketplace to disadvantage rival robot vacuum makers.
With this Ring move, Amazon is once again putting robots capable of mapping interior spaces into customers' hands, reviving some of the privacy questions raised during its failed iRobot acquisition.

As Amazon explains in Tuesday’s press release, both new Ring robots are powered by AI Pilot, “a custom-built system that uses the devices’ cameras, specialized vision models, on-device sensors, and cloud processing to see, think, and navigate autonomously.”
To help the Ring robots understand where they're operating, the devices generate floor plans of interior spaces, according to Amazon.

“Carry Ring Drone through your space or let Ring Rover autonomously explore, and it turns what it sees into a floor plan,” the company explains of the setup process. AI Pilot takes the reins in identifying the types of rooms it sees and suggests key patrol areas it should focus on, which users can add to in the Ring app.

Amazon claims that videos captured by these new flying and free-wheeling cameras will be protected by an encryption scheme it calls Throw Away the Key Encryption (TAKE). The system temporarily allows Ring's cloud services to access recordings for enabled features before the relevant encryption keys are deleted. Ring announced the scheme in August, presenting it as a way to limit access to customer recordings without sacrificing cloud-powered features.

“With TAKE, your Ring videos are protected with unique, rotating encryption keys,” Amazon explained. “A copy of the keys is temporarily held inside a secure enclave within the cloud; think of it as a sealed vault that can only provide Ring access to the key under strict, limited conditions.”

The keys, Amazon claims, are later deleted so that only users and those they allow access to can see videos, with Ring only retaining them “to power the intelligent features that you have active on your account.”

“We take privacy concerns seriously, and we believe privacy and customer control are fundamental to building products people trust,” a Ring spokesperson told The Register when asked about prior privacy concerns. “That is why customers decide where these devices go and when.”
We asked about floor plan security, but didn’t get an answer about that.

As for when those devices will be available, the Rover Cam will start shipping on December 16 at a price of about $1,000, but the Drone Cam might not ever actually make it to homes. Amazon’s announcement mentions a release date of January 27, 2027, but that’s subject to the FCC giving its blessing.

“Ring Drone Cam has not been authorized as required by the rules of the FCC,” Amazon’s release states. “This device is not, and may not be, offered for sale or lease, or sold or leased, until authorization is obtained.”
Amazon told us that the Drone Cam would still start shipping in January, luckily giving everyone a few months to figure out how to deal with this new, more mobile, invasion of privacy. ®
