2dcde4b665668871: Our modern world runs on math, from social media algorithms, package delivery, and weather prediction to medical imaging and machine learning. The rise of computers helped fuel its dominance, enabling us to work with increasingly large numbers that would otherwise be beyond the capacity of our finite human brains. But with the rise of large language models, AI chatbots, and, soon, quantum computing, so-called "big math" is beginning to outstrip its creators entirely. What that means, and how we might adapt, is the focus of a new book, Big Math: The Hidden Codes That Run Our World, by applied mathematicians Steven Strogatz and Alex Townsend.

Strogatz is perhaps best known in his field for his co-authorship of a seminal 1998 paper with Duncan Watts on the collective dynamics of small-world networks. He has also studied chaos theory as applied to physics, the geometry of supercoiled DNA, and the biological collective oscillators, such as swarms of synchronously flashing fireflies and crickets that chirp in unison. In 2005, Strogatz extended his study of synchronicity to the crowds that caused the wobbling of London's Millennium Bridge.

An award-winning communicator, Strogatz wrote three series of columns on mathematics for The New York Times in 2010, 2012, and 2025 and hosted a podcast for Quanta magazine from 2020–2021. He has written four popular books: Sync (2003), The Calculus of Friendship (2009), The Joy of X (2012), and the New York Times bestseller Infinite Powers (2019).
a5443af359df1d11: They are learning how to be drivers of change locally
Originally published on Global Voices
Participants of the Voices of Democracy project in Kyiv, Ukraine. Photo by beYOUnd. Used with permission.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

The war in Ukraine has created a myriad of challenges for youth and their participation in public life and democratic processes, bringing displacement and misinformation as well as decreased opportunities for political engagement, economic activity, and access to information. At the same time, there are still avenues youth can pursue to contribute to political decisions and shape the fate of their communities.

Despite the war, people can still submit petitions, participate in public consultations, or advocate for their needs online, but there is a lack of awareness about such opportunities. Furthermore, vulnerable groups — including displaced persons, minorities, and rural communities — know they have a voice, but struggle to find it.

In 2026, the local non-governmental organization beYOUnd implemented a project to help youth from vulnerable groups acquire the necessary knowledge and skills to find their voices in this new era of digital democracy. Global Voices conducted an email interview with Yevheniia Holovenko, the chairwoman of beYOUnd, to learn more about their initiative. The interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project.

Yevheniia Holovenko (YH): beYOUnd is a youth-led NGO based in Ukraine, registered in October 2025, though we’ve worked as a team long before that. Our mission is to increase the involvement of vulnerable youth, especially internally displaced people and young people facing difficult social and economic circumstances, in integration, self-realization, and civic life.

Our name reflects our philosophy: it starts with you; it goes beyond! Our team is largely made up of young people who’ve lived through the same challenges as the youth we work with, which shapes how we approach everything we do.

We joined the Digital Sparks initiative because digital democracy and civic space are exactly where Ukrainian youth need support right now. Safe, informed participation online is inseparable from resilience during war, and it matched our mission perfectly.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

YH: The war has pushed many young Ukrainians, especially internally displaced persons (IDPs), into digital spaces to stay connected, informed, and civically active, often without the tools to do so safely.
We saw a gap: young people were consuming information and even participating online, but without media literacy, digital security awareness, or confidence that their voice could shape anything.

We wanted to close this gap by developing practical digital safety and civic participation skills in displaced and marginalized youth. We wanted to give them an opportunity to share ideas on how to increase awareness of digital democracy with the involvement of young people in Ukraine.
GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?
YH: Within the project “Voices of Democracy in the Digital Era,” we ran an awareness campaign covering digital security, e-participation, and disinformation, which reached over 8,500 views.
On the education side, we delivered three webinars and three workshops on digital democracy, media literacy, civic action planning, and cybersecurity, engaging over a hundred participants.

We also organized an offline networking event in the capital, Kyiv, bringing 27 participants together in person to connect around these same topics, and build on the online learning with real, face-to-face relationships and exchange.
Together, these activities, which combined online reach with in-person community building, gave young people both the knowledge and the network to act on this newly acquired knowledge.
GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.

YH: “Voices of Democracy” reshaped how our beneficiaries see their own place in their community. As one participant shared, “I discovered new digital tools I can use to engage with my community and take part in important decisions.”
Others said the most valuable part was learning how to protect their personal data and use digital services safely in everyday life.
Several highlighted finally understanding the difference between advocacy and broader civic action, and how to build a real plan for their own initiative — skills that came alive through teamwork.

As another participant put it, “I learned to define a problem, trace its causes, and plan real steps to solve it — and I understood better what advocacy is and how it can drive positive change in a community.”
For many, this changed how they see their own ability to influence change locally.
GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed, thanks to your participation in the project?

YH: Leading this project deepened our understanding of how closely digital safety and democratic participation are linked. You can’t meaningfully engage young people in civic life online without first equipping them to navigate that space securely.
Working alongside experts in digital security and civic engagement broadened our grasp of practical tools we now use, and how we think about beYOUnd’s programming.

It also pushed us to see capacity-building more structurally: not just what we teach beneficiaries, but how we build our own organizational resilience for the long term, not just on a project-by-project basis.
GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

YH: The biggest lesson was that combining practical, hands-on content with real interaction (webinars, workshops, and offline networking) worked far better than any one format alone. Participants didn’t just absorb information; they built relationships and confidence to act on it, especially through the in-person exchange in Kyiv.
We also learned how much value there is in simple, clear, practical content. Participants consistently said what stuck with them most was information they could immediately use, not abstract theory.
Finally, working through capacity-building for our own team alongside the project reminded us that organizational resilience matters just as much as the skills we pass on to beneficiaries.
GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?

YH: We plan to keep the digital tools, advocacy frameworks, and civic action planning skills from this project embedded in how we design future programs for youth. This isn’t a one-off topic, but now a standing part of our work.
The connections built through the Kyiv networking event are something we want to keep nurturing, turning one-time contacts into an ongoing community.

On the organizational side, we’re applying what we’ve built around resilience and long-term capacity to strengthen beYOUnd as we grow, so we’re better equipped to run projects like this and bigger ones going forward.
Written by Nurbek Bekmurzaev

d773733f30a9491c: Energetic mayors and councils can help street homeless people to rebuild their lives. But the underlying affordability crisis needs tackling too Bringing an end to rough sleeping was among Andy Burnham’s first pledges after entering Downing Street – as it was when he became mayor of Manchester. As we reported last month, Reverse Engineer-Anything has made it easy for people to use AI tools to hack electronics that they own and replace a manufacturer’s software or operating system with an open source or vibecoded one. People have installed new operating systems on their smart TVs, have turned baby monitors into AI assistants, have unbricked internet-of-things devices that were abandoned by their manufacturers, and have installed new software on very old hardware. At the time, I wasn’t sure how I felt about the trend, but as I’ve seen people take ownership and control back over the devices that manufacturers have purposefully bricked, turned into spyware, or have placed artificial limitations on, I have come to see AI-powered reverse engineering of electronic devices as one of the few LLM uses genuinely worth getting excited about. And so big companies have immediately taken steps to restrict this behavior.

The policy tweaks show that big AI corporations will protect other big corporations when their users find ways to use LLMs to circumvent the artificial constraints that hardware manufacturers put on their devices. AI-powered copyright circumvention is OK with big tech when it’s a massive company scraping the entire internet to build their LLMs, but is not OK when people then use those tools to liberate their internet-of-things devices. It’s not the end of AI-powered reverse engineering, but people suddenly getting locked out of their accounts for asking AI to reverse engineer their gadgets suggests that the future of this practice lies in open weight, local, and uncensored models, making it less accessible to the masses and the people who could probably benefit from it most.

Tarun Gogineni, an OpenAI engineer, tweeted that people are not supposed to have their OpenAI accounts restricted for reverse engineering: “these blocks are mostly accidental and a result of difficult decision boundaries; there is no prohibition against reverse engineering with codex. it’s getting fixed,” he tweeted.

But people who are doing AI-powered reverse-engineering suggest that they are moving away from big companies’ models to alternatives where they aren’t going to have their accounts disabled or have to figure out how to work around AI company guardrails.
4ac67656f256b571: From Jamaluddin Aziz

The announcement that the Islamic development department (Jakim) and central committee for applications for filming and performances by foreign artistes (Puspal) are investigating alleged elements of ritualistic worship at The Weeknd’s recent concerts at the Bukit Jalil national stadium highlights a recurring cultural tension in Malaysia.
As a critical media scholar, I view this controversy not merely as a clash over entertainment guidelines, but as a textbook case of “context collapse”.

Coined by media researcher Danah Boyd and further theorised with Alice Marwick in their seminal 2011 study in New Media & Society (“I tweet honestly, I tweet passionately: Twitter users, context collapse, and the imagined audience”), context collapse occurs when digital platforms flatten multiple, distinct audiences into a single space.

When content created for one specific cultural or artistic environment is stripped of its original framing and judged within an entirely different moral or ideological context, modern pop theatrics are easily misread as literal religious devotion.

To understand how context shapes interpretation, one need only compare The Weeknd’s Nov 4 and 5 shows with another massive event held at the exact same stadium just three weeks earlier: Konsert Tradisional Gema Bumantara by Biduanita Negara Siti Nurhaliza.
Both concerts drew tens of thousands of devoted fans who sang every lyric in unison and cheered wildly for their favourite performer.
Yet, the public and institutional reactions to these two sold-out spectacles could not have been more different.

In modern pop culture, intense audience enthusiasm is often loosely referred to as “fan worship”. Historically, words like “fan” (from the Latin fanaticus, meaning temple frenzy) and “icon” (from the Greek eikōn, meaning sacred image) do share etymological roots in ancient religious practice.
Today, however, these terms describe secular cultural admiration. When fans cheer at a stadium, they are participating in collective musical enjoyment, not a spiritual ritual.

Viewing both Bukit Jalil concerts through a critical media lens reveals three key dynamics driving these divergent reactions. First is the mechanics of context collapse. Critics of The Weeknd’s concert pointed to short social media clips showing a towering golden female robot sculpture and dancers in red hooded robes as evidence of pagan or machine-worship rituals.

As Marwick and Boyd’s framework demonstrates, when these visuals are detached from the full two-hour concert narrative and circulated online to audiences unfamiliar with Western pop-art tropes, context collapses.
Stripped of their theatrical framing, a futuristic sculpture by Japanese artist Hajime Sorayama meant to critique the hollowness of fame and materialism is flattened into a literal religious idol.

Second is embedded cultural context. In contrast, Siti’s concert operated within a shared, deeply understood local framework. Utilising classical floral visuals and orchestral staging without human statues, her performance aligned seamlessly with Malaysian cultural and religious norms.

Because audiences and regulators immediately understood the context of Irama Malaysia heritage, the collective euphoria in the stadium was celebrated as patriotic pride rather than scrutinised as spiritual misdirection.

At most, conservative critiques of such local shows rarely go beyond general moral cautions against lagha (worldly distraction or frivolous amusement), a far cry from the theological panic of syirik (idolatry) projected onto The Weeknd’s unfamiliar pop symbolism.
Third is audience literacy and intent. Context collapse assumes that audiences are passive consumers who absorb imagery literally.
In reality, modern concertgoers possess high media literacy. Tens of thousands of Malaysians attended The Weeknd’s show to experience Grammy-winning music and dystopian sci-fi stagecraft.

Treating theatrical props as acts of syirik (idolatry) ignores the crucial distinction between artistic metaphor and religious intent (niat), unfairly questioning the faith and intelligence of ordinary Malaysian fans.
Puspal plays an essential role in ensuring that international performances respect Malaysia’s laws and social harmony.
However, effective regulation in the digital age requires media literacy and a resistance to reactionary interpretations born out of viral, out-of-context video clips.

If Malaysia wishes to remain a premier destination for global live entertainment, bringing vital economic and tourism benefits to Kuala Lumpur, authorities must evaluate performances within their full artistic context.
Distinguishing between pop-culture symbolism and actual religious worship is not just good cultural policy; it is essential for fair and rational governance.
Jamaluddin Aziz is an FMT reader.

08367870b5ce119e: A series of tax cuts since President George W. Bush's 2001 legislation have helped push the national debt to US$32 trillion. AP Photo/Ron EdmondsDemocrats, set to take over Congress with robust majorities, will face at least one expensive obstacle to their policy agenda: a national debt that now equals the size of the U.S. economy. Clocking in at US$32 trillion, this debt-to-GDP ratio of 100% would likely raise alarms for other countries. But it attracted relatively little attention in an election season dominated by concerns over the economy and the cost of living. Debt has grown to these levels because over the past 25 years, the federal government has been spending more than it collects in taxes. Even as the U.S. economy grew, lawmakers have cut taxes repeatedly, sometimes with bipartisan support, instead of paying down debt. The series of tax cuts since 2001 has added over $10 trillion to the debt, according to an analysis of Congressional Budget Office data by the Center for American Progress. In fact, without these series of cuts, the debt-to-GDP ratio would be decreasing, the study found. The debate over taxation often falls along partisan lines, with arguments focusing on which income groups are affected or the potential impact on economic growth. But as a public policy scholar, I believe that important context is often overlooked. Under conditions of strong gross domestic product growth and low debt, tax cuts may have a relatively benign fiscal impact. But today, because debt as a share of GDP is so much higher, and interest rates are steeper, the cost of adding new debt is much greater than 15 or 20 years ago, whether through additional spending or through tax cuts. I believe Democrats will have to wrestle with this math as they try to advance a policy agenda focused on affordability that minimizes the risk of further borrowing. It’s all relative Proponents of fiscal austerity argue that lower spending should accompany tax cuts so that debt doesn’t rise. U.S. federal spending, however, has remained relatively flat – outside of emergencies like the 2009 recovery package and COVID-19 stimulus funds – even as GDP has risen. At the same time, each round of tax cuts over the past quarter century has actually gotten smaller over time if they’re assessed as a share of GDP, as a study by the Tax Foundation, a nonpartisan think tank, noted. President Ronald Reagan’s 1981 tax cuts were the most expensive in history, reducing annual federal revenue on average by 2.9% of GDP, according to the Tax Foundation’s analysis. The next two biggest cuts occurred in 1945 and 1948, when the government rolled back the wartime hikes that helped pay for World War II. President Barack Obama’s 2012 legislation, extending most of the temporary tax cuts passed under President George W. Bush, comes in fourth at 1.8% of GDP, while cuts passed under President Lyndon Johnson in 1964 rank fifth. Coming in sixth place at 1.2% of GDP: President Donald Trump’s sweeping policy and tax legislation in 2025, which made permanent most of his 2017 tax cuts. Costly extensions While the Trump cuts amounted to a relatively small share of GDP, they had a much larger effect on the national debt due in part to the higher cost of borrowing. The original 2017 legislation was projected to increase public debt from 91.2% to 97.1% of GDP by 2027, with an overall 10-year cost of $1.5 trillion. That was based on the assumption the cuts would expire after 2025. But just like the earlier round of Bush tax cuts, Congress was loathe to let those provisions lapse. In 2025, the narrow Republican majority pushed through Trump’s legislation that extended or made permanent the 2017 cuts. The Congressional Budget Office, the independent government scorekeeper of legislation, estimated that the 2025 bill would add another $3.4 trillion over 10 years. And it projected that increasing deficits would push debt to 116% of GDP by the end of 2034. Why deficits and economic growth matter so much A basic calculation explains when debt stays stable, and when it does not. If a government runs a “primary” budget surplus – that is, excluding interest payments – and economic growth is higher than the interest rate on government bonds, debt remains stable. The problem for the U.S. is that budget deficits have been growing faster than the economy, while interest payments on government debt are rising as well. This math explains why the trajectory of economic growth is so important in understanding the impact of tax cuts. When taxes were cut after World War II, the economy was booming, the U.S. carried little debt, and reducing taxes didn’t further add to it. By contrast, government spending ballooned under Reagan, thanks in large part to defense outlays. Combined with lower tax revenue due to tax cuts, the national debt tripled during Reagan’s time in office. In 2000, the economy was surging again. That was the last time the U.S. took in more tax revenue than it spent and began paying down the debt. President George W. Bush cited this surplus to justify his first round of major tax cuts in 2001, which also drew support from some Democrats. It remains to be seen how much leverage the results of the midterms will grant Democratic lawmakers in the next two years as they try to enact legislation under Trump. But I believe lawmakers of all stripes will have to confront the hard choices that the U.S. national debt imposes on policy directions going ahead, thanks to a long series of decisions made over the past quarter century. 1b207d990733aaf1: Nearby stores might not actually win out with extra shoppers if a Walmart shutters. Mark Ralston/AFP via Getty ImagesShoppers often greet the closure of a Walmart with dismay, while competitors find cause to celebrate. Among critics of the big-box behemoth, a long-held assumption is that once a Walmart disappears, shoppers seeking groceries, household goods, meals and services will flow to businesses down the road. But what if the economic downside of a closure is bigger? We are marketing scholars who have studied dozens of Walmart closures in the United States. We found that nearby stores saw a slump in both monthly shopper traffic and sales revenue by roughly a quarter in contrast to comparable stores near Walmart locations that remained open. Our sample covered 39 Walmart stores that closed across 20 states from 2019 to 2026. This finding suggests a large retailer can play two roles at once. Walmart competes with neighboring businesses for shopper visits and spending. But it can also act as an anchor, giving people a reason to travel to a shopping area in the first place. When that anchor disappears, the loss of shared shopper traffic can outweigh the benefit of having one less competitor. The benefits of an anchor Our finding underscores that retailers don’t operate as isolated dots on a map. Shoppers often decide where to go before deciding which stores they’ll visit once they get there. A trip to Walmart can generate a stop at a nearby restaurant, pharmacy, salon, specialty retailer or service business. Economists call this kind of benefit an agglomeration effect: Businesses can gain from being near other businesses because the location itself attracts shoppers. Shopping center owners have long recognized this logic by using prominent stores to anchor a mix of tenants. Other researchers have found that Walmart’s entry into a shopping area causes sales in nearby existing stores to drop. But these shops can adjust their product assortment, prices and promotions to mitigate this effect, follow-up studies suggest. What has not been studied until now is what happens when a Walmart store – or any other anchor store – closes. A Walmart closure creates a tug-of-war between two forces, we argue. Competitive relief helps nearby businesses because a formidable rival is gone. But agglomeration loss hurts them because fewer shoppers have a reason to visit the area. This means a store can capture a larger share of local consumer demand after Walmart leaves and still end up worse off if the total pool of shoppers arriving in the area shrinks enough. Developers often place an anchor store in a bigger retail center to attract more foot traffic overall, which in turn goes to other stores. David Cooper/Toronto Star via Getty Images What happened after a Walmart closed We combined closure dates with monthly store-level shopper traffic and spending data. For each closed Walmart, we identified nearby non-Walmart businesses and compared their post-closure performance with that of businesses near Walmarts that stayed open. We discovered not just a sizable decline in both shopper traffic and sales revenue after closure but a worsening trend in both over time. Specifically, following a Walmart’s closure, nearby stores experienced a roughly 5% drop in the following month and 6% in the month thereafter. The decline keeps getting worse, reaching about 17% in the ninth month and 20% a year after the anchor store closes. That parallel movement in traffic and sales matters. If nearby stores were simply selling less to the same number of shoppers, we would expect spending per visit to fall. Instead, what was also happening is that fewer shoppers visited nearby businesses after the anchor disappeared. In short, competitive relief didn’t overcome the loss of traffic that would have been generated by trips to the anchor store. But not all nearby businesses were affected equally. Stores that competed more directly with Walmart had better post-closure sales than noncompeting stores. That is what we would expect if competitive relief is real: Grocery stores and other close substitutes are better positioned to capture some of the displaced consumer demand. Well-known brand stores also fared relatively better than unbranded businesses. A recognizable brand can give shoppers an independent reason to visit, reducing reliance on traffic generated by the nearby anchor. And stores surrounded by more outlets with its own brands also had more favorable post-closure sales. Another important factor is digital reach. Not surprisingly, the more a business engages with customers online, the less it depends on people physically traveling to a cluster of stores. We found that stores with a higher share of revenue from online orders saw a less severe drop in sales after a Walmart closed. These patterns suggest that managers have options and can act: Opening another location or expanding online sales can protect a retailer from an anchor closure. Why a store closing can become a neighborhood shock A large retailer decides whether to keep a store open based primarily on what makes sense for its own portfolio. But the surrounding businesses face a different calculation. A location that looks weak from the anchor retailer’s perspective can still drive valuable traffic to neighboring stores. That creates what economists call an externality – a positive or negative effect of an economic activity that impacts other parties even though market prices don’t reflect it. In this case, some of the economic value produced by an anchor sits outside the anchor’s own sales and profits. For neighboring businesses, the lesson is not to assume that a powerful competitor’s departure will create a windfall. Rather, managers need to know how many customers arrive because of the broader shopping destination, not merely how much their store’s products overlap with the anchor’s. Meanwhile, commercial property owners should treat losing an anchor as more than risking an empty storefront. It can also hurt the rest of their portfolio by reducing consumer demand. Replacing the tenant quickly matters, but so does finding a replacement that can generate trips to the area. Finally, local governments and economic development organizations need to understand that a major retail closure may affect businesses with no contractual relationship to the closed store. So their responses should extend beyond the vacant property itself – whether it’s speeding redevelopment, coordinating with local businesses and property owners to improve shoppers’ access, or helping create a new destination that restores shopper traffic. 85e2d6b966948461: Pro-monarchists celebrate after the 1953 Iranian coup. Intercontinentale/AFP via Getty Images“Very little gets into, or out of, Iran!” President Donald Trump claimed on Nov. 8, 2026, in a social media post that also lauded “history’s greatest Naval Blockade.” It followed the unveiling of Task Force Iron Gate – the Trump administration’s latest plan to isolate the Iranian economy in a bid to coerce the government in Tehran to bend to Washington’s will. At the same time, Trump has suggested that a return to open war with Iran is “highly unlikely.” From my perspective as an expert on Iran’s relations with the wider world, I believe that the U.S. war in Iran – now into its ninth month – is increasingly resembling an earlier episode of Iranian-Western conflict. In the early 1950s, the British imposed a two-year blockade and embargo against Iran after Iran’s then-prime minister, Mohammad Mossadegh, nationalized the country’s U.K.-controlled oil industry. These efforts culminated in a 1953 British- and American-backed plot to stir up protest in Iran and eventually overthrow Mossadegh. Seventy-three years later, many of those themes – oil, economic coercion, political intervention – ring true again. Trump’s stated and shifting justifications for the war include imminent threat preemption and nuclear nonproliferation. Yet his main motivations seem to be choosing Iran’s leader and controlling its oil. Having failed to achieve this through direct military force, Trump’s main means for achieving the objectives are now a naval blockade and economic isolation – much like the British some seven decades earlier. But there the analogy may end. Unlike during the Mossadegh era, Iran has shown it can fight back against foreign intervention and coercive economic actions through asymmetric warfare and economic disruption. From oil nationalization … In March 1951, one month before becoming prime minister and while serving as a parliamentary representative, Mossadegh persuaded the Iranian parliament to pass legislation that nationalized the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company. While popular with many Iranians, who perceived it as a long overdue measure to reclaim the nation’s independence and control its wealth, the move was considered by the British a breach of contract and a theft of its largest overseas asset. The U.K. filed complaints with the newly created United Nations Security Council. But in July of that year, negotiations stalled and tensions escalated between Mossadegh – now the prime minister – and the British. Economic coercion began with the British obstructing Iran’s oil sales by informing Iranian tankers that their receipts – issued when cargo is loaded on board – would not be accepted on the international market. In August, the U.K. stepped up the campaign by imposing a naval blockade against Iran. In the process, they intercepted oil tankers off the Persian coast and prevented Iran from exporting petroleum to other countries. The British also prohibited the export of key commodities to Iran – such as sugar and steel – and froze Iranian bank accounts and assets in the U.K. That same month, the U.K. evacuated its British technicians and closed Anglo-Iranian Oil Company refineries and other installations in the city of Abadan. Mossadegh and his government assumed they could replace the technicians with those from other countries while training Iranians to fill the void. However, through legal threats and agreements, the British convinced other international oil companies in the United States and Europe, except Italy, to refrain from sending personnel. … to Operation Ajax Due to the British blockade and embargo, Iran’s petroleum production declined by about 96% and its oil income to almost zero between 1950 and 1952. At the same time, foreign oil companies like British Petroleum and Saudi Aramco doubled their production to offset the economic impact to the U.K. and the world of reduced or nonexistent production and exports from Iran. Amid the economic crisis, Mossadegh’s inability to alleviate poverty, among other issues, caused his political coalition to fracture and fueled the British and American propaganda campaign against him ahead of his overthrow in Operation Ajax on Aug. 19, 1953. A year later, the Shah of Iran, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, consolidated power and signed an oil agreement with the British. In it, Iran’s share of the profits increased slightly, while an overwhelming majority of between 75% and 79% continued to be claimed by British and American companies. In exchange, the British lifted the blockade and enabled Iran to resume exporting oil on the international market. The difference of deterrence The U.K.’s campaign to pressure Iran and oust its leader contains parallels with the current conflict. Now, just as then, a Western power is hoping to bring Iranian leadership to its knees – and encourage widespread anti-government protests – through coercive economic actions. But contrary to the 1950s, Tehran today is better placed to deter its foreign adversary. While Washington has drastically degraded Iran’s conventional military capabilities, including its air force and navy, Tehran has effectively employed drones, missiles and proxies to repeatedly strike U.S. assets in the region. Back in the 1950s, Iran had no network of sympathetic regional militias like it has today, and it lacked the sufficient technology to hit back at a conventionally superior military. Iran can also counter economic measures. Since the war began in February 2026, Tehran and its partners have continuously targeted the tanker traffic and civilian and energy infrastructure of the Arab Gulf states. Consequently, it has caused Gulf kingdoms to rethink remaining under the U.S. security umbrella and diversify defense partnerships to include other powers inside and outside the region. A crude oil tanker unloads cargo in Greece after departing Fujairah Anchorage, a major Middle Eastern oil export hub outside the Strait of Hormuz. Nicolas Koutsokostas/NurPhoto via Getty Images Iran has also asserted control, to different degrees, over the critical choke points of the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab Strait in cooperation with the Houthis in Yemen. By attacking the Arab Gulf states and disrupting commercial vessels in the region, Iran has driven up the price of oil and other commodities and exerted economic and political pressure on the United States and other countries. And while the U.S. sanctions and other measures have exacerbated the formidable economic challenges facing Iran that predated the war – record currency devaluation, runaway inflation and contracted growth – the regime in Tehran has seemingly weathered the serious social unrest that transpired right before the conflict, during which thousands of protesters and other citizens took to the streets and were killed by the security forces. Unlike Mossadegh, the current leaders of Iran have had decades to build up a resilience to outside pressure. And while it took two years of economic pressure to push Mossadegh from power, years of sanctions have to date failed to bring Iran’s Islamic Republic to its knees. There is no guarantee that increasing the pressure now will change that. Eric Lob is affiliated with the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

Today’s materials challenges are different from those of the 20th century, but why are critical metals still produced using largely the same scientific foundations?

EvoMaterials, a technology platform developed by Outokumpu—the global leader in sustainable stainless steel and the producer of ferrochrome with 67% lower carbon footprint than the industry average—is exploring that question by rethinking how metals can be extracted:

“We decided to go beyond the current constraints and look fundamentally at what’s the best way to do this with the benefit of the scientific engineering knowledge and hindsight that we have today,” says Caspar Stinn, technical director for extractive metallurgy at Outokumpu. “We’re looking at how we can reimagine metals production.”
A supply chain problem disguised as a materials problem

As economies expand and the world becomes increasingly electrified, data and scientific models point to rising demand for many minerals, driven by technologies ranging from data centers to aerospace, water treatment, energy systems, and defence. According to Antoine Allanore, professor of metallurgy at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) this coincides with many Western economies having reduced their domestic processing capacity for the very metals those industries depend on.
Metallurgy is now strategically important, shaped not only by cost and availability but also by carbon footprint, geographic origin and supply-chain resilience.

That reality is particularly relevant for chromium and other specialty metals used in high-temperature and extreme environments. Chromium-based materials play a critical role in aerospace systems, power generation, corrosion-resistant infrastructure and defense technologies, where materials must perform under demanding conditions.
Beyond optimization

For decades, metallurgical innovation largely focused on improving yields, energy efficiency and process control. EvoMaterials is based on the idea that some metallurgical processes may benefit from entirely different chemical pathways.

The platform originates from research into sulfidation-based processing technologies, initially pursued to reduce carbon emissions associated with ferrochrome production. Laboratory work revealed broader potential.

Lab-scale trials demonstrated that these alternative process chemistries could potentially do more than lower emissions. They could recover valuable metals from lower grade resources and industrial side streams while fundamentally altering how separation processes are performed. The opportunity is to rethink how mineral resources are used and how much value can be extracted from them, bringing in greater resource efficiency and stronger industrial competitiveness.
Understanding traditional smelting vs. new proprietary technology

Development of the technology began in the United States in 2021 for chromite from Outokumpu’s Kemi mine in Finland, the only chrome mine in the European Union and one of the few such operations across the Western world. Since then, Outokumpu has evolved the technology through extensive research and development, combining new process chemistries with proprietary metallurgical expertise, supported in part by a non-exclusive patent license agreement from MIT.

“The technology is a new application for separating metallic elements from materials,” explains Allanore. Historically, that separation has been achieved using carbon- and energy-intensive approaches. The new method creates a different chemical environment that enables more efficient extraction with fewer losses and fewer unwanted by-products, recovering critical materials from resources considered waste.
Innovation happens at the boundaries

EvoMaterials sits at the intersection of several scientific disciplines, a combination that strongly resonates with Stinn, who completed his PhD in Materials Science and Engineering at MIT, where his research focused on low-carbon metals processing and recycling technologies.

Modern materials innovation draws on a growing mix of chemistry, materials science, physics, computational modeling, and engineering. With advanced simulation tools and AI helping researchers identify promising directions, scientific discovery still depends on experimentation and testing in the lab—on getting your hands dirty and doing the hard work.

“Science today is much more interdisciplinary than it was, and the collaboration across disciplines reveals new scientific opportunities,” says Stinn. Engineering can translate those opportunities into more efficient and cost-competitive metals production.
Building a technology platform

A technically significant aspect of EvoMaterials is that it’s not a single process, but a technology platform. Allanore compares EvoMaterials to platform technologies in other industries, where a single scientific breakthrough can enable multiple downstream applications.

Once a new extraction pathway has been mastered for one material system, the same scientific principles may be adapted to entirely different metals and mineral resources. The initial application becomes only the starting point.
“The future and the potential impact might be much broader than the original and current developments that are happening,” Allanore explains.
That possibility is increasingly important as industries seek secure supplies of nickel, chromium, molybdenum, and other strategic materials needed for advanced manufacturing.
The future of materials companies

The broader implication extends beyond metallurgy. Companies that develop proprietary process technologies may create value through production but also through intellectual property and scientific expertise.

Based on Outokumpu’s technology leadership, that transition could create entirely new categories of value, enabling the production of high-value critical materials from ores and resource streams that previously appeared uneconomical or inaccessible.

The result would be a fundamental shift in how metals are manufactured, where sustainability, resource efficiency, supply security, and economic value become outcomes of the same technological architecture rather than separate objectives.

The next step for EvoMaterials is pilot-scale validation, with a pilot plant in New Hampshire to begin operations in the first half of 2027. The facility will scale the proprietary technology from laboratory to one-ton production, providing a step toward industrial-scale deployment targeted for 2030. Beyond producing low-CO2, chromium-enriched ferrochrome and chromium metal, the platform could be adapted to other strategic materials, including nickel and molybdenum.
The work raises a broader question—how many of today’s metallurgical processes would look the same if they were invented from scratch? Or could those routes be designed differently today?
The next revolution in materials may begin by rethinking how to extract the metals that society depends on.

4f02c191dd33421c: Sean Gallup / Getty ImagesJensen Huang, the chief executive and co-founder of chipmaking company Nvidia, recently admitted to an extramarital affair. However, it’s not just a tabloid story: the woman involved, Alice Huang, has been accused of being a Chinese intelligence agent. Computer chips – specifically the chips used to produce and run artificial intelligence (AI) systems – have become a key front in the United States’ rivalry with China for geopolitical power and influence. The most powerful chips are needed for the most advanced AI, and the US has tried to maintain its edge over China by restricting access to those chips. While the Chinese government rejects claims of espionage, Alice Huang has reportedly been under investigation by the US for years. So what’s so special about Nvidia? What’s in it for China? And if Jensen Huang goes down, what else could go down with him? The world’s biggest AI chip company Nvidia is the world’s biggest supplier of the high-end chips used for AI and data centres, with some estimates putting its market share over 80%. The now multi-trillion-dollar company got its start making chips called graphic processing units (GPUs), used largely for video games. However, these chips – and their successors – turned out to be ideal for the kind of number-crunching needed for training and using AI models. Other companies such as Google and AMD have tried to make chips that can compete with Nvidia for speed and efficiency, however neither has been able to displace Nvidia from its dominance of the AI market. Read more: What is a GPU? An expert explains the chips powering the AI boom, and why they’re worth trillions Why China may be interested As a consequence, Nvidia has played a key role in the US government’s strategy to stall China’s development of AI. Sales of Nvidia’s most powerful chips to China have been restricted since 2022 – though the restrictions were somewhat relaxed last year. However, Chinese enterprises have repeatedly tested the boundaries of US sanctions. Southeast Asian companies including Megaspeed, Alice Huang’s former employer, have been accused of buying up Nvidia chips and exporting them into China. Jensen Huang has lobbied intently for a relaxation of US chip export restrictions, which is being seen in a new light after the revelation of his relationship with Alice Huang. Skipping the sanctions Trade records indicate over US$3 billion in chips crossed from Singapore to China in a single year, alongside similar volumes from Malaysia. Selling access to banned Nvidia chips to Chinese companies has also become a growth industry. Nvidia’s value has soared with the AI boom. However, its share price has fallen after the disclosure of the Huang incident, with some analysts asking whether the company propped up sales figures by ignoring sanctions. It has also been reported that an Nvidia executive leaned on US officials to halt an investigation into the firm’s relationship with Megaspeed. Regulatory impact Nvidia’s share price tumbled after the affair was revealed. Now the company is reportedly under criminal investigation. At the same time, US technology regulators are mobilising, with Congress requesting Jensen Huang explain his interactions with Alice Huang, and how Nvidia protects itself against foreign espionage. If Nvidia is forced to guarantee its chips don’t enter China, its sales pipeline may grind to a halt. And if Nvidia hits trouble, the financial impacts could be much wider. The AI sector is notorious for the amount of circular financing going on – where companies invest in their own suppliers or customers. Nvidia is a key player in this loop. Investors are already fretting over whether the enormous amounts of money sunk into AI can ever return profits. While leading AI model builders Anthropic and OpenAI are moving toward public listings or fresh funding rounds, both face harsh reality checks. OpenAI has delayed its own planned stock market listing, while Anthropic’s expected share market listing is rumoured to face a “junk bond” rating, meaning it’s a high-risk investment. Data centre firms too are losing value as they face community pushback and soaring energy costs. Governance crisis So what now? Clearly Nvidia faces a crisis, with a backlash against AI and data centres sweeping the US, US investigators looking at it closely, and the company’s own board of directors investigating its chief executive. On top of this, Nvidia has been inseparable from Jensen Huang’s personal brand for decades – and that brand is now somewhat tarnished. Until now, investors have supported the company, and Jensen, as visionary underwriters of the entire AI ecosystem. If that changes, or the company otherwise loses its way, a shortage of GPUs may be the least of the AI industry’s problems. 8c4f85be22873ce3: Au Kam San's international legal representative called the trial a ‘sham’ with ‘manufactured allegations’
Originally published on Global Voices
Au Kam San. Photo from Au Kam San's Facebook page.

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

The Chinese territory of Macau recorded its first conviction under the city’s national security law on November 6, 2026, sentencing 69-year-old former lawmaker Au Kam San to 12.5 years in prison. The Macau Court of First Instance tried the case behind closed doors, and international observers and rights groups have criticized the verdict, calling it a “bogus prosecution” that included “serious violations of his right to a fair trial.” The case raises broader questions about how justice is carried out in Macau, and whether its courts offer a fair, open way to challenge the state.

Au served in Macau’s legislature for over 20 years and remained an outspoken current affairs commentator after his retirement in 2021. He was convicted on one count of subverting state power, three counts of contacting foreign organizations to endanger national security, and one count of violating confidentiality.
According to the court’s statement, the closed-door trial was held on September 16 and 18. Au was prosecuted under Macau’s domestic security law, enacted on March 3, 2009, and tightened in 2023.

He was accused of cooperating with hostile foreign organizations to collect and disseminate “numerous political propositions that were clearly permeated with [the intent of] subversion of state power” and to assist in the collection and dissemination of false information that intended to incite hatred against the central government, overthrow and undermine the fundamental national system established by the Chinese Constitution, cause foreign countries to take hostile actions against China and Macau, and disrupt the Macau Chief Executive election in 2024.
Au’s family members, several media outlets, and dozens of citizens attended the court’s public sentencing.

Au’s wife, Cheng Miu-shan, responded to the sentencing with an open letter, stating that the closed-door hearing and public sentencing were politically motivated and a baseless persecution to humiliate and smear her husband’s character.
Au’s daughter, Cherry Au, defended her father’s innocence in her interview with UK-based media outlet, the Independent:

“What saddens me the most is seeing him being portrayed as a villain by the very government that he served for so many years,” she said. “I hope people remember the person they knew throughout his career, the reason why they placed their trust in him and elected him time and again. Right now he is facing profound injustice. I hope those who remember his years of service will stand by him.”

Au Kam San has been detained since his arrest in July 2025. He was initially charged with three counts of “subverting state power,” three counts of “establishing contacts with organizations, groups or individuals outside the Macau Special Administrative Region to commit acts that endanger national security,” and one count of “violating confidentiality.” The court reduced the subversion charge to one count after the closed-door hearing.

After the public sentencing, the court issued a press release stressing that it appointed a lawyer to defend Au and that during the trial, Au did not dispute most of the facts and acknowledged that his collusion with and conspiracy with multiple overseas organizations constituted a crime.

It also pointed out that Au did not stop colluding with foreign and overseas organizations to subvert state power after the 2023 amendment of Macau national security law. The amendment has expanded the definition of subversive acts from “violent means” to “any illegal means,” to more closely align with Hong Kong’s 2020 version of national security law.
However, Au’s daughter told the press that her father had been barred from contacting his family and accessing a private lawyer to represent him in court.

Michael Polak, director of Justice Abroad, who has represented Au to submit an official complaint to the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention, called Au’s trial a “sham” with “manufactured allegations” which brought Macau “in line with the most repressive state around the world, where the executive has the power to imprison those with whom it disagrees, with no semblance of a proper, fair legal process.”

In a statement following Au’s public sentencing, Polak also criticized that the private “hearing” had prevented any scrutiny of the Macao Authorities’ so-called evidence, thus creating a scenario where they could present anything, or nothing at all, to the Court and a conviction was inevitable.

So far, the public has not had any information about which foreign organizations, groups, or individuals Au Kam San conspired with to endanger national security and what distorted information he had spread to incite hatred against the Macau government, or undermine China’s socialist system.
The EU also issued a statement criticizing the conviction as “the erosion of political pluralism and freedom of speech” in Macau. It also expressed regret concerning the closed-door trial:
“We regret that access for the public, press and diplomats was restricted. After his arrest on July 30, 2025, Au Kam San had spent almost one year in incommunicado detention.”
Given that Au holds Portuguese citizenship, Polak called on Portugal and the EU to press for his release.

Au Kam San, a retired school teacher, is a prominent pro-democracy activist. After the 1989 pro-democracy movement, along with other pro-democracy figures such as António Ng Kuok Cheong, he established the “Macau Democratic Development Joint Committee” to “respond to the Chinese democratic movement and promote the democratic development of Macau.” They organized and participated in annual activities to commemorate China’s June 4, 1989, Tiananmen Square protests and massacre, until 2021, after the Macau authorities banned the Tiananmen vigil co-organized by Au, claiming that the event would incite state subversion.

Au started his public service career as a Macau municipal councilor from 1993 to 2001. In the first Legislative Council election after Macau’s reunification with China in 1999, Au and Ng formed a political team, “Democratic New Macau,” which won the race with 21 percent of the vote in their constituency. He was re-elected four times until 2021, when he announced his retirement. That year, the Election Committee disqualified 21 candidates from running in the legislative race, citing the Macau Court of Appeal ruling that supported Macau’s decision to ban commemoration of the June 4th Tiananmen Incident as subversive.

f60cbf1284a615ee: MIT researchers will lead an up to $53 million effort, awarded by the U.S. Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health (ARPA-H) as part of its STREAM (Systems for Tracking and Resilience in Efficient Agricultural-input Management) program, to develop next-generation weed killers that help farmers and protect human health.  More than 1 billion pounds of herbicide are used in the United States every year. Herbicides help farmers by preventing significant crop loss due to weeds, and they enable regenerative farming practices that protect the soil, but some weeds are becoming resistant to the most common herbicides.  Exposure to herbicides may contribute to increased risk of cancer, metabolic and endocrine disorders, and other adverse health outcomes. Farm workers can be exposed from frequent herbicide use, but many U.S. residents are also exposed to these chemicals in small amounts through food and drinking water.  The MIT-led research team will develop new generative artificial intelligence tools to help them discover herbicide alternatives that are more effective and developed with human health in mind. Such alternatives could also help to reduce U.S. dependency on imported phosphorus, which is a critical ingredient in a major herbicide, glyphosate. “With herbicides like glyphosate and atrazine, there’s a real crisis because of resistance mutations that are coming,” says Christopher Voigt, head of MIT’s Department of Biological Engineering. “And if you combine the resistance mutations with issues around national security of the supply chain of the precursors to herbicides, we could find ourselves without these core agrochemicals that are absolutely essential for getting the high crop yields and economical prices that the United States now sees.” Voigt is the principal investigator for the project, known as Precision Learning for On-target Weed control (PLOW). The team is also expected to include researchers from the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, the University of Tennessee at Knoxville, the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, and Robigo. The researchers are grouped into three teams that will tackle different aspects of the project, aligned with the STREAM Technical Areas. The generative AI group will develop models that can predict molecules — either chemical compounds or small interfering RNA (siRNA) — that disrupt the same plant enzymes targeted by glyphosate and other herbicides. Glyphosate kills weeds by interfering with an enzyme called EPSP synthase, which plants need to produce several critical amino acids. After many years of herbicide use, some weeds have begun to acquire genetic mutations that allow them to become resistant to those herbicides, which makes them less effective and poses a significant threat to crop yields. “There’s a real need for new herbicides because of resistance mutations that have been arising,” Voigt says. “There are also concerns about herbicides’ possible impacts on the environment and on humans, so it’s important to identify alternative ways of making herbicides, which as a general class of molecule are really critical to agriculture.” The MIT-led team plans to design generative AI models that will be able to predict molecules that can help prevent resistance from arising. The models will also optimize for other features such as low cost of synthesis, low risk of inducing resistance, and low risk of harming humans or causing ecological damage.  The group developing these AI models is led by Connor Coley, the Warren K. Lewis Associate Professor of Chemical Engineering at MIT; Regina Barzilay, the School of Engineering Distinguished Professor for AI and Health at MIT; and Alexander Tropsha, the K.H. Lee Distinguished Professor in the UNC Eshelman School of Pharmacy. The models are expected to generate billions of possible candidates, which will then be tested by a second research team. This high-throughput screening group will be led by Angela Koehler, the Charles W. and Jennifer C. Johnson Professor of Biological Engineering at MIT, and Jaime Cheah, the associate director of scientific outreach and collaborative screening in the Center for the Development of Therapeutics at the Broad Institute. “Those libraries will be screened both to identify those molecules that hit their target, but also to then provide all of that screening data back to the computational approach in order to improve it,” Voigt says. Once the candidate pools are narrowed down, researchers on a third team will begin greenhouse studies to evaluate how each molecule performs under different agricultural conditions. That team will be led by Neal Stewart and Scott Lenaghan, co-directors of the Center for Agricultural Synthetic Biology at UTK; Patrick Tranel, the Tom and Peggy Ainsworth Professor of Crop Sciences at the University of Illinois; Tim Willson, the Harold Kohn Distinguished Professor at the UNC Eshelman School of Pharmacy; and Andee Wallace PhD ’20, CEO and founder of Robigo.  The first greenhouse tests of initial RNAi candidates are expected to be complete by the end of the first year of the program. As part of this project, the research team will also develop living microbial systems that degrade agrochemicals before they reach food, soil, or waterways. Engineered bacteria, fungi, and srRNA will convert chemicals and formulation ingredients into biomass, providing a scalable strategy to reduce environmental and human exposure. This research is funded by the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health (ARPA-H) under agreement number 140D042690030. 567b0032bbdeb13b: “Pada menjalankan kuasa yang diberikan oleh Seksyen 3 Akta Penjara 1995 (Akta 537) menteri mengisytiharkan semua bangunan dan kawasan dengan keluasan 4,558.97m persegi di No 11 Jalan Langgak Duta, Taman Duta 50480 Kuala Lumpur yang terletak di atas Lot 5746, Mukim Kuala Lumpur, Daerah Kuala Lumpur, Wilayah Persekutuan Kuala Lumpur, sebagai suatu penjara bagi maksud akta bagi pemenjaraan atau penahanan orang dalam jagaan sah”.
Begitu bunyi dokumen rasmi perisytiharan termaktub dalam Warta Kerajaan Pesekutuan bertarikh 6 Nov 2026 yang disiarkan menerusi portal rasmi Jabatan Peguam Negara (AGC).
Perisytiharan berkenaan berkuat kuasa pada tarikh tersebut.

'Orang yang dalam jagaan sah' ialah Najib Razak dengan alamat tertera ialah kediamannya. Ertinya rumah Najib sekarang ialah sebuah penjara. Menteri yang disebut dalam perisytiharan itu ialah Menteri Dalam Negeri Saifuddin Nasution Ismail.
Tidak ada huraian atau penjelasan lanjut Kementerian Dalam Negeri khususnya agensinya Jabatan Penjara. AGC juga tidak memberi keterangan mengiringi perisytiharan itu.

“In the case of this Taman Duta Prison, it seems that immediate family members are allowed to share it with the inmate,” kata wartawan veteran A Kadir Jasin menerusi hantaran di Facebook, beberapa hari lalu.
Saya setuju. Menurut dokumen diwartakan seluruh rumah Najib diisytihar penjara, bukan sebahagian. Bukan bilik khas untuk Najib sahaja dijadikan penjara mengurungnya.

Maka, dengan sendirinya semua penghuni yang sememangnya tinggal di banglo mewah di Langgak Duta kekal sebagai penghuni. Ertinya, Rosmah Mansor, isteri Najib, bersama anggota keluarga terdekat akan bersama Najib dalam 'penjara' Langgak Duta. Begitu juga pembantu rumah dan sebagainya (kalau ada).

Ini keadaan berbeza dengan apa yang dikenakan oleh pemerintah Myanmar ke atas bekas pemimpin negara itu, Aung San Suu Kyi. Beliau dipindahkan dari penjara ke sebuah rumah untuk menjalani baki hukuman tahanan rumah.

Tetapi, kediaman itu bukan rumah Suu Kyi. Lokasi tidak didedah kepada umum. Sinar Harian memetik akhbar The Irrawaddy melaporkan Suu Kyi ditempatkan di sebuah rumah khas dengan kawalan keselamatan di Naypyidaw yang terletak di kawasan kediaman keluarga tentera dan dikelilingi pagar tinggi.
Hubungan Suu Kyi dengan dunia luar sangat terbatas. Pasukan peguamnya dilapor tidak dibenarkan bertemunya secara bersemuka, sejak Disember 2022.
Pada hemat saya, boleh dikatakan Suu Kyi tinggal sebagai tahanan rumah incommunicado - berseorangan.

Bagi Najib, pelawat dibenarkan dengan syarat mendapat izin terlebih dahulu secara bertulis pihak berkuasa dan dikehendaki melalui security screening mengikut prosidur biasa Jabatan Penjara. Ini saya nyatakan berdasar laporan media seperti kata Kadir.
“This whole unprecedented operation will cost tax payers additional money,” katanya.
Ikut logik, Najib sebagai seorang banduan tidak boleh memiliki atau memegang telefon bimbit atau apa-apa alat komunikasi. Namun, pada pandangan saya beliau tidak perlu itu semua.
Sebab beliau boleh jika mahu menyampaikan salam dan pesanan kepada kawan, sahabat handai, sanak-saudara, sesiapa sahaja melalui Rosmah atau anggota keluarga.
Yang kena tahan Najib bukan Rosmah. Lantas beliau dan ahli keluarga yang tinggal serumah dengan Najib bebas keluar masuk berjumpa siapa saja di luar.
Justeru, Najib boleh (saya ulangi) kalau mahu, run Umno dari rumah, beri nasihat, dan atur strategi untuk parti berdepan pilihan raya misalnya. Work from home. Silap. It should be control from home.
Cuma, jangan sampai Umno merasa mereka ada dua presiden. Sekadar friendly reminder.

Antara ciri utama konsep tahanan antarabanga banyak negara termasuk Singapura, New Zealand, dan Australia menggunakan peranti pemantauan elektronik atau gelang kaki GPS atau sistem biometrik untuk mengesan pergerakan tahanan dari jarak jauh.

Tidak dapat dipasitkan sama ada ia akan digunakan untuk Najib. Yang pasti, beliau boleh buat apa sahaja dan bergerak dalam rumah. Yakni, bebas bergaul dengan keluarga dan bergerak asalkan dalam rumah.
Untuk memastikan Najib berada dalam rumah sepanjang masa ialah tanggunjawab pegawai penjara. Penjara walaupun banglo mewah mestilah dijaga oleh pegawai penjara. Nama pun penjara.

Maka, tentulah akan ada beberapa syif 24 jam setiap hari. Tidak tahu berapa pegawai bertugas setiap satu syif. Tidak tahu berapa ramai pegawai terlibat. Setakat ini, belum ada apa apa pengumuman mengenai perkara itu.

Pasti pegawai penjara dalam satu syif yang sama perlu dibawa ulang-alik dengan kenderaan jabatan dari Penjara Kajang atau Sungai Buloh untuk bertugas di 'penjara' Langgak Duta. Bak kata Kadir a set of prison guards would have to be assigned to it.

Dan, adakah pegawai penjara boleh masuk ke dalam rumah untuk membuat kawalan atau mengawal Najib? From the inside? atau mereka hanya dibolehkan mengawal luar rumah? Mungkin kerana tidak mahu mengganggu privasi anggota keluarga Najib?
Di penjara biasa makanan untuk banduan yakni sarapan pagi, makan tengah hari, makan malam disediakan pihak penjara. Bagaimana pula di penjara 'luar biasa' di kawasan elit Langgak Duta?
Makan penjara 'biasa' dibawa masuk atau Najib boleh nikmati quinoa, ikan baung tempoyak ala hidangan Terengganu dan lain-lain kegemarannya yang dimasak di dapur Langgak Duta?
Cukup di sini meskipun ada banyak persoalan yang timbul. Umpamanya diutarakan kolumnis FMT Tajuddin Rasdi yang disiar semalam.
Apa pun Najib masih di penjara Kajang berikutan pengangguhan sementara AGC berhubung pelaksanaan tahanan rumah untuknya.
Kita tunggu saja perkembangaan seterusnya.
Artikel ini adalah pandangan penulis dan tidak semestinya mewakili FMT.
42bc912dc85d4181: Seperti parti politik di mana-mana negara termasuklah Malaysia, mempunyai parti yang memperjuangkan berbagai ideologi. Dengan ideologi ini mereka mencari pengikut. Nasionalisme, sosialisme, sekularisme termasuklah membawa idealisme agama. Fahaman ini disebar kepada rakyat agar menyokong agenda mereka yang mereka percaya terbaik untuk semua.

Tetapi, dalam usaha mengekalkan sokongan, manipulasi tetap berlaku. Paling sedap guna agama. Alasan, dalil dan nas dipakai untuk mencari kelebihan ataupun menutup kelemahan sendiri. Pahala, dosa, syurga dan neraka dijadikan modal niaga untuk mengabsahkan tindakan mereka.

Seorang pemimpin politik sebuah parti agama dalam ceramahnya beberapa minggu lalu menjawab kritikan mengapa negeri yang ditadbir oleh mereka selama 36 tahun lambat maju dengan jawapan yang mudah. "Kita bukannya nabi." Senang, kan?

Pasti penyokong mereka terpesona dan kagum dengan jawapan itu. Tiada yang benar melainkan benar belaka hujah itu. Betullah tu, kita bukan nabi, kata penyokong mereka. Kita tak sempurna. Tetapi, bila kerajaan persekutuan atau kerajaan negeri lain yang ditadbir oleh musuh politik mereka lambat, dalam hal banjir di Selangor misalnya apa yang penyokong mereka tak hentam? Kenapa tak letak hujah pemimpin kamu itu kepada keadaan pihak lain?
"Benda bukan boleh selesai sehari dua, kita bukan nabi, kan?"

Terbaru, minggu lalu seorang lagi pemimpin parti itu dalam hantaran yang dibuatnya di Facebook menulis orang yang menderma untuk membantu bekas perdana menteri Najib Razak membayar denda RM50 juta boleh mendapat pahala. Beliau mengaitkan sumbangan itu dan segala bantuan berkaitan dengannya adalah usaha memudahkan urusan. Memudahkan urusan orang dapat pahala. Peh!

Kenyataan ini sangatlah menarik. Bukanlah sebab kita baru sahaja mengetahui bahawa menderma merupakan amalan yang baik dalam Islam. Sejak kecil kita sudah diajar begitu. Masukkan duit ke dalam tabung masjid, bantu anak yatim, beri makan orang miskin, semuanya amalan mulia. Tangan yang di atas lebih baik daripada tangan di bawah. Semua itu telah kita belajar.

Tetapi, apabila derma dikaitkan dengan seorang tokoh politik yang telah disabitkan kesalahan oleh mahkamah, persoalannya menjadi sedikit berbeza. Adakah setiap amalan derma yang kita buat kepada semua pihak itu sama nilainya? Itu yang lebai-lebai politik harus ajar pengikutnya. Selain nilai dan jumlah, perlu dididik juga tujuan sesuatu sumbangan itu apakah ia benar-benar dituntut dalam agama. Apakah ia membantu permasalahan ummah? Apakah akan memberi kebaikan dan keberkatan kepada bangsa, agama dan negara? Dari segi keadilan sejagat, apakah tindakan ini sesuai?

Maaflah, saya tak boleh terima bab seorang ahli politik merasakan dia ada autoriti untuk menentukan seseorang itu boleh mendapat pahala atau dosa. Kalau tolong pihak mereka, dapat pahala. Kalau buat perkara yang sama untuk pihak lain, berdosa. Sewaktu bermusuh habis semua pihak bergelumang dosa. Bila berbaik, kutip dalil untuk menyucikannya. Jika tempat orang ditimpa banjir itu murka Allah, jika tempat mereka kena, itu ujian. Ini amat memalukan jika kita fikir dengan akal yang waras. Saya mahu bertanya, ke mana penyokong kamu hendak dibawa? Barangkali ada segelintir penyokong parti kamu yang berasa malu juga dengan kenyataan ini.

Soal dosa pahala ini bukan perkara yang sedap-sedap jadi bahan mainan. Dalam kehidupan beragama, pahala dan dosa merupakan antara asas yang membentuk pertimbangan manusia. Orang melakukan kebaikan dengan mengharapkan ganjaran tuhan, manakala menjauhi kejahatan kerana takut akan balasan-Nya. Tapi mengapa bagi kamu, pahala dibuat seperti mata ganjaran untuk tebus barang di kedai serbaneka. Kita jadi ahli kedai, dapat kad keahlian, kemudian jika ada tawaran promosi, kita pun beli barang. Daripada pembelian barang, kita dapat 'point' (pahala) yang boleh ditebus kemudiannya. Macam itu? Gila betul.

Begini, biar saya jelaskan. Dalam isu duit denda Najib, saya boleh faham jika ada penyokongnya yang bersungguh-sungguh mahu membantu beliau. Dalam politik, kesetiaan atau ketaasuban bukan sesuatu yang pelik. Semua parti ada penyokong fanatik. Mereka akan bermati-matian mempertahankan pemimpin mereka. Dan dalam isu Najib ini, ada juga yang bersimpati terhadapnya dan ada juga yang mengenang jasa ketika beliau berkuasa lalu mereka pun menderma. Itu hak mereka. Pemimpin parti lain, jika kalah saman pun akan ada penyokong mereka yang bantu buat kutipan dana.

Tetapi, mengusik sentimen penyokong dengan mempergunakan ganjaran pahala ini agak teruk, bagi saya jika kita fikir dalam-dalam. Apakah boleh kita guna 'fatwa' yang sama untuk kutip derma dan permudahkan urusan ratusan bekas banduan yang sudah bebas supaya urusan mereka dipermudahkan? Mereka terpaksa bergelut kesusahan dalam mendapat pekerjaan. Di mana seruan buat pahala kamu? Apakah manusia seperti mereka tak berguna di mata kamu? Bukankah mereka juga berhak kembali ke pangkuan masyarakat untuk menyumbang bakti dan tenaga? Kenapa berpilih-pilih? Di mana keadilannya kalau begitu?

Di luar sana, berapa ramai orang yang memerlukan bantuan untuk membayar kos rawatan, membeli keperluan sekolah anak atau menyelesaikan hutang akibat kesempitan hidup? Berapa ramai rakyat memerlukan air bersih di rumah? Apa usaha dan inisiatif kamu untuk memudahkan urusan mereka? Takkan kepada marhaen asyik dijual pahala dan syurga sahaja demi nak menutup kemalasan kamu berkhidmat? Jika kamu sebagai pentadbir negeri bekerja keras memberikan kemudahan urusan rakyat di bawah kamu, bukankah kamu juga akan mendapat pahala yang besar? Tapi kamu berhelah, 'kita bukan nabi'. Ini sangat teruk!

Apabila seorang ahli politik memakai jubah dan kopiah bercakap tentang pahala, kenyataannya tentulah akan diterima oleh penyokong mereka. Apatah lagi seseorang ahli politik itu mempunyai latar belakang pendidikan agama atau berasal daripada keluarga ulama yang dihormati. Itu akan jadi lebih kuat.

Tetapi, ayuhlah berfikir secara realistik, kita memang tidak tahu apakah dapat pahala atau tidak jika seseorang itu menderma kepada Najib. Jika dapat pun kita tak tahu bagaimana bentuknya, besar mana atau apa rupanya. Itu bukan kita yang tentukan.

Pemimpin yang fatanah seharusnya lebih tahu memilih perkataan sesuai dalam menyampaikan maksudnya. Tetapi, dek kerana miskin kata-kata dan hujah, maka modal niaga paling sesuai ialah menjual agama dan meletakkan pahala di atas meja. Apakah ahli politik merasakan bahawa tuhan memberikan mereka kuasa juga dalam mengagih pahala?
"Kepada sesiapa yang hendak menderma kepada Najib, dibolehkan kerana itu hak anda. Bersimpati, menolong dan memudahkan urusan orang lain adalah amalan yang digalakkan."
Hah! Saya rasa ayat sebegitu sudah cukup. Nampaklah bijak tanpa menanggalkan ciri ‘keustazannya’, kan?

Dalam sinis, saya tetap menganggap menjual pahala dan dosa dalam permainan politik adalah menghina kebijaksanaan rakyat. Kalau ahli politik pun boleh menentukan siapa dapat pahala, alamatnya selepas ini manifesto pilihan raya mungkin tidak lagi menjanjikan pembangunan, pekerjaan atau kos sara hidup yang lebih rendah. Cukuplah dengan janji pahala atau menggunakan alasan 'kita bukan nabi' seperti alasan seorang lagi pemimpin politik parti yang sama.
Malulah sikit. Kalau tak malu dengan tuhan, malulah sikit dengan segelintir penyokong parti kamu sendiri yang lebih bijak daripada kamu. Takkan kamu nampak mereka semua lekeh daripada kamu?
